title: Network pharmacology-guided investigation of the anti-angiogenic mechanisms of Spatholobus suberectus Dunn stem in rheumatoid arthritis.
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a severe systemic autoimmune disease characterized by progressive joint destruction. Spatholobi Caulis (SC), derived from the vine stem of Spatholobus suberectus Dunn, has a long history of clinical application in traditional Chinese medicine for activating blood circulation and relieving rheumatic arthralgia. However, its pharmacological material basis and anti-angiogenic mechanisms for treating RA remain insufficiently elucidated. To systematically investigate the active constituents of SC and elucidate its anti-angiogenic mechanisms in RA using an integrated approach combining chemical profiling, network pharmacology, and in vivo experimental validation. The chemical profile of SC was characterized using HPLC-QE-MS. A network pharmacology approach-incorporating target screening, protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis, and GO/KEGG enrichment-was utilized to predict core targets and pathways. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) were performed to evaluate the binding stability between key active compounds and hub targets. Finally, the anti-arthritic and anti-angiogenic effects were validated in a collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) rat model using micro-CT, H&E, immunohistochemistry (CD31), ELISA, and Western blot analysis. Additionally, to directly verify the predicted interactions, the effects of the core compound 7,3',4'-trihydroxyisoflavone (THIF) on TNF-α-induced MH7A cells were assessed. Cell proliferation, VEGF secretion, migration, and protein expression of EGFR and PIK3CB were evaluated after 24 h treatment with THIF. HPLC-QE-MS identified 24 active ingredients in SC. Network analysis identified key hub targets including SRC, PIK3CB, AKT1, EGFR, and ESR1 and revealed that SC predominantly modulates the PI3K/AKT, HIF-1α, and VEGF signaling pathways. Molecular docking, MD simulations and SPR demonstrated strong binding affinities and high structural stability between core compounds (e.g., THIF, Hesperetin, Afzelechin, (-)-Maackiain) and key hub targets (e.g., PIK3CB, EGFR, ESR1). In vivo, SC administration significantly alleviated joint swelling, preserved bone morphology (increased BV/TV and BMD via micro-CT), and reduced the organ indices of the thymus and spleen. Crucially, SC remarkably suppressed synovial neovascularization (decreased CD31-positive vessels), downregulated systemic inflammatory and angiogenic cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, VEGF, TGF-α), and significantly inhibited the protein expression of SRC, STAT3, EGFR, PI3K, AKT, and HIF-1α in synovial tissues. In vitro experiments demonstrated that SC effectively inhibits the proliferation of MH7A cells. Flow cytometry analysis confirmed that SC significantly induces apoptosis in MH7A cells; However, this pro-apoptotic effect was alleviated upon addition of the PI3K inhibitor LY294002. Further in vitro validation with the pure compound THIF showed that it dose-dependently suppressed TNF-α-induced MH7A cell proliferation, reduced VEGF secretion from 292.18 to 80.32 pg/mL, and inhibited cell migration. Western blot analysis confirmed that THIF significantly downregulated the protein expression of EGFR and PIK3CB in a dose-dependent manner, directly validating the SPR binding results and demonstrating targeted inhibition of the downstream pathological signaling pathways associated with RA. SC effectively ameliorates RA progression by mitigating synovial inflammation and preventing structural joint damage. Its therapeutic efficacy is primarily driven by the suppression of pathological angiogenesis via the targeted dual-inhibition of the EGFR/PI3K/AKT/HIF-1α signaling axes.

title: Strategies and tools for enhancing early detection of pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAC) remains the most lethal malignancies, with a 5-year survival rate of only around 12%. The dismal prognosis is largely attributable to late diagnosis, as early PAC is frequently asymptomatic and radiologically inconspicuous. Contemporary international guidelines recommend surveillance for well-defined high-risk groups, particularly carriers of pathogenic germline mutations such as BRCA2, STK11, and CDKN2A, as well as familial pancreatic cancer kindreds. In these settings, endoscopic ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging are the recommended surveillance modalities. Recent advances in biomarker discovery, including circulating tumor DNA, methylation signatures of cell-free DNA, and extracellular vesicles, have demonstrated encouraging results, particularly when combined with CA19-9. Paraneoplastic phenomena such as pancreatic cancer-associated diabetes and cancer-induced cachexia provide additional opportunities for earlier clinical recognition. Parallel progress has been achieved in artificial intelligence-driven radiomics analysis and deep learning algorithms, which can increase the sensitivity of cross-sectional imaging for small or otherwise occult lesions. The integration of clinical risk stratification, molecular biomarkers, and AI-enhanced imaging represents a promising framework to shift diagnosis toward surgically resectable stages. This review synthesizes the current evidence, highlights recent advances, and discusses practical considerations for physicians to facilitate earlier detection of PAC.

title: [Atypical presentation of ocular syphilis].
abstract: We report the case of a 55-year-old man who presented with a sudden decrease in visual acuity in the left eye, revealing ocular syphilis associated with asymptomatic neurosyphilis. Ophthalmological examination showed mild anterior uveitis of the left eye associated with focal peripheral retinitis displaying a ground-glass appearance, multiple creamy-white superficial retinal precipitates, and obliterative retinal arteritis. Multimodal imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography (OCT), demonstrated full-thickness retinal involvement with retinal layer disorganization, retrohyaloid inflammatory deposits, and hyperreflective preretinal inflammatory condensations. The infectious workup revealed positive syphilis serology (TPHA and VDRL), while HIV serology was negative. An anterior chamber paracentesis excluded other infectious causes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis confirmed asymptomatic neurosyphilis in the absence of neurological symptoms and with a normal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan. Treatment with intravenous penicillin G (24 million units per day for 14 days), combined with corticosteroid therapy, resulted in a favorable outcome, with regression of inflammatory signs and clinical improvement. This case illustrates an unusual presentation of ocular syphilis characterized by ground-glass retinitis associated with retinal vasculitis and superficial retinal precipitates. It highlights the value of multimodal imaging, particularly OCT, in facilitating early diagnosis and emphasizes the importance of systematically investigating neurosyphilis, even in the absence of neurological manifestations.

title: Predictive factors of functional and anatomical response to dexamethasone implant in refractory diabetic macular edema.
abstract: Background To identify clinical and spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) biomarkers predictive of functional and anatomical response to intravitreal dexamethasone implant in refractory diabetic macular edema (DME). Methods This prospective longitudinal study included 185 eyes of 98 diabetic patients with center-involving DME refractory to a mean of 7.1±2.8 prior aflibercept (2mg) injections. All eyes received a 0.7mg intravitreal dexamethasone implant and were followed for at least 6 months, with a mean follow-up of 12.9±2.1 months. Functional outcome was assessed by best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA, logMAR) and anatomical outcome by central macular thickness (CMT) on SD-OCT. Baseline OCT biomarkers included CMT, serous retinal detachment (SRD) height, integrity of the ellipsoid zone and external limiting membrane (ELM), and disorganization of retinal inner layers (DRIL). Results Baseline BCVA was 0.72±0.31 logMAR, and CMT 432±128μm. At 6 months, BCVA improved to 0.55±0.28 logMAR, and CMT decreased to 301±96μm (both P<0.001). Functional and anatomical responses were observed in 56% and 70% of eyes, respectively. Lower baseline CMT (OR=1.42, P=0.003), smaller SRD height (OR=0.76, P=0.005), fewer prior injections (OR=1.31, P=0.010), preserved ellipsoid zone (OR=2.18, P=0.002), and intact ELM (OR=1.94, P=0.004) were independently associated with favorable functional outcomes. Conclusion Baseline SD-OCT biomarkers are significant predictors of treatment response in refractory DME and may support individualized therapeutic decision-making.

title: Abnormal left ventricular mass as a prognostic marker for outcomes in infants and children with cirrhosis.
abstract: Background/aims Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy (CCM), a clinically consequential comorbidity of cirrhosis, remains undefined and underappreciated in children. This study aimed to characterize myocardial structural, functional, morphometric, and histopathologic features in pediatric cirrhosis and objectively derive a reliable echocardiographic (2DE) metric to predict perioperative adverse events, including mortality. Methods 2DE, morphometry, histopathology, and vasoactive-inotropic score (VIS) were compared between children with (n=226) and without (n=160) cirrhosis listed for liver transplantation (LT) over 2011-2021. Discriminatory performance of left ventricular mass index (height) 2.7 (LVMI g/m 2.7 ) for predicting waitlist decompensation, composite serious adverse events post liver transplant and mortality was assessed using ROC analysis, with AUCs and optimal thresholds compared against PELD-Cr/MELD scores. title: Spleen stiffness to rule out high-risk varices in advanced chronic liver disease: an individual patient data meta-analysis.
abstract: Background & aims Management of esophageal varices (EV) is of critical importance in compensated advanced chronic liver disease. We conducted an individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis to (i) investigate the performance of spleen stiffness measurement (SSM)-based algorithms using vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) to rule out high-risk varices (HRV); (ii) develop a new model for diagnosing any grade EV. Methods We systematically searched databases for studies reporting endoscopy and SSM-VCTE data in adult patients, collecting their IPD. The main outcome was ruling out HRV. The tested algorithms were: i) Baveno-VI criteria, liver stiffness measurement (LSM) <20 kPa and platelet count (PLT) >150x10 9 /L); ii) SSM ≤40 kPa; iii) combined Baveno-SSM criteria ≤40 kPa in patients outside Baveno VI criteria. We developed and internally validated logistic regression models to diagnose any grade EV. Results Twenty studies comprising 2257 patients were included, with a summary HRV prevalence of 25%. The Baveno VI algorithm showed 100% (95%-CI:97-100%) sensitivity and 100% (95%-CI:95-100%) NPV; the rate of spared endoscopies was 17% (95%-CI:15-18%). The combined Baveno VI-SSM criteria performed best for ruling out HRV: 97% (95%-CI:94-99%) sensitivity, 98% (95%-CI:96-99%) NPV and rate of spared endoscopies of 35% (95%-CI: 34-38%). These results were robust in all sensitivity analyses, including patients with non-viral etiology (n=637) and studies using the 100 Hz module. We developed new logistic models with excellent accuracy for the diagnosis of EV, but the ability to identify patients at low risk (<10%) of EV was limited. Conclusion This large, multicenter, international study validated spleen stiffness measurement as an accurate tool to assess high-risk esophageal varices. The combined Baveno-SSM algorithm performed best in ruling out HRV. Impact and implications Spleen stiffness has been recommended to rule out high-risk varices, but the evidence supporting its use is of low-quality. Our individual patient data meta-analysis, which included more than 2200 patients with compensated cirrhosis, showed that spleen stiffness ≤40 kPa can rule out high-risk varices with a very low rate of false negatives. Its combination with Baveno VI criteria was the most efficient triage strategy, doubling the rate of endoscopies that could be safely avoided compared to using the Baveno VI criteria alone. The findings of our study strengthen the level of evidence supporting the use of spleen stiffness as an additional screening tool for high-risk varices.

title: Percutaneous Versus Open Approach to Intramedullary Nailing of Metacarpal Shaft Fractures: A Comparison of 12 Week Functional Outcomes.
abstract: The optimal surgical approach for retrograde intramedullary fixation (rIMF) of metacarpal fractures remains unclear. We hypothesized that a percutaneous approach for rIMF of metacarpal shaft fractures would exhibit improved functional outcomes compared to an open approach without increased incidence of extensor lag. A retrospective cohort of patients who sustained a closed metacarpal shaft fracture and underwent rIMF through either a percutaneous or an open approach were identified. Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (QuickDASH) scores, total active motion (TAM), grip strength (% of contralateral) and visual analog scale pain scores were collected at 1, 2, 4, 6, and 12 weeks after surgery. Additional outcome measures included surgical time, radiographic alignment, and instances of extensor lag. At a single level one trauma center, 54 patients, comprising 56 metacarpal shaft fractures, were retrospectively identified. Patients treated with a percutaneous approach demonstrated significantly improved TAM (248° ± 10° vs 228° ± 19°, P < .05), grip strength (95 ± 4 % vs 75% ± 6%, P < .05), and QuickDASH scores (2.5 ± 2.6 vs 10.5 ± 4.0, P < .05) through 2 weeks after surgery, with differences dissipating by 4 weeks, and no cases of extensor lag seen. Additionally, the percutaneous approach yielded significantly shorter intraoperative times (9.5 minutes vs 18.6 minutes, P < .05). A percutaneous approach for rIMF of metacarpal shaft fractures significantly improved outcomes including TAM, grip strength, and QuickDASH scores through the 2-week postoperative period and demonstrated lower initial visual analog scale pain scores. Additionally, the percutaneous cohort experienced no cases of extensor lag at any time point. Therapeutic III.

title: Artificial Intelligence Techniques for Diagnosing and Quantifying Vitiligo: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The utilization of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) for vitiligo, particularly in image and object recognition, allows for the creation of innovative techniques that may match the precision and accuracy of current clinical methodologies. This systematic review seeks to explore how imaging-based artificial intelligence (AI) models may improve the accuracy of vitiligo diagnosis, severity assessment, and monitoring. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, IEEE Xplore, EMBASE, Compendex, and Cochrane. Fifty-four studies from January 1, 2000, to October 10th, 2024, focusing on vitiligo diagnosis, classification, treatment, or disease severity were included in this review. Meta-analysis showed models achieved high diagnostic accuracy with an area under the curve of over 0.90 and lesion segmentation with a Dice score of 0.84. Often results matched human expert performance. Studies comparing AI models with experts reported AI could perform equally to that of human experts. These studies highlight the ability of ML models to accurately detect vitiligo and provide quantitative data on the extent of lesions. While AI has shown considerable potential for the improvement of vitiligo management, larger, more diverse publicly available vitiligo datasets and studies focusing on vitiligo segmentation with full-body images are needed for full clinical integration.

title: Nucleic acid technologies in crustacean disease management: Diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance.
abstract: Crustacean aquaculture, particularly shrimp, crab, and lobster production, contributes around US$10 billion annually to the global food supply but remains highly vulnerable to viral and bacterial diseases. Pathogens such as White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV), Yellow Head Virus (YHV), Taura Syndrome Virus (TSV), and Vibrio species continue to cause substantial economic losses, and conventional management based on visual inspection, histopathology, and antimicrobial treatment is often slow and insensitive. This review examines how nucleic acid technologies are reshaping diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance in crustacean health management. Molecular diagnostic platforms including PCR, quantitative PCR, reverse transcription PCR, loop mediated isothermal amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification, and multiplex assays allow rapid, sensitive, and specific detection of pathogens, often before clinical signs appear. RNA interference shows strong therapeutic promise against viral pathogens, with experimental studies reporting 40 to 80% reductions in cumulative mortality, although stability, dosing, delivery, and production cost continue to limit commercial use. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) and Cas (CRISPR-associated) has emerged as a powerful platform for functional genomics, immune gene characterisation, and the future development of disease resistant strains, though application in crustaceans remains largely proof of concept. Environmental DNA and molecular biosurveillance enable early pathogen detection through water and sediment sampling, supporting proactive biosecurity and precision aquaculture. Persistent barriers include scalability, infrastructure gaps in producing regions, regulatory uncertainty, and public acceptance. Future progress will rely on improved delivery systems, expanded crustacean genomic resources, and integration of molecular tools with digital farm management to deliver sustainable disease control.

title: A diagnostic model integrating clinical, magnetic resonance imaging, and arthroscopic findings accurately identified hypermobile lateral meniscus: Development and internal validation.
abstract: Background To develop and internally validate a diagnostic model for hypermobile lateral meniscus (HLM) integrating clinical symptoms, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings, and dynamic arthroscopic assessment. Methods A retrospective diagnostic model study was performed, including 100 consecutive patients evaluated for suspected lateral meniscal pathology at a tertiary knee surgery center. All patients underwent standardized clinical examination, preoperative MRI, and arthroscopic assessment of lateral meniscal mobility, which served as the reference standard. Candidate predictors were restricted to preoperative clinical and MRI variables, including intermittent locking, posterolateral McMurray test, meniscocapsular gap, and suspected meniscotibial discontinuity. Arthroscopic findings were used exclusively to establish the reference-standard diagnosis and were not entered into the diagnostic model. A penalized logistic regression model with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) selection was used to identify independent predictors and construct the Hypermobile Meniscus Index (HMI). Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling, and robustness was assessed with Monte Carlo simulation. Results HLM was confirmed arthroscopically in 47% of patients. The final model included five independent predictors and demonstrated excellent discriminative performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.84 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83-0.95). At the optimal cut-off (≥5 points), sensitivity was 81%, specificity 79.2%, positive predictive value 77.6%, and negative predictive value 82.4%. Calibration analysis showed good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities (calibration slope 0.94, intercept 0.03; and Brier score 0.13). Bootstrap validation yielded an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.82. Monte Carlo simulation confirmed stability of model performance across varying prevalence scenarios, with consistent sensitivity and specificity ranges. Conclusion A diagnostic model combining clinical and MRI findings demonstrated internally validated performance for identifying HLM as defined by dynamic arthroscopy. The HMI provides a structured framework to improve preoperative recognition and guide targeted arthroscopic assessment in patients with mechanical lateral compartment symptoms and inconclusive imaging. External validation is required prior to routine clinical implementation. Level of evidence Level III, diagnostic study.

title: Knee Morphometry in Asian and Western Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Related Parameters.
abstract: Importance Intercondylar notch dimensions, anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) width, and posterior tibial slope (PTS) are recognized as important anatomical factors associated with ACL injury risk, and anatomical reference values for these parameters are derived predominantly from Western cohorts. Individual studies suggest that ACL-related knee morphology may vary across populations, but whether such differences are consistent between Asian and Western populations across commonly assessed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-measured parameters remains uncertain. Aim To determine whether MRI-measured knee morphology differs between geographically defined Asian and Western adult populations with radiologically intact ACLs across six prespecified parameters: femoral notch volume (FNV), notch width (NW), notch width index (NWI), medial tibial slope (MTS), lateral tibial slope (LTS), and ACL width. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement and prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) [CRD420261403854]. Four electronic databases were searched from inception to 11 June 2026 for MRI studies reporting eligible morphometric outcomes in adults with radiologically intact ACLs. Studies were classified as Asian or Western by country of cohort recruitment, reflecting geographic origin rather than verified individual ethnicity. Single-arm random-effects meta-analyses using restricted maximum likelihood estimation were pooled separately by cohort and compared using the Q test for subgroup differences. Meta-regression evaluated geographic cohort, measurement technique, mean age and sex composition as potential sources of between-study variation. Statistical significance was defined as two-sided p < 0.05. Results Thirty-one studies (2,463 knees; 15 Asian, 16 Western) were included. No statistically significant between-cohort differences were identified for FNV (7.26 versus 7.64 cm 3 , p = 0.78), NW (20.13 versus 19.86 mm, p = 0.77), NWI (0.28 versus 0.24, p = 0.45), MTS (5.66° versus 6.04°, p = 0.67) or LTS (5.73° versus 6.24°, p = 0.53). ACL width also did not differ statistically significantly (5.20 versus 7.62 mm, p = 0.08). Heterogeneity, quantified using the I 2 statistic, was substantial across all outcomes (I 2 = 75-100%) and prediction intervals were wide and overlapping between cohorts. Geographic cohort was not a statistically significant moderator of any outcome (p = 0.09-0.82). Measurement technique was associated with LTS (p = 0.03), explaining 44% of the between-study variance (R 2 ), but with no other outcome (p = 0.28-0.89), whereas study-level sex composition was associated with NW (regression coefficient [β] = 6.48 mm, p = 0.02), FNV (β = 5.34 cm 3 , p = 0.04) and mean cohort age was associated with both MTS (β = 0.11°/year, p = 0.02) and LTS (β = 0.11°/year, p < 0.01). Within Asian cohorts, males had statistically significantly greater FNV than females (7.65 versus 5.66 cm 3 , p < 0.01). Conclusion MRI measures of femoral notch morphology, PTS, and ACL width did not differ statistically significantly between Asian and Western populations with radiologically intact ACLs (p = 0.08-0.78). Given the substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals, these findings indicate an absence of detectable differences in the available literature rather than anatomical equivalence between populations, and clinically important differences cannot be excluded. Clinically, geographic origin alone should therefore not be considered a surrogate for individual knee morphology when assessing ACL-related anatomical risk or planning reconstruction. Although study-level sex composition, mean age and measurement technique may contribute to variation in the measured parameters, these associations should be interpreted cautiously given the ecological nature of the analysis. Level of evidence Level IV (systematic review and meta-analysis of Level III-IV observational studies).

title: Multimodality imaging of the right heart: Translating quantitative assessment into therapeutic strategy.
abstract: The right heart is a crucial determinant of prognosis across a broad spectrum of cardiovascular diseases, including pulmonary hypertension, tricuspid regurgitation, and heart failure. In the contemporary era of transcatheter device-based therapies, accurate assessment of right ventricular (RV) and right atrial anatomical and functional remodeling is critical for clinical decision-making. Although echocardiography remains the cornerstone of right heart evaluation, its interpretation is often limited by complex geometry of the RV and the load dependency of some parameters. Recent advances in multimodality imaging have enabled more robust and quantitative characterization of right heart structure and function. Three-dimensional echocardiography and RV strain provide improved functional assessment beyond conventional parameters of RV function. Cardiac magnetic resonance offers reference-standard quantification of RV volumes and mass, enhancing reproducibility and risk stratification. Computed tomography contributes complementary anatomical, functional and volumetric information, particularly relevant in structural heart interventions and evaluation of systemic venous congestion. Importantly, imaging biomarkers reflecting RV-pulmonary arterial coupling, atrial remodeling, and systemic venous congestion have demonstrated incremental prognostic value. Integration of these quantitative metrics into clinical practice may refine risk stratification, optimize timing of intervention, and identify patients unlikely to benefit from invasive therapies. This review summarizes contemporary advances in right heart imaging and proposes a practical framework for integrating echocardiography, Cardiac magnetic resonance, and computed tomography into therapeutic strategy in patients with right heart disease.

title: RF-based ultrasound elastography image reconstruction using biomechanically informed deep learning.
abstract: Breast cancer remains one of the most prevalent and lethal malignancies among women worldwide, with current diagnosis methods relying on preliminary imaging, followed by a breast biopsy if deemed necessary. Among imaging techniques developed to reduce imaging false positives, ultrasound elastography (USE) was developed to enable physicians to characterize tissue stiffness alteration which is known to be a signature of pathology. This is done through analysis of tissue deformation under mechanical loading to reconstruct tissue stiffness images using mathematical data inversion frameworks. However, conventional USE image reconstruction pipelines require sequential displacement estimation, strain map computation, and a computationally involved data inversion process, limiting its practicality for real-time use in clinical workflows. The proposed work addresses this limitation by presenting a deep learning framework capable of elastography image reconstruction from pre- and post-compression radiofrequency (RF) frames. Using a convolutional neural network (CNN) which includes a custom temporal encoder and a U-Net decoder architecture, the network is able to bypass the traditional demanding computational pipeline of USE. To train the proposed model, a biomechanically informed RF dataset was generated using anatomically accurate finite element modeling (FEM) of breast tissue deformation, including realistic ligament structures such as the Cooper's ligaments along with clinically derived boundary conditions. The proposed framework demonstrated strong agreement with a maximum error of 2% between reconstructed and ground-truth USE images, while accurately preserving relative inclusion-to-background stiffness contrast. This contrast, rather than absolute stiffness, constitutes the decision variable used in clinical lesion characterization. Additionally, a matched biomechanical comparison performed with and without ligament inclusion further demonstrated measurable changes between displacement, strain, and elastography fields, demonstrating the importance of the inclusion of the Cooper's ligaments. These results demonstrate the potential of this work as a biomechanically informed deep learning approach for a previously computationally expensive inverse elastography reconstruction, whilst maintaining clinically relevant stiffness contrast necessary for meaningful lesion characterization.

title: Pelvic splenosis and endometriosis in adolescent with hereditary spherocytosis.
abstract: The patient is a 16-year-old with a history of hereditary spherocytosis. At age 12, she underwent a laparoscopic partial converted to total splenectomy for intraoperative bleeding. The spleen was placed in a retrieval bag and removed via morcellation. She first reported abdominal pain at age 8, with dysmenorrhea after menarche at age 13. Her dysmenorrhea was managed with a progesterone IUD. Due to worsening pain, she underwent MRI which showed multiple lobulated structures throughout the pelvis and ventral abdomen, suggestive of endometriomas versus splenules. Laparoscopy revealed dozens of black-blue nodules coating the anterior abdominal wall and multiple multi-centimeter nodules attached to the sigmoid colon, descending colon, jejunum, and ovarian fossae, with vesicular lesions deep in pelvis. Abdominal wall and pelvic lesions were excised; removal of the nodules adherent to the colon and small bowel was deferred given inadequate bowel preparation. Frozen section and final histopathology confirmed splenosis throughout the abdomen and pelvis, with presence of endometriosis in right uterosacral ligament and ovarian fossa. Future surgery is planned to excise remaining splenules. This patient's case demonstrates that splenosis and endometriosis can exist simultaneously and are difficult to differentiate from one another symptomatically, on imaging, and even under direct visualization. Gynecologic surgeons should include splenosis in the differential diagnosis of pelvic nodular masses, particularly in patients with a history of splenectomy.

title: Differentiation of common liver tumors using tumor-to-liver contrast on routine non-contrast T 2 -weighted magnetic resonance imaging.
abstract: Introduction Accurate classification of liver tumors requires contrast-enhanced MRI. However, contrast agents are contraindicated in patients with renal impairment or allergies. Concerns regarding the environmental impact of gadolinium-based agents have increased. Thus, classification using non-contrast MRI is desirable. This study evaluated whether tumor-to-liver contrast (TLC) derived from T 2 -weighted imaging (T 2 WI) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), along with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), can differentiate common liver tumors: hepatocellular carcinomas (HCCs), metastases, and hemangiomas. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 119 patients with 122 liver tumors undergoing liver MRI. We calculated TLC from T 2 WI and DWI (b = 1000 s/mm²), and measured ADC values. Tumors were classified as HCCs, metastases, or hemangiomas based on radiological or pathological findings. Analyses were stratified by liver function using the albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score. Group differences were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis and Steel-Dwass tests. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using one-versus-rest receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results T 2 WI-derived TLC differed significantly among tumor types (p < 0.05) and was highest in hemangiomas, followed by metastases and HCCs. DWI-derived TLC and ADC values differed in some tumor comparisons but showed greater variability and overlap. These patterns persisted after ALBI stratification. ROC analysis showed that T 2 WI-derived TLC performed well for hemangiomas (AUC = 0.975) and HCC (AUC = 0.839), whereas ADC performed best for metastases (AUC = 0.716). Overall, T 2 WI-derived TLC outperformed DWI-derived TLC. Conclusions TLC derived from non-contrast T 2 WI may serve as a practical, observer-independent marker for differentiating liver tumors, particularly in patients who cannot receive contrast agents. Plain language summary MRI scans with contrast agents are often used to identify different types of liver tumors, but some people cannot safely receive these agents. This study reviewed MRI scans from people with liver tumors and examined whether measurements from standard non-contrast MRI images could help distinguish between common tumor types. This study found that a measurement taken from T 2 -weighted MRI images was particularly effective at differentiating liver tumors, especially hemangiomas and hepatocellular carcinoma, without the need for contrast agents. This matters because non-contrast MRI methods may help support diagnosis in people who cannot receive contrast agents and may reduce reliance on these substances.

title: Embedding research within advanced radiotherapy practice: A qualitative multi-centre study of UK radiotherapy departments with international implications.
abstract: Introduction Research is recognised as one of the four pillars of advanced practice, yet its integration within radiotherapy roles remains uneven. This study explored how research was embedded within Advanced Practice Research Radiographer (APRR) roles across UK radiotherapy services and identified organisational conditions associated with more formalised implementation. Methods An interpretivist qualitative multi-centre study was undertaken in five UK radiotherapy departments from January to December 2025. Purposive sampling recruited 28 participants from radiography, oncology, nursing and physics roles. Data were generated through non-participant observations, contemporaneous field notes and semi-structured interviews; interviews were documented in field notes rather than audio-recorded. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, supported by iterative team triangulation, and reported in line with Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research guidance. Results Four themes were identified: strategic integration of research; governance and professional identity; protected research capacity; and clinical-academic integration. Research was most effectively embedded where organisations aligned role expectations with service strategy, provided clearer governance and role definitions, protected research time, and supported collaboration across clinical and academic settings. Conversely, variable titles, inconsistent job planning and limited backfill reduced role clarity, sustainability and influence. A key limitation is that interviews were not audio-recorded, and the analysis therefore relied on contemporaneous field notes. Conclusions Embedding research within advanced radiotherapy practice depends on transferable organisational conditions: strategic leadership, governance, protected capacity and clinical-academic connectivity. Although derived solely from UK data, these findings may inform workforce and policy development in other settings; Singapore is one illustrative example of a system seeking to adapt such principles without contributing empirical data to this study. Plain language summary Research helps healthcare professionals improve care, but it is not always easy to include in everyday clinical roles. This study examined how research was built into advanced radiographer roles in radiotherapy departments in the United Kingdom. This study found that research was more successful when staff had protected time, clear responsibilities, supportive leadership, and strong links with academic partners. This matters because these conditions may help healthcare teams produce and use research that improves patient care and professional practice.

title: Large-domain histology-based diffusion MRI simulation via independent local simulations.
abstract: Diffusion MRI simulations based on realistic tissue microstructure provide a means to validate biophysical models and optimize acquisition protocols, but their computational cost restricts most studies to domains far smaller than a clinical voxel. The objective of this study was to develop an automated and scalable framework that converts whole-slide histology into diffusion MRI simulations at clinically relevant spatial scales while remaining feasible on standard workstation hardware. We present an end-to-end pipeline integrating two-dimensional whole-slide cell segmentation, mesh generation, and finite element Bloch-Torrey simulation. To enable simulations at large spatial scales without prohibitive memory growth, we introduce a subdomain tiling strategy in which the tissue domain is partitioned into extended subdomains simulated independently under no-flux boundary conditions. Signals are aggregated only from the central regions of each subdomain to minimize boundary artifacts. For an 800 μm × 800 μm histology-based domain, the aggregated signal differed by 0.07% from the corresponding full-domain finite element simulation while reducing wall-clock time from several days to hours and maintaining bounded memory usage independent of global domain size. When applied to a 2016 μm × 2016 μm heterogeneous region approximating the in-plane dimensions of a clinical voxel, the apparent diffusion coefficient obtained from the full domain differed from values computed in smaller dense and sparse subregions, demonstrating the influence of structural heterogeneity at clinically relevant scales on derived diffusion metrics. The proposed framework establishes an automated and memory-stable approach for generating diffusion MRI simulations directly from routine histology.

title: A novel and adaptable method to prepare samples for postmortem imaging with artifact reduction.
abstract: Background Postmortem MRI enables ultra-high-resolution image acquisition and subsequent biomarker validation. This approach requires that postmortem specimens be suspended in solution, which is not required for in vivo MRI. Susceptibility artifacts occur at surface-air interfaces and around air bubbles that remain in and around the sample, leading to image distortions. New method We set forth our protocol, the Seven Seals Method, whereby we prepare brain specimens for MRI scanning, with special attention to removing artifact-causing air bubbles. This protocol evolved over twenty years of ex vivo imaging experience. The method uses freezer bags to create a custom-shaped container for brain samples with a temporary reservoir pocket that collects air for removal. The protocol provides step by step instructions with diagrams and videos, a history of experimentation, and a troubleshooting guide. Results We have successfully applied this method to whole brains, brain hemispheres and blocked brain specimens, and have prepared samples in a variety of solutions. Comparison with existing methods The strengths of the Seven Seals Method include its high adaptability for shape and size fit, proven air bubble removal techniques, and inexpensive packing materials that do not require the use of a 3D printer. The tailored container minimizes motion and allows for closer proximity of the specimen to the coil elements than when using hard sided plastic containers, which yields better signal-to-noise ratio for structure visualization. Conclusions We anticipate this rigorous protocol will enable other groups to optimize their ex vivo scans for validation studies.

title: Artificial intelligence prediction of implant placement difficulty based on bone morphology and anatomical constraints.
abstract: Background Accurate preoperative assessment of implant placement difficulty is essential for effective surgical planning and minimizing complications. Conventional evaluation using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) relies heavily on clinician interpretation and is often subjective and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising approach for objective and reproducible prediction of surgical complexity using quantitative imaging parameters. Objective To develop and evaluate an AI-based model for predicting implant placement difficulty based on bone morphology and anatomical constraints derived from CBCT imaging. Methods A prospective observational study was conducted on 250 implant sites. Bone morphology parameters-including bone height, width, cortical thickness, and density-along with anatomical constraints such as proximity to vital structures, were assessed using standardized CBCT analysis. Implant placement difficulty was categorized intraoperatively as low, moderate, or high. Machine learning models, including logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost, were developed using Python libraries. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, and calibration metrics such as the Brier score. Results Moderate difficulty cases were most common (41.6%), followed by low (36.8%) and high (21.6%) difficulty. Reduced bone dimensions and density were significantly associated with increased difficulty (p < 0.001). XGBoost showed the best performance (AUC 0.91, accuracy 87.6%, sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.89, Brier score 0.108). Conclusion AI models, particularly XGBoost, can reliably predict implant placement difficulty and enhance clinical decision-making and treatment planning.

title: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance derived myocardial strain: applications, acquisition techniques, analysis, and reporting. A Scientific Statement of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance, Radiological Society of North America, and the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging of the ESC.
abstract: Myocardial strain imaging enables quantification of cardiac deformation. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) is well suited for strain assessment due to the ability to image in any given plane with high spatial and contrast resolution. CMR strain measures have incremental diagnostic and prognostic utility over conventional clinical imaging parameters across disease states. Routine integration of CMR strain assessment in clinical practice has been hindered by the lack of agreement on imaging protocols and analysis methods, variability due to noise sensitivity, and a paucity of robust normative age-, sex- and ethnicity-specific reference ranges. In recognition of the expanding applications of strain techniques in clinical and research CMR, this joint SCMR/RSNA/EACVI scientific statement integrates data from original research studies, guidelines, and opinions from experts across the field to guide responsible and evidence-based utilization of CMR strain.

title: Robust Approach to Measure Time-Resolved Septal Curvature in Pediatric Pulmonary Hypertension Patients Using Standard Short-Axis Ventricular Volume Contours: A Retrospective, Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Background Right heart catheterization is the gold standard for diagnosis and monitoring of pediatric pulmonary hypertension (PH). Noninvasive cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) and echocardiography can additionally provide volumetric and functional assessment of the right ventricle and possibly serve as a non-invasive method for surveillance of PH severity using ventricular septal curvature (SC), interventricular septal (IVS) angle, or eccentricity index (EI). However, these septal wall measurements require manual interaction and can be observer dependent. This study presents the results of a robust, contour-based SC computation and assesses interobserver variability and performance as a candidate marker of RV afterload as compared to manually measured SC, IVS angle and EI. Methods This cross-sectional, retrospective study enrolled PH patients with mixed etiology (idiopathic/heritable and congenital heart/connective tissue disease-associated PH) and similar-age controls who underwent clinical CMR and catheterization (catheterization only for patients). A standard short-axis CMR stack was processed on commercial image-processing software to semi-automatically extract the relevant contours for the endo- and epicardial ventricular walls. SC was computed based on the contours and the minimum value in the cardiac cycle was obtained (SC contour ). For comparison, SC (SC manu ), IVS angle and EI were manually obtained from the CMR images. The relationship between septal wall measurements and invasive pressure measurements by catheterization was evaluated via Spearman correlation. Association with adverse events (death, lung or heart and lung transplant, and Potts surgery) was evaluated via univariate Cox proportional hazard model. Interobserver agreement was analyzed using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Results Analysis was performed on 24 patients and 14 controls (median age 16.4 [12.3 - 18.9] and 15.9 [14.7 - 17.4] years respectively). SC contour demonstrated moderate-strong correlations with RVSP (ρ=-0.79), RVSP/SBP (ρ =-0.65), and mPAP (ρ=-0.80) and had the strongest correlation in idiopathic/heritable PH patients (ρ = -0.74 - -0.83). SC contour demonstrated a higher ICC (0.96 (95% CI 0.93 - 0.98; p<0.001) versus SC manu (0.89 (95% CI 0.80 - 0.94; p<0.001)). In the exploratory prognostic analysis, significant associations with adverse events were not observed for any septal wall measurements. Conclusions The contour-based SC approach demonstrated strong correlation with invasive pressure measurements, with less manual interaction and observer dependency than manual measurements.

title: A Visual LGE Extent Cutoff for Mortality Risk Stratification in Ischemic Cardiomyopathy.
abstract: Background Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) extent has been linked to adverse outcomes in ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM). While quantitative methods of LGE assessment are widely accepted, semi-quantitative methods remain debated but still hold value. This study aimed to determine an optimal LGE segments cutoff for ICM patients with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <50% in a large bicentric cohort. Methods This bicentric retrospective French study included 3,591 patients with ICM (defined by prior myocardial infarction and/or coronary revascularization), LVEF <50%, and ischemic-LGE on cardiovascular magnetic resonance performed between 2008 and 2022. Ischemic LGE extent was assessed semi-quantitatively using the 17-segment model. An optimal cutoff for LGE extent was derived in the derivation cohort (Center 1, N=2,900) using a conditional inference tree and externally validated in an independent cohort (Center 2, N=691). The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Prognostic performance was compared between a conventional model based on LVEF ≤35% alone and a combined model integrating LVEF ≤35% with the newly identified ischemic-LGE cutoff. Model discrimination and reclassification were assessed using Harrell's C-index, continuous net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). Results During a median follow-up of 9 years, 549 patients (15.3%) died. The optimal cutoff of visual LGE extent to predict mortality was 5 segments. Patients with high ischemic LGE extent (>5 segments) had a markedly increased risk of all-cause mortality compared with those with ≤5 segments (adjusted hazard ratio, 3.8; 95% CI: 3.0-4.8; p<0.001). Survival discrimination according to this cutoff was consistent across derivation and validation cohorts. Compared with the conventional LVEF ≤35% model alone, the combined model integrating the >5 ischemic-LGE segment cutoff significantly improved risk discrimination and patient reclassification (ΔC-index: +16%; continuous NRI: +36%; IDI: +4%; all p<0.001). Conclusion In patients with ICM, reduced LVEF (<50%), and detectable ischemic LGE, a visually assessed segment-based cutoff of >5 ischemic-LGE segments was independently associated with all-cause mortality and validated in an independent second-center cohort. This pragmatic, software-independent assessment may complement conventional risk stratification, although prospective studies are required before integration into clinical decision-making.

title: The Prognostic Value of Entropy from T1 Mapping in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension.
abstract: Background The prognostic value of left ventricular (LV) entropy from T1 mapping in pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) remains unexplored. Study design and methods This prospective study enrolled patients with PAH who underwent cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) within 72h of right heart catheterization (RHC). Myocardial native T1, extracellular volume fraction (ECV) and entropy were calculated in mid-ventricular short-axis slice. The primary endpoint was defined as all-cause mortality or lung transplantation. Outcomes were further analyzed across groups stratified by survival status using Cox proportional hazards regression and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Results A total of 312 patients were analyzed over a median follow-up of 36.10 months, with 59 deaths. Elevated LV entropy was positively correlated with log-transformed NT-proBNP, right ventricular (RV) end-systolic, end-diastolic volume indices, LV native T1 and ECV, and inversely correlated with RV ejection fraction (all P < 0.01). LV entropy did not differ significantly across etiological subgroups, whereas LV entropy without IPs was higher in congenital heart disease-associated PAH. Both LV entropy ≥8.60 and LV entropy without IPs ≥8.30 independently predicted all-cause mortality (HR, 2.207; 95% CI, 1.324-3.678; P = 0.002; and HR, 2.357; 95% CI, 1.405-3.955; P = 0.001, respectively) and were associated with reduced survival (both log-rank P < 0.005). Adding LV entropy improved ESC models (χ²: 55.79 to 60.61, C-statistic: 0.782 to 0.801) and ESC-CMR models (χ²: 35.31 to 41.77, C-statistic: 0.805 to 0.813). Conclusions Elevated LV entropy was related to disease severity, RV dysfunction, and adverse clinical outcomes, and served as an independent predictor of all-cause mortality in patients with PAH. title: Automatic 3D TOF-MRA Intracranial Aneurysm Segmentation using SAM-Guided Multi-View Decoding Network.
abstract: Background Deep learning-based aneurysm segmentation using 3D time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA) offers promising non-invasive screening, but its accuracy and generalizability remain limited. Purpose To develop a deep learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection and segmentation on MRA, and evaluate its multicenter performance against the digital subtraction angiography (DSA) gold standard and radiologists of varying experience. Materials and methods MRA images from patients suspected of harboring unruptured intracranial aneurysms were retrospectively collected from Jinhua Municipal Central Hospital for model development. An external test set, with DSA as the reference standard, was gathered from Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine. Manual segmentation of cerebral arteries and aneurysms was performed using 3D-Slicer software. Performance was evaluated via Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), sensitivity, and F1-score, and compared against independent clinical evaluations from radiologists with different experience levels. Results The internal dataset comprised 1,560 patients (1,554 aneurysms), including 421 patients (522 aneurysms) for testing. The external test set included 208 patients (224 aneurysms). On the internal test set, the model achieved a lesion-level sensitivity of 86.0% (95% CI: 82.8 - 88.7), a precision of 87.4% (95% CI: 84.2, 90.0), and a DSC of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.84, 0.90). On the independent external test set, the model demonstrated robust generalizability with a sensitivity of 83.4% (95% CI: 75.9, 88.0) and a DSC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.79, 0.87). The model achieved an overall detection F1-score of 86.7, significantly outperforming junior radiologists (P <.001) and was comparable to mid-level radiologists (P >.05), with an average processing time of approximately 72seconds per exam. Conclusion The proposed deep learning model demonstrated robust multicenter performance for intracranial aneurysm detection and segmentation. Achieving diagnostic accuracy comparable to mid-level radiologists, it holds potential as an efficient assistive tool for MRA interpretation in clinical workflows.

The model achieved an overall detection F1-score of 86.7, significantly outperforming junior radiologists (P <.001) and was comparable to mid-level radiologists (P >.05), with an average processing time of approximately 72seconds per exam.

Conclusion

title: Prospective Cardiac MRI study comparing Recovered COVID-19 patients with Recovered Non-COVID-19 Viral Respiratory Infection Patients (R-COVID-CMR).
abstract: Objective Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has been associated with subclinical myocardial inflammation. Post-COVID-19 infection, there are concerns about subsequent heart failure and persistent myocarditis. It is unknown how COVID-19 infection compares with non-COVID-19 viral infections in terms of myocardial inflammation based on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) assessment. This prospective longitudinal study aims to determine and compare the extent and severity of myocardial involvement in patients with COVID-19 infection versus non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infections (control). Method Recruited recovered COVID-19 (RCOVID) patients and recovered non-COVID (non-COVID) patients from several hospitals and COVID-19-designated clinic underwent three CMR examinations for functional assessment, native T1, T2, and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification, with corroborating blood markers (NT-proBNP, white cell count, c-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and high sensitivity cardiac troponin T). CMR scans took place (i) within 2-week of confirmed recovery, (ii) 3-month, and (iii) 12-month post-recovery. Linear mixed model with Bonferroni correction was used for analysis. Results 152 participants were recruited, 112 RCOVID outpatients (mean age: 41.0; 58.9% female) and 40 non-COVID inpatients (mean age:45.0; 37.5% female). Non-COVID infections included influenza virus, rhinovirus/enterovirus, parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and human metapneumovirus. At all three time points, blood results and cardiac function parameters were not significantly different between RCOVID and non-COVID patient groups (p-value not significant). Both patient groups had no significant differences for native T1/T2 values, ECV, late gadolinium enhancement, T2 short tau inversion recovery, and overall fulfilment of the 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria at each time points. Conclusion In this prospective longitudinal study with CMR examinations, COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse myocardial inflammatory response than non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infection in terms of CMR parameters, and blood markers. Plain english summary During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreaks, some COVID-19 patients were incidentally found to have inflammation of the muscular layer of the heart. Healthcare professionals were concerned the inflammation will lead to heart not delivering enough blood to meet body demands (ie. heart failure) in the long run. Therefore, we designed this study to better understand the extent and severity of cardiac involvement in patients with COVID-19 by comparing them to patients with other types of viral respiratory infections, such as influenza, which we were more familiar with. We recruited two groups of patients, one group with patients recovered from COVID-19, the other group with patients recovered from other types of viral respiratory infections. For each patient, we arranged three assessments at 2 weeks, 3 months, and 12 months after their recovery respectively. During each assessment, they had blood taken and underwent a cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) scan, a type of medical imaging used for assessment of heart function. 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria (LLC) is a set of criteria for diagnosis of myocardial inflammation recommended by a group of experts. We compared the two groups of patients at each time point according to LLC, as well as their blood markers and heart function. In our study, we found that COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse heart muscle inflammatory response than other types of viral respiratory infections. This is reassuring as patients with previous COVID-19 infections will likely not develop inflammation of the heart muscle nor develop heart failure.

title: Accelerated 3D Late Gadolinium Enhancement Pulse Sequence with Isotropic Spatial Resolution, Self-Navigation of Respiratory Motion, and Arrhythmia Rejection for Quantification of Left Atrial Fibrosis in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation.
abstract: Background The left atrium (LA) is a thin structure (1.5-2.5mm). Conventional 3D late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) pulse sequences for imaging the LA typically have limited through-plane resolution (2.5-5mm) or prolonged scan times (10-15min), resulting in poor image quality and limited clinical translatability. We sought to develop and test whether a 3D LGE pulse sequence featuring 1.5mm³ isotropic spatial resolution and a predictable scan time of 600 heartbeats can produce diagnostically acceptable image quality at 1.5T for quantification of LA structural remodeling in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Methods A 3D LGE pulse sequence was developed using gradient-recalled echo (GRE) readout, stack-of-stars k-space sampling with variable density along the partition direction, retrospective arrhythmia rejection, and XD-GRASP reconstruction with self-navigation of respiratory motion. Thirty patients with AF (twenty imaged prior to first-time ablation, ten prior to repeat ablation) and twenty healthy controls were scanned using this pulse sequence. The upper limit of normal image intensity ratio (IIR) was derived from the control group; specifically, 2 standard deviations (SDs) above the mean. Suspected LA fibrosis was quantified by one rater. Two cardiothoracic radiologists independently graded the image quality across three categories (conspicuity, artifacts, noise) using a 5-point Likert scale per category, with a score of 3 considered clinically acceptable. Results The proposed pulse sequence produced diagnostically acceptable image quality scores in all three categories for AF and control cohorts. Retrospective rejection of data acquired during ectopic heartbeats significantly (p<0.05) improved contrast-to-noise ratio (+3.7%) and sharpness (blur metric -3.2%) metrics, albeit at the expense of a significantly reduced signal-to-noise ratio (-4.4%). The upper limit of normal IIR was 1.43. Using this cutoff value to identify suspected LA fibrosis, compared with the control group (2.47 ± 2.24%), the first-time ablation group (7.45 ± 7.38%) was not significantly different (p = 0.14), whereas the repeat ablation group (14.94 ± 13.83%) was significantly different (p < 0.05). Conclusion The proposed pulse sequence produces diagnostically acceptable image quality at 1.5T and provides evidence of LA structural remodeling in AF patients, including greater suspected LA fibrosis burden, relative to control subjects.

title: Visualization of post-STEMI myocardial infarction and microvascular obstruction with non-contrast, free-breathing whole- heart iT 2 prep-IR BOOST.
abstract: Background Clinical adoption of cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) for risk stratification in ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is often limited by long scan times and the requirement for breath-holding and contrast agents. Objectives This study aimed to validate a non-contrast, free-breathing 3D whole-heart T1/T2 CMR method (iT 2 prep-IR BOOST) for rapid assessment of myocardial injury in STEMI patients, hypothesizing that this technique provides promising diagnostic accuracy and quantitative assessment to conventional contrast-enhanced CMR. Methods A free-breathing 3D isotropic whole-heart iT 2 prep-IR BOOST sequence was performed with a scan time of <8minutes. Sixty-four STEMI patients underwent CMR, including iT 2 prep-IR BOOST, clinical T2-STIR, late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and T1/T2 mapping. The diagnostic performance of iT 2 prep-IR BOOST was evaluated against LGE and T2-STIR to assess myocardial infarction (MI), microvascular obstruction (MVO), and edema. Subgroup analyses further investigated the association between MVO detected by iT 2 prep-IR BOOST and left ventricular (LV) remodeling at 1-year follow-up. Results In 60 STEMI patients, the acquisition was completed in 7.2 ± 0.6min as a single free-breathing 3D whole-heart scan. Patient-level analysis showed high sensitivity and specificity for MVO (100.0% / 87.5%) and segmental MVO detection (95.8% / 97.8%). T 2 prep-IR BOOST yielded robust image contrast for MI comparable to LGE, while offering comparable edema visualization to T2-STIR. Volumetric and transmurality quantifications of MVO, MI, and edema showed excellent agreement with reference standards (all r > 0.90, p < 0.001), supported by significant biophysical correlations with native T1/T2 values (p < 0.001). Furthermore, in a 1-year follow-up cohort (n=51), baseline T 2 prep-IR BOOST-derived MVO volume was associated with adverse left ventricular remodeling, showing significant correlations with both ΔLVEDVI (r = 0.305, p = 0.029) and ΔLVESVI (r = 0.293, p = 0.037). Conclusions In this preliminary single-center study, iT 2 prep-IR BOOST showed promising diagnostic performance and close quantitative agreement with conventional LGE and T2-STIR in stable STEMI patients. Further prospective validation in larger, independent, and more heterogeneous cohorts, including patients unable to undergo contrast-enhanced CMR, is required before this technique can be considered an alternative to standard LGE and T2-weighted sequences.

title: Prognostic Value of Late Gadolinium Enhancement Findings in Isolated Left Ventricular Dilatation and Dilated Cardiomyopathy.
abstract: Background Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and isolated left ventricular dilatation (ILVD) are defined as left ventricular (LV) dilatation, with reduced or preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), respectively. We aimed to assess the prognostic value of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) findings, including LGE extent, location, and number of areas to predict all-cause death in ILVD and DCM, separately. Methods Between 2008 and 2021, we conducted a bicentric retrospective study including all consecutive ILVD and DCM patients referred for cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR). The primary outcome was all-cause death. A propensity-score matching was performed to balance characteristics between ILVD and DCM populations. Cox regressions were performed to determine the prognostic value of each LGE feature. Results Of 2,752 patients (age 52±8 years, 56% males), 408 (15%) patients died after a median (interquartile range) follow-up of 9 (7-12) years, including 268 (16%) of 1,668 DCM patients and 140 (13%) of 1,084 ILVD patients. Overall, 737 (27%) patients had LGE, including 472 (28%) of 1,668 DCM patients and 265 (24%) of 1,084 ILVD patients. After propensity-score matching, in ILVD patients with LGE (N=265), the LGE extent (hazard ratio [HR] 1.38, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.06-1.78, p=0.015), multiple LGE areas (HR=3.39, 95% CI: 1.66-6.92, p<0.001), and its septal location (HR=2.68, 95% CI: 1.59-4.52, p<0.001) were strong prognosticators of death after adjustment. Similarly, after propensity-score matching, in DCM patients with LGE (N=277), the LGE extent (HR=1.39, 95% CI: 1.06-1.83, p=0.018), multiple LGE areas (HR=2.70, 95% CI: 1.20-6.08, p=0.017), and its septal location (HR=2.82, 95% CI: 1.47-5.41, p=0.002) were strongly associated with death. The CMR LGE score performed well in participants with LGE (area under the curve [AUC] at 10 years, 0.79 [95% CI: 0.69-0.89]). Conclusions LGE findings were strongly and independently associated with death in both ILVD and DCM patients, with each successive LGE characteristic providing significant incremental prognostic value beyond traditional prognosticators, including LVEF.

title: Multi-center study of CMR versus cardiac catheterization with endomyocardial biopsy for pediatric transplant surveillance: study protocol.
abstract: Notwithstanding advances in post-transplant care, acute allograft rejection (AR) remains the leading cause of mortality in pediatric heart transplant recipients (PHTX). Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) continues to be the standard of care for AR detection, despite being invasive, costly, and associated with patient discomfort and potential complications. Non-invasive alternatives, including cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) with T1 and T2 parametric mapping and blood biomarkers (BB) such as cell-free DNA (cfDNA) and microRNA (miRNA), have shown promise in the adult transplant population, but their validation in the pediatric transplant population is lacking. The "Predictive Modeling of Acute Rejection in Pediatric Heart Transplant Recipients" (PEACE) study is a prospective, multicenter trial aiming to assess the diagnostic accuracy of CMR and BB in comparison to EMB. The goal of this manuscript is to describe the purpose and experimental protocol of the PEACE study. The PEACE study's overarching hypothesis is that CMR and BB can consistently and accurately detect myocardial abnormalities, potentially guiding the need for EMB. Secondary objectives include cost-analyses of CMR and BB, as well as a biomarker performance evaluation in biopsy-negative, but symptomatic and suspected AR cases. PEACE will enroll PHTX ages 6-25 years, across approximately 20 U.S. pediatric hospitals. All subjects will undergo EMB for surveillance or suspected AR as standard of care. As part of the research protocol, subjects will undergo blood collection for BB prior to the EMB and CMR within 5 days of EMB. Central core labs will conduct blinded analysis for imaging, pathology, and biomarkers to ensure consistent data interpretation. PEACE represents a critical step in reducing reliance on invasive biopsies in the clinical care of PHTX. By validating non-invasive tools in a large, diverse population, the PEACE study could transform AR detection, resulting in improvement of the patient experience and outcomes in this vulnerable population. (Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07770659, Non-invasive Prediction of EArly Cardiac rEjection (PEACE)).

title: Myocardial Alterations in Major Depressive Disorder with Anxious Distress: Evidence from Oxygenation-Sensitive CMR and Entropy Analysis.
abstract: Background Patients with major depressive disorder with anxious distress (MDD-A) frequently experience cardiovascular symptoms (CVS), which are associated with impaired quality of life and poorer long-term prognosis. This study aimed to quantitatively evaluate myocardial alterations in MDD-A patients using oxygenation-sensitive cardiovascular magnetic resonance (OS-CMR) and mapping-derived entropy analysis, and to explore their associations with CVS as well as the severity of depressive and anxiety symptoms. Methods In this prospective study, 58 consecutively enrolled medication-naïve patients with MDD-A diagnosed according to DSM-5 criteria and 61 healthy controls were included. All participants underwent CMR examinations at 3.0T. Left ventricular (LV) function, native T1 and T2 values, T1-entropy and T2-entropy, LV strain parameters, and oxygenation-sensitive signal intensity change (OS-SI%) were measured and compared between the two groups. Associations between CMR-derived parameters and CVS, anxiety symptom severity, and depressive symptom severity were assessed separately. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Compared with healthy controls, patients with MDD-A exhibited significantly higher T1-entropy (8.3 ± 0.3 vs. 7.5 ± 0.3, p < 0.001) and T2-entropy (9.2 ± 0.4 vs. 8.1 ± 0.3, p < 0.001), whereas OS-SI% was significantly lower (11.4 ± 7.5% vs. 14.5 ± 4.5%, p = 0.007). After adjustment for age, sex, smoking status, and heart rate, multivariable regression analyses revealed that OS-SI% was inversely associated with HAMD scores (β = -0.205, p = 0.043) and HAMA scores (β = -0.453, p < 0.001), and inversely associated with CVS (OR= 0.801, p = 0.002). T1-entropy (β = 4.105, p = 0.022) and T2-entropy (β = 2.793, p = 0.042) were positively associated with HAMD scores. Conclusion OS-SI% and mapping-derived myocardial entropy measures may serve as valuable noninvasive imaging biomarkers for assessing early myocardial alterations in patients with MDD-A.

title: The Right Ventricle in Focus: State-of-the-Art CMR Imaging - Challenges, Standards, and Innovations.
abstract: The right ventricle (RV) is recognized as a critical contributor to cardiovascular outcomes. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) has emerged as the reference standard for comprehensive RV assessment, enabling precise evaluation of ventricular volumes, function, flow, and tissue characterization. In this review, we provide a state-of-the-art overview of RV imaging using CMR. We first outline the anatomical and physiological features that distinguish the RV from the left ventricle. Next, we highlight the key technical challenges in imaging the RV, notably its complex geometry, prominent trabeculation, and thin myocardial wall. We then summarize current clinical CMR approaches, including cine imaging for volumetric assessment, phase-contrast techniques for flow quantification, and methods for tissue characterization such as late gadolinium enhancement. Additionally, we discuss advanced and emerging CMR techniques aimed at overcoming current RV imaging limitations, including high-resolution three-dimensional cine imaging, four-dimensional flow imaging, parametric mapping, and novel reconstruction strategies. These innovations hold promise for improving accuracy, reproducibility, and mechanistic insight into RV structure and function. Finally, we review the clinical role of CMR in major RV pathologies, including congenital heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, and tricuspid regurgitation. Across these conditions, CMR provides vital diagnostic and prognostic information, with growing evidence supporting its role in guiding clinical management. As technical advancements continue and standardization improves, CMR is poised to transform RV evaluation from a historically challenging endeavor into a precise and impactful component of cardiovascular care.

title: Endovascular stenting of extracranial cervical artery dissections: A two-center study.
abstract: Purpose Extracranial arterial dissections (EAD) are uncommon in the general population but represent a relatively frequent cause of ischemic stroke in young adults. Most EAD have a favorable prognosis and are managed conservatively with antithrombotic therapy, with current guidelines supporting either antiplatelet or anticoagulant treatment. Endovascular stenting is reserved for selected high-risk cases, and this article reports a multicenter experience with this approach and reviews the available literature. Materials and methods Eighty-four EAD patients who underwent stenting were included. A standardized follow-up protocol at 12 months consisting of a clinical neurological assessment accompanied by imaging studies, including either Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Digital Subtraction Angiography was adopted. Results In our cohort, most dissections were spontaneous (81 %) and predominantly involved the internal carotid artery (85 %), with acute stroke being the most common indication for stenting. Technical success was achieved in 85.7 % and complications occurred in 10 %. Three patients with initial stent implantation failure underwent successful secondary attempt. No significant predictors of technical success were identified. At discharge, good functional outcome was observed in 83 % of patients and at 12 months most followed patients showed favorable radiological results with high stent patency (86 %) and excellent clinical outcomes (mRS 0-2 in 97 %). Conclusion The results of our study suggest that for selected patients with medical therapy failure or hemodynamic compromise, stenting is a reasonable alternative. Given the limited evidence on indications, safety and efficacy, further randomized studies comparing stenting with medical management are warranted.

Purpose

Extracranial arterial dissections (EAD) are uncommon in the general population but represent a relatively frequent cause of ischemic stroke in young adults. Most EAD have a favorable prognosis and are managed conservatively with antithrombotic therapy, with current guidelines supporting either antiplatelet or anticoagulant treatment. Endovascular stenting is reserved for selected high-risk cases, and this article reports a multicenter experience with this approach and reviews the available literature.

Materials and methods

Eighty-four EAD patients who underwent stenting were included. A standardized follow-up protocol at 12 months consisting of a clinical neurological assessment accompanied by imaging studies, including either Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Digital Subtraction Angiography was adopted.

Results

In our cohort, most dissections were spontaneous (81 %) and predominantly involved the internal carotid artery (85 %), with acute stroke being the most common indication for stenting. Technical success was achieved in 85.7 % and complications occurred in 10 %. Three patients with initial stent implantation failure underwent successful secondary attempt. No significant predictors of technical success were identified. At discharge, good functional outcome was observed in 83 % of patients and at 12 months most followed patients showed favorable radiological results with high stent patency (86 %) and excellent clinical outcomes (mRS 0-2 in 97 %).

The results of our study suggest that for selected patients with medical therapy failure or hemodynamic compromise, stenting is a reasonable alternative. Given the limited evidence on indications, safety and efficacy, further randomized studies comparing stenting with medical management are warranted.

title: Basal forebrain glioma: Clinical characteristics and surgical treatment.
abstract: Background Surgical resection of basal forebrain (BFB) gliomas involving the anterior perforated substance (APS) is associated with a high risk of surgical complications due to multiple perforating arteries that traverse this region. Despite these challenges, surgery in this region serves several important purposes, including cytoreduction, histopathological diagnosis, and seizure control. Methods This study included a consecutive series of 67 patients with gliomas either confined to the BFB (13 cases) or extending to adjacent anatomical regions (54 cases) who underwent surgery at the Burdenko Neurosurgery Center between 2016 and 2023. Three main approaches were used: transsylvian, anterior interhemispheric, and supraorbital subfrontal. In 5 cases, the tumor was removed using a microsurgical burr-hole technique. Results BFB tumors were classified according to 2 features: 1) involvement of anatomical regions adjacent to the BFB and 2) localization of the tumor within the BFB: the septal region (S), anterior APS segment (Pa), and posterior APS segment (Pp). Isolated BFB tumors were found in 13 cases (19.4%), including 4 localized to the septal region. Among 59 patients with early postoperative MRI, median EOR was 82%. EOR 70-90% was achieved in 23 of 59 patients (39.0%), and EOR ≥ 90% in 25 of 59 (42.4%). With extension into the Pp segment, EOR ≥ 90% was achieved less often than in the remaining cohort: 8 of 31 (25.8%) versus 17 of 28 (60.7%), respectively (p = 0.009). title: Implementation and early experience with tubular retractor-assisted minimally invasive parafascicular surgery for deep brain tumors.
abstract: Minimally invasive parafascicular surgery using tubular retractors (tr-MIPS) has emerged as a strategy to access deep intra-axial lesions while minimizing white matter disruption. However, practical guidance on institutional implementation and integration with modern intraoperative adjuncts remains limited. We describe our early institutional experience with tr-MIPS, with a focus on workflow adoption, multimodal adjunct integration, and feasibility. Demographic, radiographic, operative, and postoperative data were collected, with particular attention to extent of resection, neurological outcomes, and use of adjunctive technologies. Six patients underwent tr-MIPS for deep intra-axial tumors of varied histology. Gross or near-total resection was achieved in four cases. Five patients experienced no new postoperative neurological deficits, and one had transient dysphasia. Median length of stay was 3.5 days. A range of adjuncts including diffusion tensor imaging, 5-aminolevulinic acid fluorescence, intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring, and depth-electrode electroencephalography were successfully incorporated without workflow disruption. Notably, intraoperative depth-electrode EEG was used to guide resection of an epileptogenic lesion, representing a novel adjunctive application in the tr-MIPS setting. tr-MIPS can be implemented within a modern neurosurgical practice and feasibly integrated with multiple intraoperative adjuncts. We demonstrate feasibility with the addition of this technique to our center's armamentarium. Beyond facilitating access to deep lesions, its compatibility with technologies such as tractography, neurophysiologic monitoring, and EEG expands its functional utility. These findings support the feasibility of a broader adoption of tr-MIPS and highlight opportunities for multimodal, precision-guided minimally invasive neuro-oncologic surgery.
