title: Comparing Diagnostic Ability of Two Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models with That of Endodontists for Teeth Requiring Initial Root Canal Treatment: A Multicenter Retrospective Investigation.
abstract: Introduction Despite growing interest in large language models (LLMs) for endodontic diagnosis, prior studies have used simulated cases, examination formats, or small selected series. This multicenter retrospective study compared the diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-5.2 and Gemini 3.0 with that of calibrated endodontists across 645 teeth requiring initial root canal treatment. Methods Cases were evaluated across four endpoints: pulpal diagnosis, periapical diagnosis, treatment planning, and case difficulty. Standardized clinical summaries and radiographs were submitted to endodontists and both LLMs using a fixed single-pass protocol. Exact-match accuracy, Cohen's κ, Gwet's AC1, macro-averaged F1 score, McNemar tests, and generalized estimating equations were used for statistical comparison. Results Endpoint accuracies ranged from 74% to 88%. Macro F1 was highest for periapical diagnosis (ChatGPT-5.2, 0.724; Gemini 3.0, 0.719) and lowest for treatment planning (0.385; 0.550), where both models showed lower observed performance in minority categories, interpreted as suggestive given small subgroup sizes. Composite accuracy across the three clinical endpoints was 61.1% (95% CI, 57.4%-64.8%) and 59.4% (95% CI, 55.3%-63.3%), and four-endpoint accuracy was 47.3% (95% CI, 43.3%-51.2%) and 46.2% (95% CI, 42.3%-49.8%), indicating at least one clinically relevant error in about half of cases. Treatment planning was the only endpoint differing between models after Holm-Bonferroni correction, favoring Gemini 3.0 (OR, 1.457; adjusted p = .003). Conclusions Both models performed acceptably on individual endpoints and common presentations, but performance was endpoint-specific and substantially reduced on integrated assessment and low-prevalence categories. These findings support use of LLMs in endodontic diagnosis and treatment planning as adjunctive tools, but not without expert supervision.

title: ASSESSMENT OF TREATMENT RESPONSE RESPONSE AND THE ROLE OF COMPLETION SURGERY AFTER CONCURRENT CRTAND BRACHYTHERAPY FOR LOCALLY ADVANCED CERVICAL CANCER - A REVIEW FROM THE FRENCH CERVICAL CANCER GUIDELINES GROUP.
abstract: Concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by brachytherapy is the standard of care for locally advanced cervical cancer. However, post-treatment management remains challenging. Accurate response assessment is essential because it informs subsequent management, particularly the indication for completion surgery. Radiation-induced tissue changes may impair the reliability of clinical examination and conventional imaging, while the respective roles of advanced imaging modalities and completion surgery remain debated. Functional lumbopelvic MRI incorporating diffusion-weighted and perfusion sequences is the reference imaging modality for response assessment and provides greater diagnostic performance than clinical examination alone. FDG PET-CT offers complementary information, particularly regarding nodal disease and early metabolic response, but the routine combination of FDG PET-CT with MRI has not been shown to improve diagnostic accuracy. MRI performed early during CRT may help differentiate responders from nonresponders based on changes in the apparent diffusion coefficient. However, the optimal timing of MRI after treatment completion remains uncertain. Available evidence does not support the routine use of conization for response assessment. Completion surgery provides no prognostic benefit and increases morbidity in patients with squamous cell carcinoma who achieve a complete response after CRT and brachytherapy. Evidence remains insufficient to establish its role in adenocarcinoma. When completion surgery is indicated, delaying the procedure until at least 6-8 weeks after CRT may reduce postoperative morbidity. Simple hysterectomy should be favored over radical hysterectomy, which increases morbidity without improving survival. Current evidence demonstrates no superiority of minimally invasive surgery or laparotomy in terms of oncologic outcomes or overall morbidity.

title: Accuracy of Diagnostic Methods for Peripheral Trigeminal Nerve Injuries: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background Post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy following oral and maxillofacial procedures may cause persistent neurosensory disturbances and neuropathic pain, yet the diagnostic performance of the available assessment methods remains uncertain. Purpose This systematic review evaluated the accuracy of diagnostic methods used to detect peripheral trigeminal nerve injuries in the maxillary and mandibular regions after oral and maxillofacial procedures. Study selection PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases were searched in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines. Diagnostic accuracy and observational studies evaluating clinical, neurophysiological, or imaging-based methods for peripheral trigeminal nerve injuries were included, while non-English and nonhuman studies, reports lacking relevant diagnostic performance data, studies outside the maxillary or mandibular regions, and nonoriginal research were excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2. Results The search identified 2914 records, of which 10 studies (0.3%) were included in the final synthesis, comprising n = 520 participants and k = 514 injured or evaluated nerves. The included studies comprised 5 prospective diagnostic accuracy studies, 2 retrospective diagnostic accuracy studies, 2 case-control diagnostic accuracy studies, and one cross-sectional observational study. Clinical neurosensory testing showed 96% accuracy, 100% sensitivity, 62.5% specificity, 95% positive predictive value (PPV), and 100% negative predictive value (NPV) for lingual nerve (LN) injuries, compared with 73% accuracy, 85% sensitivity, 47% specificity, 77% PPV, and 60% NPV for inferior alveolar nerve injuries. The tongue somatosensory evoked magnetic field laterality index showed 95.7% accuracy, 92.3% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% PPV, and 90.9% NPV for LN injury. Conclusions and relevance Clinical neurosensory testing was widely used but had variable diagnostic performance, with lower values for inferior alveolar nerve injuries. Quantitative sensory testing and neurophysiological methods provided more balanced diagnostic profiles, especially when combined. Magnetic resonance neurography demonstrated high specificity but variable sensitivity, with greater clinical value for high-fgrade injuries. The highest single-test accuracy was reported for tongue somatosensory evoked magnetic fields in LN injury. Overall, these findings support a multimodal diagnostic approach when objective confirmation, injury grading, anatomical localization, or treatment planning is required.

title: Computed Tomogrpahy-Guided Management of High-Risk Mandibular Third Molars: A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background Coronectomy is used to reduce the risk of inferior alveolar nerve (IAN) injury in high-risk mandibular third molars, but comparative studies rarely account for preoperative risk stratification. Purpose To compare postoperative outcomes following coronectomy and complete removal in a computed tomography (CT)-guided, risk-adapted treatment pathway. Study design, setting, and sample This prospective cohort study included consecutive patients with high-risk mandibular third molars treated at Amstelland Hospital, Amstelveen, the Netherlands (2019-2025). All subjects underwent CT assessment after panoramic radiography. Subjects aged < 18 years or with previous surgery, incomplete records, inability to complete follow up, American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status > III, or acute infection were excluded. Predictor variable Planned treatment modality (coronectomy vs complete removal). Main outcome variables The primary outcome was postoperative IAN or lingual nerve sensory disturbance. Secondary outcomes included postoperative complications and treatment-related outcomes, including successful coronectomy, intraoperative conversion to complete removal, and subsequent interventions involving retained roots. Covariates Age, sex, smoking status, American Society of Anesthesiologists classification, impaction classification, and pathology. Analyses Primary comparative analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle, with converted cases retained in the planned coronectomy group. Intraoperative conversion was analyzed as a treatment-related outcome. Effect estimates with 95% CIs were calculated as appropriate. Statistical significance was set at P < .05. Results A total of 1,727 subjects (2,450 mandibular third molars; median age 25 years [interquartile range, 22-31 years]; 1,064 [61.6%] female) were included. 1,387 (56.6%) were treated with planned coronectomy and 1,063 (43.4%) with planned removal. Among planned coronectomies, 1,337 (96.4%) were completed as intended, 27 (1.9%) involved partial root removal, and 23 (1.7%) converted to complete removal. IAN hypoesthesia occurred in 29 molars (1.2%) and lingual nerve hypoesthesia in 8 (0.3%). IAN injury increased with impaction depth (P < .001) and occurred in 3 (13.0%) converted molars versus 6 (0.6%) removals (P < .001). IAN hypoesthesia resolved in 25 cases (86.2%). Secondary root removal was required in 36 (2.6%) of 1,364 performed coronectomies. Conclusions and relevance In this CT-guided, risk-adapted pathway, neurosensory complications were uncommon. Intraoperative conversion was associated with increased IAN injury risk and represents an important intraoperative risk marker.

title: Tumor-induced osteomalacia caused by a mandibular phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor misdiagnosed as giant cell reparative granuloma: case report.
abstract: Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) is a rare syndrome caused by FGF23-secreting phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors (PMTs). Clinicians frequently misdiagnose mandibular PMTs due to their histological mimicry of giant cell lesions. We report a 16-year-old female with mandibular PMT-induced TIO who endured a 5-year diagnostic delay across eight hospitals. Two factors confounded her diagnosis: histological mimicry of giant cell reparative granuloma and an incidental SMARCAL1 variant misdirecting clinical attention toward a genetic disorder. Ultimately, integrated histopathologic evaluation and focal FGF23 immunohistochemistry supported the diagnosis of PMT, with serum P1NP reaching 435.00 ng/mL and β-CTX exceeding 6.00 ng/mL at peak disease severity, while ¹⁸F-AlF-NOTA-TATE PET/CT localized the lesion. Tumor resection with fibula free flap reconstruction achieved early postoperative improvement in serum phosphate levels and symptoms, although long-term clinical, biochemical, and radiographic follow-up remains necessary to assess durable remission and monitor for recurrence. This case illustrates multiple diagnostic pitfalls in TIO with mandibular PMT, emphasizing that a high index of suspicion and integration of biochemical, histological, and imaging findings are essential to avoid delayed diagnosis.

title: Large Osseous Choristoma of the Tongue Base: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Osseous choristoma is a rare benign lesion composed of mature bone in an ectopic soft-tissue site, most often the posterior tongue. We report a 9-year-old girl with a 1-year history of a slowly enlarging tongue-base lesion causing dysphagia and snoring during sleep. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a well-circumscribed, homogeneous bony-density lesion measuring 4.0 × 3.8 × 4.1 cm without enhancement or adjacent soft-tissue invasion. The lesion was completely excised through a dorsal tongue approach. Histopathological examination demonstrated mature osseous tissue with bony trabeculae and marrow cavities, confirming osseous choristoma. Recovery was uneventful, with no clinical recurrence at 3 months. Large tongue-base osseous choristomas may cause functional symptoms despite their benign nature. Computed tomography provides a useful diagnostic clue, while definitive diagnosis depends on histopathology. Complete surgical excision remains the treatment of choice.

title: Diagnostic Value of Tc-99m-HDP SPECT/CT in Temporomandibular Joint Osteoarthritis: Correlation with Clinical and Structural Findings.
abstract: Background This study evaluated the diagnostic utility of quantitative Tc-99m-hydroxydiphosphonate (HDP) bone single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT) in temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis (TMJ OA) by analyzing correlations among tracer uptake, clinical features, and structural imaging to detect early metabolically active disease. Methods A retrospective review included 48 patients (96 TMJs) with TMJ discomfort who underwent SPECT/CT and conventional imaging. Clinical parameters included pain duration, visual analog scale (VAS) score, joint sounds, mandibular range of motion, and occlusal findings. Radiography assessed condylar morphology and cortical erosion, and a Destructive Change Index (DCI) quantified bony changes. SPECT/CT uptake was expressed as maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax). Correlation and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed. Results SPECT/CT uptake strongly correlated with condylar cortical erosion on CT (r = 0.80) and moderately with lateral pole tenderness (r = 0.51) and pain VAS score (r = 0.40). Joint sounds and condylar morphology correlated weakly (r = 0.26 and 0.21, respectively), while other clinical factors had negligible associations. ROC analysis identified an optimal SUVmax cutoff of 3.88, yielding 91% sensitivity (95% CI: 80-97%) and 85% specificity (95% CI: 73-94%) for detecting cortical erosion. SPECT/CT revealed increased metabolic uptake in some radiographically normal joints, suggesting the possibility of early osteoarthritic change before overt structural abnormalities became apparent. Conclusion Quantitative SPECT/CT provides complementary metabolic information beyond structural imaging and may facilitate the detection of metabolically active TMJ osteoarthritis.

title: Digital volumetric planning and mixed reality-guided anterolateral thigh flap reconstruction for maxillary defects.
abstract: Background Accurate restoration of soft-tissue volume remains challenging in maxillary reconstruction. This study assessed the feasibility of a defect-oriented digital volumetric planning workflow combined with mixed reality (MR)-guided anterolateral thigh flap (ALTF) harvest. Methods Patients who underwent maxillectomy followed by ALTF reconstruction between November 2023 and January 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Preoperative CT data were imported into Mimics Medical 21.0 for three-dimensional reconstruction of the maxilla and tumor. Virtual osteotomy and defect simulation were performed to calculate the simulated recipient-defect capacity, designated as V1. Flap dimensions were then designed using V1 and donor-site adipose thickness. MR guidance was used intraoperatively for perforator localization and flap harvest. Intraoperative flap volume was measured by water displacement (V2), and postoperative flap volume was quantified on CT imaging (V3). Secondary outcomes included flap utilization rate, complications, speech intelligibility, patient satisfaction, and University of Washington Quality of Life scores.The three related volumes were compared using the Friedman test, followed by Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Results Fifteen patients were included. Mean flap thickness was 10.80 ± 3.49 mm. Median V1, V2, and V3 values were 61.57 mL (interquartile range [IQR], 44.53), 75.00 mL (IQR, 52.00), and 64.26 mL (IQR, 40.65), respectively. The overall difference was significant (Friedman statistic = 17.200, degrees of freedom = 2; P < 0.001). V2 was significantly greater than V1 (adjusted P < 0.001) and V3 (adjusted P = 0.003), whereas V1 and V3 did not differ significantly (adjusted P = 1.000). Mean flap utilization rate was 91.13 ± 9.67%. All flaps survived. One patient developed titanium mesh exposure after radiotherapy; no other major complications occurred. Postoperative speech intelligibility and quality-of-life outcomes were generally favorable. Conclusions Digital volumetric planning combined with MR-guided ALTF harvest was technically feasible in this preliminary cohort and provided a reference for individualized flap design. The findings should be interpreted as exploratory, and comparative studies with larger samples are needed to determine whether this workflow improves clinical outcomes or reduces tissue trimming.

title: Prognostic factors in patients with lower gingival squamous cell carcinoma by computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging: an especial focus on mandibular canal invasion and masticator space invasion.
abstract: Introduction The study aimed to research the prognostic factors in patients with lower gingival squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) by computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), especially focus on mandibular canal invasion and masticator space invasion. Material & methods Forty-eight patients with lower gingival SCC underwent CT and MRI for pre-treatment. The prognostic factors were assessed by chi-square test with the Fisher's exact test. The five-year overall survival rates were analyzed by Kaplan-Meier method with log rank test. Results The results demonstrated that masticator space invasion with MRI was significant predictive variable for regional lymph node metastasis (p = 0.015), and that bone invasion with CT, masticator space invasion with MRI and T-primary tumour (TNM classification 9th Edition) were significant predictive variables for survival (p < 0.001, p = 0.004 and p < 0.001, respectively). The five-year overall survival rate in bone invasion with CT was 77.1 % for non-mandibular canal invasion and 0 % for mandibular canal invasion, respectively (p < 0.001). The five-year overall survival rate in masticator space invasion with MRI was 68.8 % for no invasion and 12.5 % for masticator space invasion, respectively (p < 0.001). Furthermore, the five-year overall survival rate in T-primary tumour was 80.9 % for T1-3 and 7.1 % for T4, respectively (p < 0.001). Conclusion This study suggested that the mandibular canal invasion with CT may be a potential prognostic factor and that further multicenter validation is needed.

title: Procedure-specific cranial base responses after surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion and Le Fort I osteotomy.
abstract: Background The biological effects of maxillary surgery may extend beyond the operative site to involve the posterior cranial base. Although biomechanical studies have suggested force transmission to the spheno-occipital synchondrosis (SOS), procedure-specific cranial base responses have not previously been quantitatively evaluated using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based radiomics. Objective To compare postoperative cranial base responses following surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE) and Le Fort I osteotomy by quantitatively evaluating the SOS using CBCT-based radiomics. Materials and methods This retrospective observational study included 25 skeletally mature patients treated with either SARPE (n = 12) or Le Fort I osteotomy (n = 13). Preoperative and three-month postoperative CBCT scans were analyzed. The SOS was manually segmented using a standardized anatomical reference framework, and 107 radiomic features were extracted according to Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative recommendations. Within-group and between-group comparisons were performed using non-parametric tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Selected radiomic features were further analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Results Radiographic SOS separation rates were comparable between the SARPE and Le Fort I groups (p > 0.05). Following false discovery rate correction, 43 radiomic features demonstrated significant postoperative alterations in the SARPE group, whereas four features showed nominally significant changes after Le Fort I osteotomy (p < 0.05), none of which remained significant after FDR correction. Nominal between-group comparisons identified four features with p < 0.05, but none remained significant after FDR correction. Linear mixed-effects analysis identified a significant Group × Time interaction for GLSZM Large Area Low Gray Level Emphasis (FDR-adjusted p = 0.024), supporting a procedure-specific longitudinal response. Heatmap and volcano plot analyzes demonstrated a broader distribution of postoperative imaging-derived changes following SARPE than after Le Fort I osteotomy. Conclusions SARPE and Le Fort I osteotomy produced distinct postoperative responses within the spheno-occipital synchondrosis, suggesting that cranial base adaptation varies according to the surgical procedure. The broader radiomic response observed following SARPE is consistent with the hypothesis that preservation of the pterygomaxillary connection may permit greater force transmission to the posterior cranial base. CBCT-based radiomics may provide a sensitive quantitative method for characterizing procedure-specific cranial base responses.

title: Comparison of the efficacy of three-dimensional printing-assisted strategy and traditional total ankle arthroplasty in the treatment of end-stage ankle arthritis.
abstract: Objective To compare perioperative parameters, early functional outcomes, and complication profiles between 3D printing-assisted total ankle arthroplasty strategy incorporating preoperative virtual planning, patient-specific osteotomy guides, and a customized talar component and conventional total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) in the treatment of end-stage ankle arthritis. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on data from 44 patients diagnosed with end-stage ankle arthritis who were admitted to our hospital between January 2021 and December 2023. Among them, 20 patients (observation group) underwent total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) using a 3D-printed patient-specific TAA strategy, while 24 patients (control group) received conventional TAA using the same tibial component and polyethylene liner but a standard off-the-shelf talar component, together with standard instrumentation. The following parameters were recorded and evaluated: operative duration, intraoperative blood loss, length of postoperative hospital stay, intraoperative fluoroscopy time, preoperative and postoperative American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) scores, visual analogue scale (VAS) scores, and ankle range of motion (ROM). Additionally, the occurrence of soft tissue-related complications was monitored. Results The AOFAS score, VAS score, and ankle range of motion (ROM) in both groups showed significant improvement postoperatively compared to preoperative values (P < 0.05). However, no statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups (P > 0.05). With regard to surgical outcomes, including operative time, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative hospitalization duration, and the intraoperative fluoroscopy time, the observation group demonstrated significantly better results than the control group (P < 0.001). Concerning postoperative complications, the observation group experienced only one case of superficial infection, whereas the control group had two cases of superficial infection and one case of wound edge necrosis. Although the total complication rate was slightly lower in the observation group, the difference between the two groups was not statistically significant (P = 0.389). Postoperative radiographic analysis confirmed significantly improved alignment accuracy of the tibial component in the observation group compared to the control group (P < 0.05). Conclusion The 3D printing-assisted TAA strategy appears to improve perioperative efficiency and short-term radiographic alignment accuracy compared with conventional TAA, whereas short-term functional outcomes and wound-related complication rates remain comparable between groups. Given the additional preoperative preparation time and cost, its theoretical promise for patients with complex deformities and its potential effect on long-term implant survival require further confirmation through prospective, randomized studies with long-term follow-up.

title: Multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy for quantitative morphomechanical assessment of articular cartilage.
abstract: Background Osteoarthritis (OA) involves progressive cartilage degeneration, while conventional white-light arthroscopy mainly provides surface morphological information and lacks quantitative functional contrast. Multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy (MMPA) may strengthen intraoperative cartilage assessment by enabling earlier identification of matrix, collagen, and biomechanical alterations that are not readily visible under white light. Methods We developed a preclinical multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy (MMPA) prototype integrating photoacoustic imaging, polarization-resolved photoacoustic imaging, and photoacoustic elasticity imaging to enable label-free, in situ microscopic-resolution assessment of cartilage composition, collagen-related structural anisotropy, and biomechanical response. Validation was performed on 300 human cartilage regions spanning multiple degenerative grades. A feature-based machine-learning classifier was developed mainly using cartilage regions with Mankin scores from 2 to 9, and an independent external validation cohort including 120 cartilage regions was used to assess model generalizability. Longitudinal in vivo monitoring was conducted in a large-animal model. MRI and white-light arthroscopy were used as comparative imaging modalities, whereas histopathological grading served as the reference standard. Results MMPA provided additional visualization of microscopic morphomechanical changes that were less apparent on conventional white-light arthroscopy. The multimodal machine-learning model achieved AUCs of 0.93 (95% CI: 0.91-0.95) internally and 0.89 (95% CI: 0.87-0.90) externally. MMPA detected 81% of lesions, compared with 78% for MRI and 72% for white-light arthroscopy, with a significant overall difference (Cochran's Q=21.00 , p=2.75×10-5 ) and significant pairwise differences (MMPA vs MRI, p=0.0313 ; MMPA vs white-light arthroscopy, p=0.000831 ). MMPA-derived scores most closely tracked histopathological severity. Conclusion This study establishes a preclinical multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy framework for quantitative intraoperative morphomechanical assessment of articular cartilage degeneration. MMPA has potential to serve as a quantitative upgrade to conventional white-light arthroscopy, assisting surgeons in earlier recognition of degenerative cartilage changes from Mankin score 2 onward, lesion evaluation, and intraoperative decision-making. The translational potential of this article : This study presents a preclinical multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy platform that provides quantitative intraoperative assessment of cartilage composition, structural anisotropy, and biomechanical properties. Rather than replacing MRI, MMPA is intended to complement preoperative MRI by offering real-time functional assessment during arthroscopy.

title: Somatic Growth Faltering Precedes Brain Growth Deceleration in Preterm Infants: A Window for Intervention.
abstract: Objective To identify the timing and clinical risk factors associated with somatic growth faltering (GF) in very preterm infants (VPI, born < 32 weeks' gestation) and explore the relationship with longitudinal brain growth throughout the extrauterine second and third trimesters. Study design Observational cohort followed with serial growth anthropometrics and brain magnetic resonance imaging at approximately 4-week intervals through term corrected age. Multivariable logistic regression identified clinical covariates associated with GF. Generalized additive models, extended linear mixed models, and multivariable linear mixed models were applied to create trajectories of nutritional intake and weight and brain growth and compare term corrected brain volumes between VPI with and without GF. Results 118 VPI (68 GF, 50 no GF) underwent 333 magnetic resonance imaging studies (195 GF, 138 no GF). Those with GF were born younger (mean [SD] 27.4 [2.2] vs 28.3 [2.3] weeks, p=0.02) and experienced more clinical comorbidities. Poor weight gain in GF VPI began after 33 weeks corrected age and was associated with early systemic steroids (odds ratio [95% CI] 3.8 [1.2,14.8], P=0.03) and gastrointestinal surgery (odds ratio [95% CI] 7.8 [1.8,53.9], P=0.01). GF infants demonstrated significantly lower lipid, caloric, and maternal milk intake trajectories than non-GF infants. VPI with GF compared with no GF experienced slower volumetric brain growth after 37 weeks corrected age in nearly all brain regions. Term corrected cerebellar (β= -1.74 [-2.95,-0.52], p=0.01) and brainstem (β= -0.29 [-0.55,-0.04], p=0.02) volumes were lower in GF infants after adjusting for significant covariates. Conclusions Brain growth is impaired during critical extrauterine periods in GF VPI, with a 4-week interval between the onset of weight faltering and subsequent brain growth deceleration that may represent an important window for clinical intervention.

title: VIRTUAL REALITY-ENHANCED FOR PREOPERATIVE ANATOMICAL ASSESSMENT OF ABDOMINAL NEUROBLASTOMA: A COMPARATIVE STUDY WITH CONVENTIONAL CT IMAGING.
abstract: Aim Accurate assessment of tumour anatomy is critical for neuroblastoma surgical planning. This study evaluated whether patient-specific virtual reality (VR) models improve the accuracy of pre-operative anatomical assessment compared with conventional computed tomography (CT) imaging. Methods CT scans from nine patients with abdominal neuroblastoma were segmented to create patient-specific VR models, which were then imported into an in-house VR application. Eleven paediatric surgeons (n=5 consultants; n=6 registrars) independently evaluated conventional CT images and VR reconstructions to assess vascular and organ involvement, image-defined risk factors (IDRFs), and operative strategies. Anatomical accuracy was quantified against intraoperative findings recorded in the International Neuroblastoma Surgical Report Form. Subjective ratings were collected using Likert scales. Mixed-effects models and non-parametric statistical analyses were conducted (p<0.05). Results VR significantly improved overall anatomical accuracy, with a mean increase of 12.4 percentage points (95% CI 8.5-16.3; p<0.0001). Improvements were observed for vascular involvement (+12.5%, p<0.001), organ involvement (+9.6%, p<0.01), and IDRF identification (+13.7%, p<0.0001). Improvements in anatomical accuracy with VR were similar between consultants and registrars. VR did not significantly alter operative planning decisions or predicted tumour resectability. Surgeons reported greater confidence in anatomical understanding and surgical planning with VR than CT (p<0.001). The VR platform received high ratings for usability, integration into the preoperative planning workflow, and perceived clinical value. Conclusion VR improved surgeons' anatomical assessment accuracy and confidence compared with traditional CT scans, highlighting VR's potential as a useful supplement to conventional imaging for preoperative evaluation in complex abdominal neuroblastoma.

title: Unfolding new horizons: Machine learning applications for pediatric intussusception - A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Pediatric intussusception is among the most common surgical emergencies in early childhood. Ultrasonography is the diagnostic standard but remains operator-dependent, and no validated machine learning (ML) tools exist for triage or prognostic stratification. We systematically evaluated ML models for diagnosis and prognosis of pediatric intussusception. Methods This PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis (CRD420251073590) included studies evaluating ML models for pediatric intussusception diagnosis or prognosis reporting sensitivity, specificity, or AUC. Risk of bias was assessed with PROBAST. A bivariate random-effects model was applied to internally and externally validated datasets, with subgroup analyses by input modality. Results Eleven studies (37 model variants; 36,863 patients) were included. Internally validated ultrasound (US) models (k=4) achieved pooled sensitivity 0.914 (0.829-0.959) and specificity 0.980 (0.939-0.994). Externally validated US models (k=3) showed sensitivity 0.946 (0.909-0.969) and specificity 0.958 (0.918-0.979). Abdominal radiograph (AXR) triage models performed lower externally (sensitivity 0.800 [0.725-0.859]; specificity 0.748 [0.662-0.819]), consistent with a screening role. Notably, AI assistance improved junior readers' specificity by 15.9 percentage points overall (up to 37.6 points for the most junior readers), and AI-assisted junior sonographers cut ultrasound examination time by 61% without loss of diagnostic accuracy. Possible publication bias was detected (Deeks' p=0.021). Prognostic AUCs ranged from 0.555 to 0.962. Conclusions US-based ML models demonstrate high, externally robust diagnostic accuracy. AXR models suit screening but need further validation. No study reported clinical endpoint data. Multicenter prospective validation outside Asia and regulatory pathway development are required before implementation. Until then, AXR-based models should be positioned as an adjunct that raises suspicion, never as a gate that determines which child receives an ultrasound. Level of evidence Level III - Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of retrospective diagnostic accuracy studies.

title: CONGENITAL HEPATOPULMONARY FUSION IN RIGHT CONGENITAL DIAPHRAGMATIC HERNIA: SURGICAL STRATEGY AND OUTCOMES IN A MULTICENTER COHORT.
abstract: Aim Congenital hepatopulmonary fusion (CHPF) is a rare anomaly associated with right congenital diaphragmatic hernia (RCDH), for which optimal diagnosis and surgical management remain undefined. This study aimed to explore the impact of surgical separation on outcomes. Methods A retrospective multicenter study reviewed neonates with intraoperatively or radiologically confirmed CHPF associated with RCDH. Demographic data, imaging, surgical strategy, and outcomes were analyzed. Patients were stratified according to whether surgical separation of the fusion was performed (CHPF-S) or not (CHPF-NS). Results Forty-three patients were included (26 CHPF-S and 17 CHPF-NS). Prenatal diagnosis of RCDH occurred in 20.9% of cases, while most diagnoses were made postnatally. Imaging findings suggestive of CHPF were identified preoperatively in a minority of patients, with computed tomography angiography providing additional information regarding vascular anatomy in selected cases. Baseline demographic characteristics, gestational age, birth weight, and CDH defect distribution were comparable between groups. The age at surgical repair differed, however not significantly, with earlier intervention in the CHPF-S group (9.0 ± 15.8 vs 17.9 ± 24.2 days, p=0.099). Complete parenchymal fusion was more frequently observed in the CHPF-NS group, whereas partial fusion was more common in the CHPF-S group. Pulmonary hypertension occurred in 55.8% of patients and extracorporeal life support was required in 7.0%. Overall mortality was 27.9%, including 7 deaths in the CHPF-NS group and 5 in the CHPF-S group (41.2% vs 19.2%, p=0.117), predominantly related to severe pulmonary hypertension. title: Utilizing light energy transformation in nanostructures for targeted diagnostic and therapeutic applications.
abstract: Theranostics, a combination of therapy and diagnostics, represents a paradigm change in precision medicine with the ability to monitor diseases in real time and deliver targeted treatment. Nanomaterials are state-of-the-art technology for photo-energy conversion-based therapeutic action and diagnostic imaging; note the remarkable temporal and spatial precision that uses light as a driving force. This review highlights recent advances in the design and application of such nanomaterials for converting light into demand responses via mechanisms including photoluminescence (PL), photothermal conversion for photothermal therapy (PTT), photoacoustic imaging (PAI), photoelectric effect, SERS-based detection, and photodynamic therapy (PDT). Such light-activated systems are versatile platforms for the treatment of various diseases like arthritis, cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and retinal degeneration. By integrating multiple therapeutic and diagnostic modalities into a single nanoscale system, photoactive nanomaterials hold the potential to achieve enhanced treatment efficacy with minimal side effects. However, rapid advances are still hindered by challenges related to maximizing tissue penetration and biocompatibility, as well as activation in physiological settings. Nevertheless, the synergy of light-based science and nanotechnology is enabling next-generation precision theranostics and dynamic tools for personalized medicine for physicians. For these intelligent nanoplatforms to reach their full potential in practical healthcare applications, more interdisciplinary research and clinical translation are required.

title: Association Between Glenohumeral Bony Morphology and Anterior Shoulder Instability: An Advanced Three-Dimensional Analysis.
abstract: Background Glenohumeral bony morphology plays an important role in anterior shoulder instability (ASI), but the specific acquired and constitutional anatomical features associated with ASI remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to quantitatively evaluate and compare glenohumeral bony morphological characteristics between patients with ASI and controls using three-dimensional (3D) computed tomography (CT) imaging analysis. Methods A total of 210 participants were included, comprising 105 patients with unilateral ASI and at least one recurrence and 105 controls. Bilateral shoulder CT scans were obtained for the ASI group, whereas unilateral CT scans were obtained for the control group. The following parameters were measured on 3D models: glenoid index (GI), glenoid version angle, glenoid inclination angle, glenoid depth, humeral head containment angle, and the humeral head-to-glenoid diameter ratio. Within-patient comparisons were performed between affected and contralateral unaffected shoulders, and the contralateral unaffected shoulders were further compared with control shoulders. Sex-based subgroup analyses were also performed. Results The affected shoulders had a greater GI than the contralateral unaffected shoulders, with a mean paired difference of 0.19 (95% CI, 0.16-0.23; Holm-adjusted P < 0.001). The humeral head containment angle was nominally smaller on the affected side, but the difference did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons (raw P = 0.013; Holm-adjusted P = 0.067). Compared with control shoulders, the contralateral unaffected shoulders demonstrated a greater GI (1.39 ± 0.11 vs. 1.32 ± 0.10; mean difference, 0.07; 95% CI, 0.04-0.09; Holm-adjusted P < 0.001) and reduced glenoid depth (2.9 ± 0.8 mm vs. 3.6 ± 0.9 mm; Holm-adjusted P < 0.001). No significant differences were observed in the remaining morphological parameters after Holm correction. In the exploratory sex-stratified analyses, greater GI and reduced glenoid depth remained significant among male participants, whereas no parameter differed significantly among female participants after correction for multiple comparisons. Conclusion ASI was associated with distinct glenohumeral bony morphological characteristics on 3D analysis. A greater glenoid index and reduced glenoid depth were the most consistent features, including in the contralateral unaffected shoulders of patients with ASI, suggesting a possible anatomical association. Level of evidence Level III, Cross-Sectional Design, Prognosis Study.

title: Proceedings from the 2025 International Consensus Meeting on Orthopedic Infections: the definition of Shoulder Periprosthetic Joint infection.
abstract: Background Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) remains one of the greatest diagnostic and treatment challenges facing shoulder surgeons and their patients. A definition for shoulder PJI was established by the 2018 International Consensus Meeting (ICM) on Orthopedic Infections, but the selection and weighting of its minor criteria relied largely on expert opinion. The purpose of this study was to present an updated, evidence-based definition of shoulder PJI generated by the 2025 ICM Shoulder Group. Methods The 2025 ICM Shoulder Group, an international panel of shoulder surgeons and infectious disease specialists, used a modified Delphi process informed by 86 systematic reviews and by a predictive statistical model derived from the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) Multicenter Revision Arthroplasty and PJI Group dataset to reconsider the 2018 ICM definition of shoulder PJI, including its major criteria, minor criteria, and diagnostic categories. Results The delegates voted to eliminate organism virulence from the definition and to retain gross intra-articular purulence and presence of a sinus tract as the two criteria defining Definite PJI. The Minor Criteria were revised to include erythema, unexpected wound drainage, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), elevated synovial neutrophil percentage, positive frozen section, radiographic humeral osteolysis, intraoperative humeral loosening, and positive culture, each statistically weighted using the predictive model. Non-definite PJI was categorized by summed minor criteria score as High likelihood (≥13 points), Moderate likelihood (7-12 points), Unknown (1-6 points), or No PJI (0 points). The final definition achieved unanimous delegate consensus (51 of 51 delegates; 100% agreement; super majority, strong consensus). Conclusions The 2025 ICM definition of shoulder PJI represents an evidence-informed evolution of the 2018 definition, combining statistical modeling of prospective multicenter data with structured expert consensus. The definition is expected to continue to evolve as further shoulder-specific data become available.

title: Preoperative Pseudoparesis Is Not Associated With Inferior Outcomes After Anterior Latissimus Dorsi and Teres Major Transfer for Irreparable Anterosuperior Rotator Cuff Tears: A Propensity Score-Matched Analysis.
abstract: Background The prognostic relevance of preoperative pseudoparesis after combined anterior latissimus dorsi and teres major transfer (aLDTM) for irreparable anterosuperior rotator cuff tears (IASRCTs) has not been examined in a matched comparison. We hypothesized that, after propensity score matching, final outcomes would not differ significantly between groups. Methods This retrospective comparative cohort study reviewed patients undergoing aLDTM for IASRCT between April 2015 and January 2024. Pseudoparesis was defined a priori as active forward elevation ≥45° and <90° with preserved passive elevation after local anesthetic injection and without neurologic deficit (n=57); active forward elevation ≥90° defined the comparator group (n=183). True pseudoparalysis (<45°) and advanced arthropathy (Hamada grade >2) were excluded. One-to-one propensity score matching on age, sex, body mass index, diabetes, hypertension, previous cuff repair, acromiohumeral distance (AHD), Hamada grade, intraoperative reparable infraspinatus tear, and fatty infiltration of the four rotator cuff muscles produced 57 pairs (all absolute standardized mean differences <0.10). Outcomes included clinical scores (VAS, ADLIR, Constant, UCLA, ASES), range of motion, strength, subscapularis-specific tests, and tendon integrity on 2-year postoperative MRI. Mean follow-up was 57.0 ± 20.0 months. Results Both groups improved in clinical scores, forward elevation, abduction, internal rotation, and most strength measures (all adjusted P < .001); external rotation range of motion did not change significantly. Final clinical scores, range of motion, and strength showed no significant between-group differences (all adjusted P ≥ .569). The pseudoparesis group showed larger gains in forward elevation (69° ± 26° vs 35° ± 28°, adjusted P < .001) and abduction (48° ± 29° vs 29° ± 27°, adjusted P = .007). Subscapularis-specific tests and AHD did not differ between groups. Retear on 2-year postoperative MRI occurred in 3/57 (5.3%) and 4/57 (7.0%) (adjusted P = 1.000). Conclusion In this propensity score-matched analysis, the pseudoparesis group had lower baseline elevation by definition, whereas final clinical, range-of-motion, strength, and structural outcomes did not differ between groups after aLDTM for IASRCT. These findings should not be extrapolated to true pseudoparalysis or advanced arthropathy.

title: Predictive Modeling of Clinically Apparent Shoulder Periprosthetic Joint Infection (PJI).
abstract: Introduction The first International Consensus Meeting (ICM) definition of shoulder periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) introduced a tiered framework of PJI categories based on weighting of minor criteria for those cases not having major criteria of Definite infection. The selection of minor criteria and weightings was based on expert opinion and limited available evidence. The purpose of this study was to use prospective, multicenter data to develop a predictive model for clinically apparent shoulder PJI to inform a more evidence-based understanding of minor criteria and PJI categories. Methods Prospective data were collected on 861 consecutive revision shoulder arthroplasty cases within the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) Revision Shoulder Arthroplasty and PJI Multicenter Research Group. Presence of a sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis and intra-articular purulence were identified as pathognomonic indicators of infection (major criteria) and used as the primary outcome for multivariable analysis. Logistic regression modeling was performed, with model specification guided by information criteria. Variable selection emphasized optimal model fit while balancing complexity, focusing on: (1) markers of host inflammatory response, (2) universally available and commonly utilized diagnostic tests, (3) minimizing the total number of variables, and (4) preserving model usability despite missing data. Results Among 861 cases, 97 shoulders (11%) met the outcome of interest (sinus tract or intra-articular purulence). The final model incorporated seven variables spanning clinical findings, laboratory values, imaging, intraoperative assessment, and microbiology. These variables were erythema, unexpected wound drainage, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP), radiographic humeral osteolysis, synovial neutrophils ≥70% or positive frozen section (≥5 polymorphonuclear cells in ≥5 high-powered fields), intraoperative humeral loosening, and ≥2 positive cultures with the same organism. The apparent concordance statistic in the development cohort was 0.90 (95% CI 0.87-0.94). A nomogram was subsequently developed to estimate the probability of PJI, defined by the presence of a sinus tract or intra-articular purulence. Conclusion Using prospective, multicenter data, this study proposes a seven-factor nomogram to estimate the probability of clinically apparent shoulder PJI. The model showed strong apparent discrimination for clinically apparent infection in the development cohort. External validation will be necessary to confirm performance, and consensus will be required to establish weighting and diagnostic thresholds for tiers of non-definite shoulder PJI.

title: The medial collapse sign is associated with cubitus varus after pediatric supracondylar humeral fracture fixation: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Background Cubitus varus deformity is a common complication following pediatric supracondylar humeral fractures and rarely remodels spontaneously. However, surgeons lack a reliable intraoperative radiographic sign that directly reflects inadequate medial column reduction. This study aimed to evaluate whether the medial collapse sign (MCS) on immediate postoperative anteroposterior radiographs is associated with postoperative cubitus varus. Methods A retrospective cohort study included pediatric patients who underwent surgical treatment for supracondylar humeral fractures consecutively between January 2016 and March 2024. Fifty-two patients treated with reduction and cross pinning and followed for at least 6 months were included. Patients were categorized according to the presence or absence of cubitus varus at final follow-up (n = 20 and n = 32, respectively), which was radiographically defined as a side-to-side carrying-angle difference ≥5° on standing anteroposterior radiographs. Univariable and multivariable analyses were performed using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Results Presence of the MCS was strongly associated with cubitus varus (OR 155.4, 95% CI 24.8-1965.5; Holm-adjusted P < .001). MCS remained associated after adjustment for medial cortical comminution (OR 47.5, 95% CI 6.6-590.4, Holm-adjusted P < .001). The large effect size should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited sample size. Sensitivity and specificity were 90.0% and 96.9%, respectively. Interobserver reliability was almost perfect (κ = 0.919). Conclusion The medial collapse sign is strongly associated with postoperative cubitus varus and may reflect inadequate medial column reduction. Recognition of the same medial cortical morphology on intraoperative fluoroscopy may prompt reassessment of alignment and reduction. Level of evidence Level III, Retrospective cohort comparison, prognosis study.
originalAbstract:
Background

Cubitus varus deformity is a common complication following pediatric supracondylar humeral fractures and rarely remodels spontaneously. However, surgeons lack a reliable intraoperative radiographic sign that directly reflects inadequate medial column reduction. This study aimed to evaluate whether the medial collapse sign (MCS) on immediate postoperative anteroposterior radiographs is associated with postoperative cubitus varus.

Methods

A retrospective cohort study included pediatric patients who underwent surgical treatment for supracondylar humeral fractures consecutively between January 2016 and March 2024. Fifty-two patients treated with reduction and cross pinning and followed for at least 6 months were included. Patients were categorized according to the presence or absence of cubitus varus at final follow-up (n = 20 and n = 32, respectively), which was radiographically defined as a side-to-side carrying-angle difference ≥5° on standing anteroposterior radiographs. Univariable and multivariable analyses were performed using Firth's penalized logistic regression.

Results

Presence of the MCS was strongly associated with cubitus varus (OR 155.4, 95% CI 24.8-1965.5; Holm-adjusted P < .001). MCS remained associated after adjustment for medial cortical comminution (OR 47.5, 95% CI 6.6-590.4, Holm-adjusted P < .001). The large effect size should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited sample size. Sensitivity and specificity were 90.0% and 96.9%, respectively. Interobserver reliability was almost perfect (κ = 0.919).

Conclusion

The medial collapse sign is strongly associated with postoperative cubitus varus and may reflect inadequate medial column reduction. Recognition of the same medial cortical morphology on intraoperative fluoroscopy may prompt reassessment of alignment and reduction.

Level of evidence

Level III, Retrospective cohort comparison, prognosis study.

title: Idiopathic Granulomatous Mastitis in Mexican Women: 11-Year Clinical, Imaging, and Pathology Review.
abstract: Introduction Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM) is a rare chronic inflammatory breast disease that mimics malignancy, often leading to delayed diagnosis and mismanagement. Data on IGM in Latin American populations are scarce. Materials and methods We conducted a retrospective study of 39 women diagnosed with IGM between 2013 and 2024 at a specialized breast center in Mexico. Clinical, radiological, pathological, and treatment data were extracted from records. All patients provided informed consent for participation in the study. Patient confidentiality was maintained throughout the study, and all data were analyzed in a deidentified manner. Results The mean age was 35 y; 91.9% were premenopausal and 79.5% had a history of pregnancy. Palpable mass (66.7%), pain (61.5%), and fistulas (33.3%) were common. Ultrasound revealed hypoechoic tubular lesions in 70.8%. Histology confirmed non-necrotizing granulomas in 92.3%, with frequent squamous metaplasia and plasmacytic infiltration. Corticosteroids were used in 94.9%; surgery in 5.1%. At 12 mo, 87.1% showed remission; 51.3% had residual breast deformity. Conclusions IGM in Mexican women presented with hallmark histological features but often at advanced stages. Early diagnosis is key to reducing long-term cosmetic sequelae.

title: Evaluation and Management of Adolescent Breast Masses: A Systematic Review From the American Pediatric Surgical Association Outcomes and Evidence-Based Practice Committee.
abstract: Intoduction The evaluation and management of breast masses in the adolescent population is not standardized with most guidance extrapolated from adult data. We sought to review existing literature to inform practice in this unique population when presenting with a breast mass. Methods A systematic review of English language articles published between 1993 and 2024 was conducted to address management of adolescent patients (age 13 to 18 y) with breast masses: 1) What characteristics of breast masses prompt intervention? 2) Which surveillance strategies should be implemented if a biopsy is not pursued? and 3) What is the prognostic value of Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) classification of breast masses in adolescent patients? Results Of 9600 manuscripts initially identified, 11 met the inclusion criteria. Reporting of biopsy modality (incisional versus excisional) and indications was inconsistent across studies. A biopsy was most commonly pursued in the setting of an enlarging mass, large lesion size (>5 cm), nipple discharge, patient anxiety, or family history. Ultrasound was the primary imaging modality used; no patients underwent magnetic resonance imaging or mammography. Surveillance strategies varied widely. Given the low incidence of malignancy in adolescent patients, available data suggest BI-RADS classification may have limited applicability and may not accurately stratify cancer risk in this population. Conclusions Current evidence does not demonstrate a standardized approach to the evaluation of breast masses in adolescent patients and provides limited guidance regarding nonoperative surveillance strategies. Current literature supports the use of ultrasonography as the imaging modality of choice for adolescent breast masses, but frequency of surveillance is not well-defined. Adult BI-RADS classification is likely not appropriate for adolescents and warrants further study.

title: Management of Brachial Plexus Neurogenic Tumors: A Retrospective Study of 25 Cases.
abstract: Introduction To investigate the clinical characteristics of cervical brachial plexus neurogenic tumors and enhance the diagnostic and therapeutic management of this condition. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on the clinical data of 25 patients diagnosed with brachial plexus neurogenic tumors who were treated at a tertiary teaching hospital between January 2019 and December 2024. Clinical manifestations, treatment strategies, and follow-up outcomes were systematically summarized. Results A total of 25 patients were included, treated across multiple departments: otorhinolaryngology-head and neck surgery, neurosurgery, orthopedics, thyroid surgery, and vascular surgery. There were 13 male and 12 female patients, aged 16-76 y, with a disease duration ranging from 1 wk to 2 y, defined as the interval from symptom onset to initial clinical evaluation. The primary presenting symptom was a neck root mass in 21 patients, among whom seven experienced ipsilateral upper limb numbness, soreness, or electric shock-like pain upon palpation and four reported sensory disturbances in the upper extremity or shoulder-back pain. All patients underwent cervical contrast-enhanced computed tomography, and 18 additionally received 3.0 T magnetic resonance imaging. Preoperative ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration cytology was performed in all cases, revealing spindle cell tumors with morphological features suggestive of schwannoma. Of the 25 patients, 23 underwent surgical resection, while two with small tumors (<2 cm), no neurological symptoms, and cytologically benign findings opted for conservative management with close observation. Surgical approaches included the anterior supraclavicular approach, the posterior cervical paravertebral approach, and clavicle-splitting (transclavicular) approach. Postoperative pathological examination confirmed benign schwannoma in 22 cases and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor in one case. Follow-up duration ranged from 12 to 60 mo. Transient postoperative neurological dysfunction occurred in five patients, manifesting as limited shoulder abduction, reduced wrist extensor strength, or limb numbness; all deficits resolved within 6 mo following structured rehabilitation programs. Conclusions Brachial plexus neurogenic tumors commonly present as a mass in the neck root, with a subset of cases accompanied by neurological symptoms. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are valuable modalities for tumor localization and qualitative characterization. Preoperative fine needle aspiration cytology enables a preliminary assessment of tumor histology. The selection of an appropriate surgical approach should be guided by tumor location and anatomical involvement. Intralesional enucleation is a key strategy for preserving neurological function, and when combined with microsurgical techniques and intraoperative nerve monitoring, even transient postoperative neurological deficits can be effectively managed through structured rehabilitation programs.

title: Histological Stages of Appendicitis Associated With Imaging Characteristics: A Computed Tomography and Ultrasound-Based Comparative Study.
abstract: Introduction Appendicitis diagnosis relies heavily on medical imaging procedure studies; however, a definite diagnosis is obtained through histological assessment. Understanding the imaging characteristics and their relation to various histological phases enhance the quality of treatment recommendations. This study analyzed imaging characteristics of acute appendicitis in relation to its histological severity. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted using data from a third-level hospital. Appendectomy specimens from patients with prior computed tomography (CT) scans or ultrasound (US) imaging were included. Histological stages were categorized into simple, suppurative, abscessed, and perforated phases, depending the presence of edema, vascular congestion, neutrophilic infiltrate into the muscular layer, microabscess formation, mucosal ulceration, purulent exudate, macroscopic pus, and perforation with transmural inflammation. Imaging features as fat stranding, presence of free fluid, contrast enhancement within the appendix, appendicolith detection, reactive lymph nodes in the vicinity, appendix diameter itself, increased echogenicity, and detecting heightened perfusion via Doppler imaging were compared across these stages. Results Among 760 patients included (51.4% women, mean age 30.1 ± 5.3), 196 (25.8%) had CT scans and 361 (47.5%) had US. CT confirmed appendicitis in 59.2% of cases, yielded a negative result in 19.4%, and provided an inconclusive diagnosis in 21.4% of cases, commonly identifying fat stranding, free liquid, and contrast enhancement. US diagnosed appendicitis in 67.6% of cases, whereas 32.4% were reported as negative, with findings including increased echogenicity, Doppler perfusion, appendix identification, and free liquid in the right parietocolic gutter. All imaging characteristics were less prevalent in early stages compared to advanced stages, with a higher negativity rate in earlier stages. Conclusions Imaging findings are associated with the histopathological severity of appendicitis. Increased histopathological severity is associated with greater frequency of CT and US findings. These relations suggest the potential for managing appendicitis based on the histological phase suspected from imaging findings. Further research is warranted.

title: Understanding Colorectal Cancer Screening Gaps Among Adults Aged 45-49.
abstract: Introduction The United States Preventative Task Force recommends initiating colorectal cancer (CRC) screening at age 45, but screening rates among 45-49 y-olds has been lower than older age groups. Reasons for low screening rates among younger individuals are not clear. Methods Using Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data from 2022 to 2024, we investigated factors associated with CRC screening among adults aged 45-49; stratified analyses were conducted among the insured and uninsured. Among screened individuals, associations with undergoing endoscopy versus another screening modality were studied. We characterized preventative care behaviors including seeking primary care, time since last checkup, and completion of other age-appropriate cancer screening. Results Of 50,132 individuals, 21,566 (42.6%) underwent CRC screening. Those with primary care physicians had higher odds of screening (odds ratio = 1.71; 95% confidence interval = 1.47-1.98, ref: no primary care physician), but increasing time since one's last visit was associated with decreasing odds of screening at all time intervals (5+ y ago: odds ratio = 0.29; 95% confidence interval = 0.23-0.38, ref: <1 y). Lower income, rural residence, no insurance, and lower educational attainment were associated with lower odds of screening. CRC screening was completed in only 41.3% of women who had mammograms and 48% who were screened for cervical cancer. Conclusions Uptake of CRC screening lags in adults aged 45-49, with differences in socioeconomic factors and preventative care utilization. A majority of eligible but unscreened individuals accessed other age-appropriate cancer screening tests, directing focus to patient- and provider-specific factors as potential targets for intervention.

title: Development and Implementation of an Integrated Early Lung Cancer Detection Program in Ethiopia: A Scalable Framework for Resource-Constrained Settings.
abstract: Background In low- and middle-income countries(LMICs), barriers to early lung cancer(LC) detection extend beyond CT scanner availability to encompass participant identification pathways, digital management infrastructure, multidisciplinary coordination, and workforce capacity. Ethiopia's high tuberculosis burden, widespread biomass fuel exposure, and centralized oncology services create a distinct implementation environment. This report describes implementation and operational lessons from the first integrated LDCT-based early LC detection program in Ethiopia. Methods An integrated program was implemented at two tertiary referral centers in Addis Ababa between March 2024 and May 2026 using a phased strategy that deliberately prioritized infrastructure development before large-scale recruitment. Core components included an Ethiopian Thoracic Society-adapted ten-domain risk assessment framework incorporating locally relevant exposures, the ScreeningPLUS digital management platform, AI-assisted nodule detection, multidisciplinary review, smoking cessation counseling, and integration of tuberculosis and pulmonary medicine referral pathways into a unified detection infrastructure. Results A comprehensive early LC detection infrastructure was successfully established within existing healthcare systems. Key implementation challenges include equipment importation delays exceeding six months, digital infrastructure adaptation, variable patient identification practices, and multi-service workflow integration. The multi-pathway design proved essential: 73.9% of participants had never smoked, confirming that tobacco-based eligibility criteria alone would have excluded the majority of the target population. Following infrastructure maturation and focused outreach,enrollment increased substantially, supporting a phased approach in which operational readiness precedes large-scale recruitment. Conclusions Integrated early LC detection is achievable in resource-constrained settings when approached as a systems-level effort emphasizing phased infrastructure development, local adaptation, and pathway integration. These lessons provide a practical framework for LMIC implementation.

title: Trends in Retraction of Vascular and Interventional Radiology Research.
abstract: Retractions play an important role in maintaining the integrity of vascular and interventional radiology (VIR) literature, yet their causes and trends remain uncharacterized. A search of PubMed, Embase, and the Retraction Watch Database in April 2026 identified 142 retracted VIR articles published since 2000. The leading reasons for retraction were peer-review manipulation (21.1%), intrinsic study errors (14.8%), and submission duplication (11.3%), although 40% of notices did not specify a reason. Most articles originated from China (69%) and addressed interventional oncology (35.2%). Retractions rose sharply in recent years, with 64.7% occurring between 2023 and 2026. The median time from publication to retraction was 14.8 months, and most articles were retracted within two years. Journal impact factor ranged widely (0.60-78.50) and was not associated with time to retraction. These findings highlight peer-review manipulation as a prominent mechanism of misconduct and reaffirm the importance of rigorous peer review and editorial screening.

title: Synchronous Percutaneous Biopsy and Cryoablation for Suspicious Solitary Pulmonary Nodules.
abstract: To evaluate the feasibility, diagnostic yield, and safety of synchronous CT-guided core needle biopsy and cryoablation for highly suspicious 1-2 cm pulmonary nodules MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included 102 consecutive patients undergoing synchronous CT-guided core needle biopsy and cryoablation between August 2020 and October 2025. Treatment was undertaken on the basis of clinical and imaging suspicion before final histopathologic diagnosis. A cryoprobe was placed before biopsy to provide an intraprocedural landmark. Technical success, diagnostic yield, and adverse events were evaluated in all 102 patients; local tumor progression and overall survival were evaluated separately in 81 patients with pathology-confirmed NSCLC. Cryoablation technical success was 100% (102/102), and concurrent biopsy diagnostic yield was 87.3% (89/102). Biopsy identified 86 malignant diagnoses, including 81 NSCLCs. Mean nodule diameter was 1.52 ± 0.30 cm. Median follow-up in the NSCLC cohort was 34.5 months (IQR, 18.4-49.4 months). The cumulative incidence of recorded local tumor progression was 8.8% at both 1 and 3 years, and overall survival was 100% and 90.8%, respectively. Pneumothorax requiring chest tube drainage occurred in 20.6% (21/102), and no procedure-related deaths were reported. The synchronous biopsy and cryoablation approach was technically feasible and provided a specific histopathologic diagnosis in 87.3% of selected patients with highly suspicious 1.0-2.0-cm pulmonary nodules. Among patients with pathology-confirmed NSCLC, local-control outcomes were within the range reported in similar cryoablation-only series.

title: Pediatric Laryngeal Tumors: A Systematic Review of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms.
abstract: Background Pediatric laryngeal tumors are exceptionally rare and encompass a heterogeneous spectrum of benign and malignant neoplasms. Evidence remains largely limited to case reports and small case series. Objective To systematically characterize the histopathology, clinical presentation, treatment, recurrence, and outcomes of benign and malignant laryngeal tumors in children. Methods A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, ScienceDirect, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from January 2000 to July 2026 involving patients aged ≤18 years with histologically confirmed primary laryngeal tumors. Results Eighty-six studies were included. Among 52 patients with benign tumors, granular cell tumor was the most frequent diagnosis, followed by neurofibroma and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor. Hoarseness was the predominant symptom, and surgery, particularly endoscopic resection, was the principal treatment. Recurrence occurred in 7/44 patients (15.9%) with available outcome data. Among 69 patients with malignant or intermediate tumors, squamous cell carcinoma predominated, followed by sarcomas and lymphomas. Treatment included surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy according to histology and disease extent. Total laryngectomy was performed in nine patients, and 12 deaths were reported. Conclusions Pediatric laryngeal tumors are rare, but should be considered in children with persistent or progressive hoarseness, dyspnea, dysphagia, or other unexplained upper airway symptoms. Granular cell tumor and neurofibroma were the predominant benign lesions, whereas squamous cell carcinoma was the most frequently reported malignant neoplasm. Given the rarity of these tumors and the current reliance on case-based evidence, the establishment of international multicenter registries is warranted to generate higher-quality data and inform standardized diagnostic and therapeutic algorithms for pediatric laryngeal neoplasms.

title: Association of Completion Imaging Modalities and Carotid Endarterectomy Outcomes in the Vascular Quality Initiative.
abstract: Objective Completion imaging after carotid endarterectomy (CEA) confirms technical success and identifies defects requiring correction. However, the comparative effectiveness of imaging modalities in detecting clinically significant problems remains unclear. This study evaluated completion imaging patterns, intraoperative re-exploration as a surrogate for detection efficacy, and associated postoperative outcomes. Methods CEAs performed between 2012-2024 in the VQI were analyzed. Completion imaging was categorized as none, Doppler, duplex ultrasound, or angiography. Intraoperative re-exploration rates were compared across modalities to assess detection of technical defects requiring revision. Postoperative outcomes were analyzed among patients who required re-exploration. Inverse probability weighted (IPW) logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios. Temporal trends were also analyzed. Results Among 208,786 CEAs, 24% had no completion imaging, 48% used Doppler, 24% duplex, and 4% angiography. Angiography had the highest intraoperative re-exploration rate (none 0.9%, doppler 0.9%, duplex 2.3%, angiography 3.6%; p<0.001). Among the 2,723 patients who required re-exploration, postoperative stroke occurred in 8.3% with no imaging, 12.5% with doppler, 3.7% with duplex, and 22.5% with angiography (p<0.001). In IPW-adjusted analyses, intraoperative duplex was associated with significant reduction in postoperative stroke compared to: no imaging (aOR 0.43, 95%CI 0.27-0.69), doppler (aOR 0.28, 95%CI 0.19-0.40), and angiography (aOR 0.13, 95%CI 0.09-0.20), all p<0.001. Overall, Angiography had the worst stroke outcomes. Doppler and angiography performed worse than duplex across additional endpoints, including ipsilateral stroke, TIA, any neurological event, return to OR, and 30-day mortality. Despite the stronger safety profile of duplex, it remains underused, as most CEAs performed in the last 15 years have utilized doppler or no imaging. Conclusions Re-exploration and stroke outcomes after completion imaging reflect each modality's safety and efficacy in detecting significant technical defects. Duplex ultrasound demonstrated the lowest stroke rates and overall complications compared with angiography, doppler, and no imaging, suggesting its superior efficacy and safety. Doppler showed intermediate performance, while angiography carried the highest risk among patients who required re-exploration. Despite strong evidence favoring duplex, the majority of surgeons performing CEAs still rely on doppler or omit any completion imaging. Greater use of duplex ultrasound and incorporation of intraoperative duplex assessment into vascular training may improve intraoperative assessment, although further prospective evaluation is warranted.

title: Vascular Surgery is Overrepresented by Multiple Medical Societies Compared to its Peers.
abstract: Medical societies play an important role in representing physicians and their interests. Our objective was to compare the number, size, and fiscal strength of vascular societies compared to other cardiovascular specialties. All information was found via a systematic Internet search and with publicly available data (i.e. www.aamc.org). Medical societies representing vascular surgery (VS), cardiology (CARD), cardiothoracic surgery (CTS), and interventional radiology (IR) in the United States were compared. Board-certified physicians (www.abms.org) and publicly available financial information were tabulated (www.ProPublica.org). Board-certified vascular surgeons (n=4464) can choose to join 30 VS societies (4 national, 10 regional, 12 city/state, 4 other). In comparison, 12 societies (2 national) represent CTS (n=5869) and 16 (1 national) represent IR (n=4032) physicians. Cardiologists (n=22843) are represented by 14 (5 national) societies and an additional 27 chapters of a parent national society. The available number of vascular surgeons per national society is markedly lower than comparative specialties. Vascular societies generated $23M in revenue compared to $52M for CTS, $6M for IR, and $1.03B for CARD. CARD societies have 93% of total revenue for these four specialties and 52 times the revenues compared to VS societies. Compared to similar specialties, VS has few surgeons, yet a high number of medical societies. This segmentation may dilute the educational, governmental, societal, and patient advocacy impact of VS compared to its peers.

title: Fingerprinting the polycystic kidney: radiomics of the noncystic parenchyma for earlier ADPKD detection.
abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease risk stratification relies on total kidney volume, a validated marker of cyst burden and progression. Kremer et al.'s pilot study used rapid breath-hold magnetic resonance fingerprinting with radiomics to evaluate noncystic renal parenchyma in children and young adults. Quantitative T1/T2 texture features distinguished autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease from controls independently of total kidney volume, cyst fraction, age, or body size, suggesting early tissue changes. Small, cross-sectional, unmatched data require longitudinal validation of reproducibility, prognostic value, and clinical utility.

title: Development and validation of a deep learning-based automated Notch Width Index measurement system from anteroposterior knee radiographs.
abstract: Background The Notch Width Index (NWI), a radiographic marker of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury risk, is poorly reproducible when measured manually. We developed a fully automated NWI system combining deep learning segmentation with geometric analysis. Methods A segmentation model (U-Net++/EfficientNet-B5) and a YOLOv8 laterality classifier were trained on 384 public images. Thirty-three anteroposterior knee radiographs were each measured twice by each of two surgeons. The fully automated method (D) was compared with both surgeons, and two semi-automated methods (B, C) with Surgeon 1 to isolate each processing stage, using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and Bland-Altman analysis. The models were also applied without retraining to 500 external radiographs to assess feasibility and failure modes. Results Single-reading manual reliability was poor to moderate (ICC 0.475 and 0.562). The deterministic automated method agreed with both surgeons at ICC 0.525-0.756 (moderate to good); the semi-automated methods performed comparably (ICC 0.734 and 0.753). Segmentation reached a mean Dice coefficient of 0.975 ± 0.003, and processing was about 540 times faster than manual measurement. On the external dataset, segmentation degraded on osteoarthritic and low-quality images, so plausible values did not guarantee correct segmentation. Conclusion The method achieved moderate-to-good agreement with expert measurement while ensuring deterministic, examiner-independent reproducibility. Because it was never trained on surgeons' readings, this reflects reproduction of the geometric definition rather than overfitting. The principal barrier is segmentation under domain shift, not the algorithm; the method is best regarded as a reproducible standardization tool for routine anteroposterior views.
