title: Comparative accuracy of large language models and orthopaedic clinicians in knee osteoarthritis and tibial plateau fracture classification systems.
abstract: Background Multimodal large language models (LLMs) can process radiographic images, but their accuracy across orthopaedic classification systems requires further evaluation. This study compared the classification accuracy of four LLMs with that of orthopaedic surgeons and residents. Methods This cross-sectional study included 100 cases obtained from Radiopaedia, with 20 cases each for the Kellgren-Lawrence, Ahlback, Schatzker, Hohl and Moore, and AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association (AO/OTA) classifications. Each case comprised anteroposterior and lateral radiographs. Five orthopaedic surgeons, five residents, and four LLMs assessed the same cases, yielding 1400 classification assessments. Three independent senior orthopaedic surgeons established the consensus reference standard. AI evaluations were conducted in April 2026 using a standardized Turkish-language prompt, without classification definitions or examples. Only the first response was recorded. Analyses were descriptive because paired case-level classifications were unavailable. Results Overall accuracy was 91.2% (456/500) for orthopaedic surgeons, 70.2% (351/500) for residents, and 51.0% (204/400) for LLMs. LLM accuracy was 70.0% for Kellgren-Lawrence, 68.8% for Ahlback, 67.5% for AO/OTA, 28.8% for Hohl and Moore, and 20.0% for Schatzker. Model-specific accuracy was 58.0% for Claude Opus 4.1, 57.0% for GPT-5.5, 45.0% for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 44.0% for DeepSeek-VL2. Orthopaedic surgeons achieved the highest observed accuracy across all five classification systems. Conclusion LLM classification accuracy varied across systems and was lower overall than that of orthopaedic surgeons and residents. These findings are limited to the selected educational dataset and evaluation conditions. They do not establish educational or clinical utility; validation in larger, representative datasets is required.

title: Artificial intelligence-supported diabetic retinopathy screening in Tanzania: a randomised controlled trial.
abstract: Background Non-attendance after referral from screening is one of the major challenges for diabetic retinopathy screening programmes in Africa. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for the identification of diabetic retinopathy can provide point-of-screening results and therefore enable immediate counselling. We aimed to investigate whether AI-supported diabetic retinopathy screening, with a point-of-screening result and face-to-face counselling, increased the proportion of people with true referable diabetic retinopathy who attended the central ophthalmology referral clinic when compared with standard diabetic retinopathy screening with deferred human grading and telephone counselling. Methods This two-arm, parallel-group, individually randomised controlled trial was conducted at non-communicable disease or diabetic clinics in 24 hospitals in the Kilimanjaro and Arusha regions of Tanzania. Eligible participants (aged ≥18 years) had diabetes and attended diabetic retinopathy screening. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either AI-supported diabetic retinopathy screening with a point-of-screening result and face-to-face counselling (the AI-intervention group) or standard-of-care diabetic retinopathy screening with deferred human retinal image assessment and telephone counselling (the standard-of-care group). Participants had retinal photographs taken of both eyes. Images from the AI-intervention group were submitted to the AI software, and these participants were given their screening result (non-referable, referable, or ungradable) plus face-to-face counselling before leaving the photography room, with a referral to the central ophthalmology clinic if the AI output was referable or ungradable. Participants in the standard-of-care group received their screening result, along with appropriate counselling, by telephone a few weeks later. The primary outcome was attendance at the central ophthalmology clinic within 8 weeks of screening among participants classified by masked UK-certified graders as having true referable diabetic retinopathy. This trial was registered with the ISRCTN Registry, ISRCTN18317152, and is complete. Findings Between March 8, 2023, and Aug 31, 2024, 2439 participants were assessed for eligibility and 2378 were enrolled, of whom 1192 were randomly assigned to the AI-intervention group and 1186 to the standard-of-care group. 904 participants had true referable diabetic retinopathy, comprising 437 in the AI-intervention group and 467 in the standard-of-care group. Of the participants in the AI-intervention group, 157 (35·9%) of 437 attended the central ophthalmology clinic within 8 weeks, compared with 85 (18·2%) of 467 in the standard-of-care group, an absolute difference of 17·7 percentage points (95% CI 12·0-23·4; odds ratio 2·52 [95% CI 1·86-3·42]; p<0·0001). Interpretation AI-supported screening, with a point-of-screening result and face-to-face counselling, increased the proportion of people with true referable diabetic retinopathy that attended the central ophthalmology clinic after screening compared with the standard of care in Tanzania. Such AI-enabled screening pathways have the potential to improve diabetic retinopathy screening programmes in Africa. originalAbstract:
Background

Non-attendance after referral from screening is one of the major challenges for diabetic retinopathy screening programmes in Africa. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for the identification of diabetic retinopathy can provide point-of-screening results and therefore enable immediate counselling. We aimed to investigate whether AI-supported diabetic retinopathy screening, with a point-of-screening result and face-to-face counselling, increased the proportion of people with true referable diabetic retinopathy who attended the central ophthalmology referral clinic when compared with standard diabetic retinopathy screening with deferred human grading and telephone counselling.

Methods

This two-arm, parallel-group, individually randomised controlled trial was conducted at non-communicable disease or diabetic clinics in 24 hospitals in the Kilimanjaro and Arusha regions of Tanzania. Eligible participants (aged ≥18 years) had diabetes and attended diabetic retinopathy screening. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either AI-supported diabetic retinopathy screening with a point-of-screening result and face-to-face counselling (the AI-intervention group) or standard-of-care diabetic retinopathy screening with deferred human retinal image assessment and telephone counselling (the standard-of-care group). Participants had retinal photographs taken of both eyes. Images from the AI-intervention group were submitted to the AI software, and these participants were given their screening result (non-referable, referable, or ungradable) plus face-to-face counselling before leaving the photography room, with a referral to the central ophthalmology clinic if the AI output was referable or ungradable. Participants in the standard-of-care group received their screening result, along with appropriate counselling, by telephone a few weeks later. The primary outcome was attendance at the central ophthalmology clinic within 8 weeks of screening among participants classified by masked UK-certified graders as having true referable diabetic retinopathy. This trial was registered with the ISRCTN Registry, ISRCTN18317152, and is complete.

Findings

Between March 8, 2023, and Aug 31, 2024, 2439 participants were assessed for eligibility and 2378 were enrolled, of whom 1192 were randomly assigned to the AI-intervention group and 1186 to the standard-of-care group. 904 participants had true referable diabetic retinopathy, comprising 437 in the AI-intervention group and 467 in the standard-of-care group. Of the participants in the AI-intervention group, 157 (35·9%) of 437 attended the central ophthalmology clinic within 8 weeks, compared with 85 (18·2%) of 467 in the standard-of-care group, an absolute difference of 17·7 percentage points (95% CI 12·0-23·4; odds ratio 2·52 [95% CI 1·86-3·42]; p<0·0001).

Interpretation

AI-supported screening, with a point-of-screening result and face-to-face counselling, increased the proportion of people with true referable diabetic retinopathy that attended the central ophthalmology clinic after screening compared with the standard of care in Tanzania. Such AI-enabled screening pathways have the potential to improve diabetic retinopathy screening programmes in Africa.

title: Symptom-agnostic endpoints in tuberculosis vaccine efficacy trials.
abstract: Tuberculosis vaccine prevention-of-disease efficacy trials traditionally rely on symptom-triggered case detection. This approach captures only a subset of bacteriologically confirmed disease and can miss cases that occur between scheduled trial visits or outside trial procedures, slowing endpoint accrual and complicating interpretation of results. At the same time, the diagnostic landscape for tuberculosis is changing rapidly. Advances, including near point-of-care (NPOC) molecular assays using sputum and non-sputum specimens, portable chest radiography with computer-aided detection, and digital tools for decentralised monitoring, now make symptom-agnostic screening strategies increasingly feasible in large clinical trials. A 2026 WHO policy recommending the use of NPOC molecular diagnostics for tuberculosis further highlights the relevance of these approaches. In this Health Policy paper, we outlined a framework for integrating symptom-agnostic screening into tuberculosis vaccine efficacy trials and reviewed emerging diagnostic technologies that could enable this transition. Using parameters informed by the placebo arm of the M72/AS01 E phase 2b trial, we present a worked example illustrating a possible effect on endpoint detection and case-verification burden. In this illustrative scenario, an NPOC-based symptom-agnostic screening strategy was estimated to increase detection of bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis endpoints by approximately 1·4-fold, as compared with that by symptom-based screening alone, although this finding should not be interpreted as a direct estimate of overall trial efficiency. Realising these benefits will require analytical validation of diagnostic tools, clinical qualification for trial use, and early alignment with regulators and policy bodies. If evaluated through staged evidence generation and implemented with stringent confirmation algorithms, then symptom-agnostic screening could support more interpretable assessments of vaccine impact across the bacteriological spectrum of tuberculosis disease while preserving endpoint specificity.

title: Lung cancer associated with cystic airspaces (LCCA): A comprehensive literature review undertaken as part of the British thoracic oncology group (BTOG) work programme.
abstract: Lung cancer associated with cystic airspaces (LCCA) is an increasingly recognised yet under-characterised presentation of non-small cell lung cancer, accounting for approximately 1-4% of cases. Despite growing awareness driven by thin-section computed tomography and lung cancer screening, LCCA remains absent from major international guidelines and classifications, including those of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer, and the World Health Organization. This narrative review synthesises the available evidence to define LCCA as a distinct clinico-radiological entity and to inform future guideline development. LCCA presents heterogeneously, with thin- or thick walled cysts, unilocular or multiloculated morphology, and variable solid components, frequently mimicking benign cysts, bullae, or emphysema. Such ambiguity contributes to diagnostic delay; in the NELSON screening trial, LCCA accounted for 22.7% of missed or delayed diagnoses. Several radiological classifications, notably that of Mascalchi, aid description and risk stratification. Conventional staging is problematic, as measurement of the solid component alone may underestimate true tumour extent, while fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography carries a high false-negative rate. Tissue sampling is similarly complicated by low diagnostic yield and false negative results, underscoring the importance of multidisciplinary team discussion. The natural history follows a stepwise progression from thin-walled cyst to wall thickening, mural nodularity, and invasive disease, with prognosis determined principally by stage, although mural nodularity and increasing solid components confer higher recurrence risk. Treatment broadly mirrors that of solid lung tumours; current guidance advocates targeting the whole cystic lesion for radical therapy rather than the solid component alone, with systemic anticancer therapy appropriate in advanced or multifocal disease. Much current practice is extrapolated from part-solid tumours; consensus on Powered by Editorial Manager® and ProduXion Manager® from Aries Systems Corporation terminology, classification, and staging, supported by prospective registry data, is required to optimise outcomes.

title: Multi-omics liquid biopsy for leptomeningeal metastases in lung cancer: from molecular mechanisms to precision diagnosis and treatment.
abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM), a serious complication of advanced lung cancer, poses significant challenges in both clinical diagnosis and treatment monitoring, and is associated with a poor prognosis. Conventional diagnostic methods include magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology; however, their sensitivity is limited, particularly in the early stages of the disease. Against this backdrop, liquid biopsy has emerged as a minimally invasive and practical approach for molecular assessment and longitudinal monitoring of LM. Recent studies have reported that, in selected cohorts of patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and LM, CSF-derived circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) detects driver and resistance-associated alterations more frequently than paired plasma, while epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM)-based CSF circulating tumor cell (CTC) assays have reported sensitivities of 76%-100% and specificities of 84%-100%, compared with a first-lumbar-puncture sensitivity of 44%-67% for conventional CSF cytology. These performance estimates should be interpreted in the context of selected cohorts and heterogeneous reference frameworks. Furthermore, cerebrospinal fluid circulating tumor cell (CSF-CTC) burden holds prognostic value, with higher CTC levels associated with poorer survival outcomes. This review summarizes recent advances in liquid biopsy biomarkers including ctDNA, DNA methylation, microRNA (miRNA), proteins, and circulating tumor cells (CTCs), focusing on their applications in the diagnosis, treatment monitoring, and prognostic assessment of lung cancer-associated LM, and provides a comparative discussion of liquid biopsy based on plasma and cerebrospinal fluid specimens. It further explores the potential, current challenges, and directions for clinical translation of multi-omics integration in the personalized management of LM.

title: Serum extracellular vesicle-associated SNORD54 adds diagnostic information to CEA and CYFRA21-1 in non-small cell lung cancer: a case-control development study.
abstract: Background Blood-based biomarkers that complement established serum markers may improve molecular classification of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). We evaluated whether SNORD54 and SNORD41 measured in a serum extracellular vesicle (EV)-enriched fraction provided incremental discrimination beyond carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and cytokeratin 19 fragment 21-1 (CYFRA21-1). Methods This single-center case-control biomarker-development study included serum samples from patients with histologically or cytologically confirmed NSCLC and contemporaneous healthy controls. Supporting expression evidence was assessed in paired lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma datasets and in 48 paired formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded NSCLC specimens. Serum analyses included gene-specific cohorts and a common complete-case cohort with SNORD54, SNORD41, CEA, and CYFRA21-1 measurements. Logistic regression models were compared using paired DeLong tests. Model parsimony, adjustment for age, sex, and smoking, locked Stage I-II and Stage I subgroup analyses, U6-normalization sensitivity analyses, and 2000-resample bootstrap internal validation were performed. Results The complete-case cohort comprised 98 patients with NSCLC and 79 healthy controls. Adding SNORD54 to CEA and CYFRA21-1 increased the AUC from 0.851(95% confidence interval [CI], 0.795-0.907) to 0.951 (95% CI, 0.920-0.982; ΔAUC, 0.100; 95% CI, 0.050-0.150; P < 0.001). At the development-derived cutoff, the three-marker model achieved 85.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity. SNORD41 did not improve the SNORD54-containing model (ΔAUC, 0.0003; P = 0.480; likelihood-ratio P = 0.953) and increased both Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. With coefficients and the cutoff fixed from the overall cohort, the three-marker model achieved AUCs of 0.904 (95% CI, 0.843-0.964) for Stage I-II disease and 0.882 (95% CI, 0.804-0.960) for Stage I disease. SNORD54 remained informative after adjustment for age, sex, and smoking. The optimism-corrected AUC was 0.948. U6 Ct values differed between diagnostic groups; associations of both snoRNAs with case status persisted in sensitivity models accounting for U6 Ct. Conclusions SNORD54 measured in a serum EV-enriched fraction provided incremental discrimination beyond CEA and CYFRA21-1 in this NSCLC case-control cohort. The parsimonious SNORD54 + CEA + CYFRA21-1 model retained discrimination in locked early-stage subgroup analyses and showed limited apparent optimism after bootstrap correction. Independent validation in cohorts that include benign pulmonary nodules and other relevant lung diseases, together with standardized EV processing and validated RNA normalization, will define the clinical transportability of this three-marker panel.

title: Spatial Proteomics Uncovers Immune Cell Neighborhoods and Tumor-Immune Interfaces in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies with dismal prognosis and limited treatment options. The complex interplay between tumor cells and their microenvironment contributes significantly to treatment resistance, yet technological challenges have hindered comprehensive spatial characterization of immune components in PDAC tissues. Here, we performed high-dimensional spatial proteomics using multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBI) to quantify 27 protein markers across tissues from twelve treatment-naïve PDAC patients who subsequently underwent adjuvant chemotherapy. We achieved confident single-cell phenotypic mapping of the PDAC ecosystem through deep-learning based segmentation and expert-validated phenotypic annotation. Our analysis revealed significant enrichment of immunosuppressive myeloid populations in patients who eventually experienced disease relapse. Conversely, cytotoxic CD8+ T cells were depleted in these relapse-prone tumors. Using spatial probabilistic topic modeling, we identified eight distinct cellular neighborhoods with unique compositions and functional states, including the enrichment of an immune suppressive neighborhood in relapsed patients. While immunogenic cell neighborhoods were present in both patient populations, analysis of the tumor-immune neighborhoods demonstrated altered functional marker expression profiles, suggesting distinct immune activation in patients who relapsed versus those who did not. Our findings provide a high-resolution spatial atlas of the PDAC immune landscape and identify prognostic microenvironmental signatures that may inform the development of novel immunotherapeutic strategies for this recalcitrant disease.

title: Longitudinal Spatial Proteomics of Breast Cancer Reveals Recurrent Phenotypic Clone States and Temporal Trajectories.
abstract: Intratumoral heterogeneity complicates treatment response and relapse in breast cancer, yet longitudinal spatial studies that preserve tissue architecture remain scarce. Here we integrated matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) with region-resolved dia-PASEF proteomics to map recurrent spatial proteomic programs across serial breast cancer specimens. Forty-seven formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissues from 16 patients were analyzed, encompassing primary tumors, relapses, and metastatic lesions. Cohort-level MSI co-segmentation provided a common reference atlas of 10 recurrent spectral states, and pathologist-guided microextraction of 201 tumor-containing regions yielded 402 extraction-level proteomic datasets. Because no genomic lineage tracing was performed, we use the term recurrent spatial proteomic state to denote a spatially localized, recurrent proteomic phenotype and not a genetically proven clone. Recurrent spatial proteomic states were observed across hormone receptor-positive, HER2-positive, and hormone receptor-negative/HER2-low disease, indicating that similar spatial programs can recur across clinical subtypes. Longitudinal analyses of representative patients showed marked state turnover during therapy, with persistence of some states and emergence of others at relapse or metastatic progression. Feature-ranking models identified proteins associated with each spatial state and with clinical sampling stage, while exploratory enrichment analyses suggested broad shifts from earlier immune- and hormone-associated programs toward later inflammatory, invasive, and stress-adapted programs. Because the cohort is modest, repeated regions from the same patient are not independent, and no external validation cohort was available, all predictive and therapeutic interpretations are presented as hypothesis-generating. These data provide a spatial proteomic atlas of recurrent spatial proteomic states in breast cancer and a framework for studying constrained, but not deterministic, evolutionary trajectories during progression and treatment.

title: Advanced neuroimaging in rare diseases: The paradigm of quantification in the era of personalized medicine.
abstract: Rare diseases frequently involve the central nervous system, posing significant diagnostic and monitoring challenges. Recent advances in Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and neuroradiology have expanded the tools available for RD assessment, encompassing improvements in image acquisition, postprocessing techniques, and functional MRI sequences. Advanced postprocessing methods allow radiologists to derive additional quantitative information from conventional morphological images, including the segmentation and volumetric analysis of brain structures such as gray matter. Functional MRI techniques, such as Diffusion Weighted Imaging, Perfusion Weighted Imaging, or Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy, further contribute objective metrics reflecting underlying pathophysiological processes, including water diffusion and tissue perfusion. Within the framework of personalized medicine, integrating these advanced neuroimaging approaches may improve diagnostic precision and support treatment monitoring, follow-up, and disease surveillance. This review highlights the application of advanced neuroimaging tools across a range of clinical scenarios relevant to rare diseases, including cranial and structural abnormalities, white matter disorders, tumor assessment, and vascular conditions.

title: A clinical evaluation of spiral 4DCT and intelligent 4DCT sequence scanning.
abstract: Accurate 4DCT imaging is essential for radiotherapy planning but is often degraded by breathing irregularities. Phantom studies show that intelligent four-dimensional computed tomography (Direct i4D) sequence scanning can significantly reduce artifacts related to breathing irregularity compared to traditional spiral 4DCT. Direct i4D is a sequence-based acquisition mode in which beam-on time is adapted in real time to an individual patient's breathing pattern to optimize projection data coverage. In this study, we compared Direct i4D and spiral 4DCT scan image quality between Direct i4D and spiral 4DCT in a paired design, with both scans acquired for the same patient during a single simulation session. Spiral 4DCT and Direct i4D scans from 33 patients with pre-identified irregular breathing patterns were collected retrospectively. Breathing irregularities included variations in amplitude, frequency, or both. Spiral 4DCT scans were used for motion evaluation, while the Direct i4D scans were acquired for treatment planning. To compare the internal target volume (ITV) on both 4DCT datasets, a radiation oncologist manually contoured all ITVs de novo. Residual sorting artifacts were visually evaluated and scored by a radiation oncologist and medical physicist on a scale of 1 to 5 (where higher scores indicate lower presence of artifacts and better image quality). Visual evaluation of 4DCT phases showed that 36% of spiral 4DCT and 3% of Direct i4D scans would require resimulation. Meanwhile, 18% and of spiral 4DCT and 27% of Direct i4D scans were artifact-free (p-value < 0.1). The ITV comparison between the 2 4DCT techniques revealed mean and standard deviation (STD) Dice similarity coefficients of 0.59 and 0.18, respectively. ITV mean CT value difference varies between 0.80 HU and 158.41 HU (Mean ± STD: 39.41HU ± 40.02 HU). Real-time adaptation of the scan time and rebinning by Direct i4D enhanced the image quality for individual 4DCT phases. Irregular breathing patterns can degrade spiral 4DCT image quality and tumor delineation. The novel Direct i4D technique provides a reliable solution to reduce such artifacts significantly.

title: Mind the Gap: Continuous magnification sampling for pathology foundation models.
abstract: In histopathology, pathologists examine both tissue architecture at low magnification and fine-grained morphology at high magnification. Yet, the performance of pathology foundation models across magnifications and the effect of magnification sampling during training remain poorly understood. We model magnification sampling as a multi-source domain adaptation problem and develop a simple theoretical framework that reveals systematic trade-offs between sampling strategies. We show that the widely used discrete uniform sampling of magnifications (0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 mpp) leads to degradation at intermediate magnifications. We introduce continuous magnification sampling, which removes gaps in magnification coverage while preserving performance at standard scales. Further, we derive sampling distributions that optimize representation quality across magnification scales. To evaluate these strategies, we introduce two new benchmarks (TCGA-MS, BRACS-MS) with appropriate metrics. Our experiments show that continuous sampling can improve downstream task performance at intermediate magnifications, with gains of up to 4 percentage points in balanced classification accuracy, and that optimized distributions can further improve performance. Finally, we evaluate current histopathology foundation models, finding that magnification is a primary driver of performance variation across models. Our work paves the way towards future pathology foundation models that perform reliably across magnifications.

title: Mind the Gap: A survey of chronic wound datasets, methods, and clinical translation.
abstract: Chronic wounds, including diabetic foot ulcers, venous ulcers, arterial ulcers and pressure ulcers, represent a growing global health challenge with significant morbidity, mortality, and economic burden. Advancements in medical image analysis have shown promise in automating wound detection, segmentation, and measurement. However, translation of these research advances into clinical practice through mobile applications remains limited. This survey presents systematic analysis of the relationship between chronic wound datasets, deep learning methods, and mobile wound assessment applications. We analyse 20 datasets (14 public/partially public and 6 private), including iterative challenge datasets that extend image pool through synthetic augmentation. We review 50 deep learning methods spanning encoder-decoder architectures to self-supervised learning approaches, and evaluate 13 mobile applications (commercially deployed clinical tools and research prototypes). We examine the alignment between publicly available chronic wound datasets and the documented capabilities of mobile wound assessment mobile applications. Our analysis reveals critical misalignments between datasets, algorithms and mobile applications. Existing datasets are typically designed for algorithm benchmarking rather than clinical deployment, and therefore lack standardised acquisition protocols, scale calibration markers, depth information, detailed tissue composition annotations, and representation of diverse skin types. Conversely, reviewed mobile applications report capabilities, including automatic tissue classification, calibrated wound measurement and depth estimation, for which publicly available data is insufficient. We map documented dataset characteristics to capabilities reported among reviewed mobile applications, identify unresolved methodological challenges, and outline key priorities for the field. Based on these insights, we propose actionable recommendations for developing clinically translatable computer vision system for wound assessment. This survey is intended to serve as a reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to bridge the gap between medical imaging methodologies and practical demands of clinical wound care.

title: A self-navigated framework for motion detection and spoke-reordering musculoskeletal dynamic reconstruction in 3D radial MRI.
abstract: Motion remains a major challenge and active research focus in MRI, as both involuntary (e.g., head movement) and voluntary (e.g., joint motion) motion can degrade image quality or, alternatively, provide opportunities for dynamic assessment. Existing motion sensing approaches - such as external tracking or navigator sequences - often require additional hardware, increase SAR, or necessitate sequence modifications, thereby limiting clinical flexibility. In this work, we propose a self-navigated motion sensing framework for 3D radial MRI. Motion surrogates are first extracted directly from multi-coil k-space data. A sliding-window summation is then applied to enhance robustness, followed by a second principal component (PC2)-based strategy to derive a 1D motion-sensitive signal that reflects subject position over time. Beyond conventional head motion correction, we demonstrate the utility of the proposed framework in improving dynamic 4D MRI of the ankle and knee under both stepwise and continuous motion protocols. By reordering spokes based on motion-derived position rather than acquisition time, the method enables motion-resolved reconstructions with improved anatomical clarity. Overall, this approach facilitates efficient motion detection and supports broader adoption of motion-aware dynamic MRI. The source code of this framework is available at https://github.com/EricLin1993/SpEMSK.

title: A unified and domain-robust framework enables controllable multimodal brain MRI synthesis.
abstract: Multimodal magnetic resonance image (MRI) synthesis can shorten examinations, reduce cost, and furnish contrasts that are difficult or impossible to acquire, but current models remain hard to control and brittle to shifts in scanner, protocol, and pathology. We present a unified, domain-robust synthesis framework that modulates spatial carriers with physically informed, domain-stable statistical guidance. A balanced soft-plus-hard conditioning scheme enables a single model to perform diverse contrast mapping, while allowing smooth user adjustment of contrast weighting. Evaluated on 991 test subjects from five public and three private datasets spanning cross-dataset, cross-protocol, and related cross-pathology scenarios, our approach matches or outperforms advanced baselines for both in-domain synthesis and inference under unseen domains without finetuning. Clinician Turing test and downstream glioma grading experiments further indicate realistic appearance, preservation of pathology-relevant information, and potential practical value under clinically heterogeneous conditions. By jointly delivering controllability, robustness to real-world variability, and physically informed, domain-stable guidance within one architecture, this work advances MRI synthesis toward deployment in heterogeneous clinical environments.

title: Performance uncertainty in medical image analysis: A large-scale investigation of confidence intervals.
abstract: Performance uncertainty quantification is essential for reliable validation and eventual clinical translation of medical imaging artificial intelligence (AI). Confidence intervals (CIs) play a central role in this process by indicating how precise a reported performance estimate is. Yet, due to the limited amount of work examining CI behavior in medical imaging, the community remains largely unaware of how many diverse CI methods exist and how they behave in specific settings. The purpose of this study is to close this gap. To this end, we conducted a large-scale empirical analysis across a total of 24 segmentation and classification tasks, using 19 trained models per task group, a broad spectrum of commonly used performance metrics, multiple aggregation strategies, and several widely adopted CI methods. Reliability (coverage) and precision (width) of each CI method were estimated across all settings to characterize their dependence on study characteristics. Our analysis revealed five principal findings: (1) the sample size required for reliable CIs varies from a few dozens to several thousands of cases depending on study parameters; (2) CI behavior is strongly affected by the choice of performance metric; (3) aggregation strategy substantially influences the reliability of CIs, e.g. they require more observations for macro than for micro; (4) the machine learning problem (segmentation versus classification) modulates these effects; (5) different CI methods are not equally reliable and precise depending on the use case. Finally, we derived practical implications of this study in the form of a decision tree which shall prove useful to the community. This paves the way for future consensus guidelines on reporting performance uncertainty.

title: Streamline pathology foundation model by cross-magnification distillation.
abstract: Foundation models (FM) have transformed computational pathology but remain computationally prohibitive for clinical deployment due to their massive parameter counts and high-magnification processing requirements. Here, we introduce XMAG, a lightweight FM developed through cross-magnification distillation that transfers knowledge from a state-of-the-art 20x magnification teacher to an efficient 5x magnification student architecture. XMAG employs a compact backbone and operates entirely at 5x, requiring 11.3 times fewer patches per whole slide image (WSI) compared to existing approaches. Our novel distillation framework incorporates dual-level knowledge transfer, aligning both global image representations and local spatial features across magnification levels through carefully designed projection heads and spatial token mapping. We trained XMAG on 3.49 million images curated from publicly available datasets and evaluated performance across seven clinically relevant histopathology analysis tasks spanning multiple cancer types. Across four WSI-level classification tasks, XMAG achieved an average AUC within 1% of substantially larger foundation models while delivering up to 29.5-fold faster encoder-level processing, corresponding to an encoder throughput of 8.8 WSIs per minute in a controlled patch-encoding benchmark. We also found that performance differences remained task-dependent, with larger gaps observed for fine-grained tasks such as ISUP grading and patch-level phenotyping. We further explore end-to-end XMAG training as a direction for task-specific adaptation of the compact model. These results suggest that cross-magnification distillation is a promising strategy for developing efficient low-magnification pathology foundation models and may support more scalable WSI analysis in computationally constrained research and translational settings.

title: ConComp: Constraining and compensating latent representations for semi-supervised medical image segmentation.
abstract: Semi-supervised learning has significantly advanced medical image segmentation under limited annotation scenarios. However, existing semi-supervised medical image segmentation (SSMIS) methods based on consistency regularization and pseudo-labeling may be affected by internal covariate shift (ICS), which may disturb feature stability and reduce pseudo-label reliability during training. In this work, we investigate how ICS affects feature stability and pseudo-label reliability in SSMIS. Based on this analysis, we propose ConComp, a unified framework that mitigates ICS from a statistical perspective by introducing distribution-aware latent constraints and compensating for latent distribution discrepancies. Specifically, we introduce a Distribution-Aware Feature Constraint (DAFC) mechanism that derives distribution-aware latent constraints from unlabeled feature statistics and residually integrates them into labeled features, thereby reducing changes in their distributions during training. In addition, we propose a Latent Distribution Discrepancy Compensation (L2DC) mechanism that treats the discrepancy between labeled and unlabeled representations as an informative signal to guide feature fusion, thereby compensating for missing structural cues and improving generalization. Extensive experiments on three challenging SSMIS benchmarks, including BraTS2019, LiTS2017, and Pancreas-NIH, demonstrate that ConComp consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/1jayyang/ConComp.

title: Anatomical prior-guided implicit segmentation of challenging thin and tubular anatomical structures in CBCT images.
abstract: Medical image segmentation has achieved promising performance with deep learning approaches like nnU-Net. However, extremely precise segmentation of challenging topological structures, particularly thin anatomical structures, remains an unsolved problem. In digital dentistry, cortical bone in the mandible and maxillary regions and the inferior alveolar nerve (IAN) represent such thin structures and tubular topologies, where accurate segmentation from Cone-beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) scans is crucial for treatment planning. To address this challenge, we propose an anatomy-guided coarse-to-fine framework. After an initial coarse CNN-based stage, we apply an implicit refinement function to enhance segmentation, focusing on uncertain regions through point-wise selection. To guide this refinement, we leverage the Signed Distance Field (SDF) of teeth as an anatomical prior, exploiting their stable spatial relationship with the target structures. Extensive evaluations on challenging dental CBCT datasets, including both cortical bone and IAN segmentation, demonstrate our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods across metrics. In particular, it achieves over 30% improvements in distance error metrics (ASD and HD). These results validate its robustness and generalization for precise thin structure segmentation in dental CBCT images. Our code is available at https://github.com/ShanghaiTech-IMPACT/Anatomical-Prior-guided-Implicit-Segmentation-of-Thin-Anatomical-Structures-in-CBCT-image.

title: Learning discriminative prototypes via Variational Information Bottleneck for multimodal cancer survival prediction.
abstract: Survival prediction is critical in cancer research for forecasting patient outcomes and optimizing treatment strategies. While integrating histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) with genomic profiles holds promise for improved predictive accuracy, two major challenges persist: (1) the inherent low signal-to-noise ratio in gigapixel WSIs, where task-irrelevant background patches often dominate standard Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) bags, and (2) the instability of unsupervised prototype initialization (e.g., K-means), which frequently converges to non-informative morphological patterns. To address these challenges, we propose DP-VIB (Discriminative Prototypes via Variational Information Bottleneck), a hierarchical framework that leverages the information bottleneck principle to learn survival-relevant prototypes in a coarse-to-fine manner. Unlike traditional approaches, DP-VIB first employs a survival-supervised Global VIB Module to learn a discriminative latent representation, filtering out nuisance variations through an information bottleneck constraint. Subsequently, Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) priors derived from this purified latent representation serve as robust initializations for fine-grained patch-level prototypes, significantly enhancing convergence and semantic quality. Finally, we introduce a tri-branch Histology-Genomics(HG) encoder followed by a cross-modal fusion mechanism to deeply fuse these VIB-guided prototypes with genomic pathway embeddings, enabling analysis of model-derived prototype-pathway associations. Extensive validation on five TCGA cancer cohorts demonstrates that DP-VIB consistently outperforms strong baselines in Concordance Index (C-index), achieving superior robustness and accuracy in individualized survival prediction.

title: KAMP-Net: Knowledge-aligned Multi-modal Prompt-tuning Network for Prostate Cancer Diagnosis from bpMRI.
abstract: Bi-parametric magnetic resonance imaging (bpMRI) is widely used for non-invasive diagnosis of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). Although the Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) standardizes interpretation through structured diagnostic criteria, clinical assessment remains highly operator-dependent. Vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, offer a promising automated solution by leveraging the imaging-language coupling inherent in PI-RADS. However, existing VLM adaptation methods generally treat medical diagnosis as a generic image-to-label matching task. This conventional "label-driven" paradigm relies on superficial semantic correlations, fundamentally failing to capture the structured reasoning, anatomical context, and sequence prioritization defined by clinical guidelines like PI-RADS. To address this fundamental limitation, we propose KAMP-Net, a multi-modal prompt-tuning network that shifts the paradigm toward "knowledge-driven" learning. Our core algorithmic novelty lies in mathematically translating structured PI-RADS criteria directly into the network's computational graph. Specifically, rather than employing generic feature fusion and global alignment, KAMP-Net utilizes zone-aware modality routing to dynamically gate heterogeneous bpMRI sequences, and enforces a hierarchical vision-language alignment that structurally mirrors a radiologist's bottom-up diagnostic workflow. Experiments on a multi-center cohort comprising two public and one private datasets, plus an external private dataset, show that KAMP-Net delivers competitive performance in both patient-level diagnosis and lesion-level localization. Beyond standalone performance, we evaluated its clinical utility in an AI-assisted workflow. Notably, for challenging equivocal cases (PI-RADS = 3), this human-in-the-loop strategy successfully reduces false positives without risking missed diagnoses, demonstrating its strong potential as a reliable decision-support tool. Code is available at: https://github.com/IsYuchenYuan/KAMP-Net.

title: Distribution matching based personalized federated learning for multi-center, cross-modal liver image registration.
abstract: In clinical liver MRI, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) imaging are commonly used and complementary sequences, particularly for liver tumor diagnosis and assessment. Accurate registration between the two modalities facilitates subsequent quantitative analysis and multi-modal image-based evaluation. Although deep learning has achieved remarkable progress in image registration, considerable challenges remain in multi-parametric liver imaging, mainly due to substantial contrast differences, pronounced respiratory motion, limited single-center training data, and inter-center heterogeneity. This study proposes a cross-modal registration framework for liver DWI and DCE across multi-center datasets. First, a multi-task synthesis-registration network (SynReg) is introduced, which integrates image synthesis and registration within a unified architecture to reduce cross-modal appearance discrepancy and facilitate deformable registration. To further improve personalized learning under cross-center heterogeneity, we propose a personalized decentralized distribution matching (PDDM) framework with SynReg as the backbone. PDDM performs compatibility-aware selective collaboration by identifying compatible external training cases and constructing client-specific collaboration relationships. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distributions are used as a lightweight compatibility descriptor, while the synthesis components remain local and the registration network is selectively aggregated among compatible clients. The framework was evaluated on six datasets collected from five medical centers and acquired on MRI systems from three vendors under both low- and high-b-value settings. PDDM consistently achieved more favorable registration performance than single-center training and representative personalized federated learning methods, while remaining closely competitive with centralized pooled-data training. In comparisons with alternative matching strategies, PDDM showed the most consistently favorable overall performance across centers, b-value settings, and registration metrics. These findings support compatibility-aware selective collaboration as an effective strategy for personalized multi-center liver image registration. Code will be available at https://github.com/ZIC-skyzrc/PDDM-SynReg.

title: A latent ODE approach to full-cycle biventricular cardiac motion modeling from cine MRI.
abstract: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) captures rich spatiotemporal information about ventricular structure and motion, but conventional risk models use only a few image-derived indices from selected cardiac phases. We present a latent dynamical model that encodes bi-ventricular anatomy and full-cycle cine motion as a continuous latent trajectory, using heart-rate-aware neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) dynamics and a graph-based mesh autoencoder to reconstruct anatomically consistent 3D+t ventricular motion. A covariate-conditioned prior defines the expected end-diastolic latent state, and a Cox proportional hazards model tests whether deviations from this prior predict incident heart failure. We studied 72,386 UK Biobank participants without baseline cardiovascular disease, including 367 incident heart failure events. In a held-out evaluation subset, adding the latent score to refitted pooled cohort equations improved the stratified C-index from 0.704 to 0.785, compared with 0.764 for seven established cardiac markers. Compared with non-graph and non-ODE approaches, the proposed model gave the best trade-off between reconstruction fidelity, generative realism, and downstream prognostic performance. These results suggest that continuous full-cycle modeling of ventricular motion provides informative cardiac phenotypes beyond conventional CMR summaries, while external validation in more representative patient cohorts is required before clinical risk-prediction use.

title: Joint segmentation of pancreatic tumors and peripancreatic vessels via a clinical risk-aware uncertainty alignment framework.
abstract: Preoperative assessment of pancreatic cancer resectability critically relies on accurate joint segmentation of tumors and peripancreatic vessels from contrast-enhanced CT. However, beyond segmentation accuracy alone, effective decision support in practice further requires task-specific characterization of peri‑tumoral infiltration risk and topological discontinuity risk. To address this, we propose a clinical risk-aware uncertainty alignment framework that achieves reliable risk characterization while maintaining high segmentation accuracy. The framework is built upon a dual-decoder architecture with evidential deep learning for joint segmentation and uncertainty estimation. Two clinically grounded alignment strategies are further designed to transform this uncertainty into task-specific risk indicators. Specifically, an infiltration-aware boundary uncertainty alignment module is proposed, which synthesizes texture, spatial, and vascular proximity factors into an infiltration-inspired prior and uses its ordinal structure to guide alignment, yielding infiltration-risk-aware uncertainty from which infiltration-aware tumor boundaries are derived for downstream invasion analysis. A topology-aware discontinuity uncertainty alignment module is further designed, which uses skeleton-mismatch regions as a connectivity-related proxy and constrains uncertainty by a three-tier ordinal relation with region-weighted supervision, yielding discontinuity-risk-aware uncertainty and improved vessel connectivity. Multi-center validation on 1058 patients from five medical centers demonstrates favorable and stable cross-institutional performance, and downstream experiments explore the utility of the aligned uncertainty for tumor-vessel invasion analysis. Overall, this study couples accurate tumor and vessel delineation with clinically grounded risk characterization, with the potential to support tumor-vessel assessment in preoperative planning. Our source code will be released at https://github.com/SJTUBME-QianLab/CRUA-Net.

title: ROI-SSIM guided framework for 3D knee MRI reconstruction under artifact degradation.
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction is highly sensitive to undersampling and acquisition artifacts. Although deep learning-based approaches have significantly improved reconstruction quality, they are typically optimized using global fidelity metrics that may not fully reflect reconstruction quality within clinically important structures such as the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), meniscus, and articular cartilage. This study proposes a region-aware MRI reconstruction framework based on a Vision Transformer autoencoder (ViT-AE) guided by an ROI Structural Similarity (ROI-SSIM) loss. The method leverages fastMRI+ bounding-box annotations and incorporates a hybrid artifact simulation framework spanning k-space and image-domain degradations. Experiments on the fastMRI knee single-coil validation set (PD contrast, R=4) show that the proposed ViT-AE achieves reconstruction fidelity competitive with established baselines (SSIM 0.823, Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) 32.4dB , Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) 0.0147), while ROI-SSIM supervision improves structural fidelity within clinically relevant annotated regions. Under mixed artifact conditions, region-specific structural similarity decreased by only 2.9% , compared with a 6.8% decrease in global SSIM. These findings support the use of region-aware supervision for artifact-robust MRI reconstruction. Overall, the method presented in this paper:Introduces ROI-SSIM supervision for region-aware MRI reconstruction.Develops a hybrid artifact simulation framework spanning k-space and image-domain degradations.Demonstrates improved anatomical preservation under artifact conditions.

title: Ex vivo fluorescence confocal microscopy for real-time margin assessment of nonmelanoma skin cancer in Mohs surgery: A prospective interventional study.
abstract: New-generation ex vivo fluorescence confocal microscopy (EVFCM) generates hematoxylin-eosin-like images directly comparable to conventional histopathology. Its interobserver performance with a novel acquisition mode in non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC) micrographically controlled surgery remains to be defined. In this prospective interventional study, 42 tumors from 39 patients undergoing Mohs surgery between January and October 2025 were examined with EVFCM. Specimens were orthogonally sectioned, stained, and acquired in digital-stain mode. Peripheral and deep margins were independently and blindly reviewed by a dermatologist and a pathologist, both trained in EVFCM interpretation. Concordant negative margins were considered tumor-free, whereas positive, discordant, or equivocal findings prompted re-excision and re-evaluation. Diagnostic agreement with histopathology was assessed using Cohen's κ statistic. A total of 261 margins were evaluated. Inter-reader agreement between the dermatologist and pathologist was almost perfect for both margin assessment (κ=0.863; SE 0.067; p<0.001; observed agreement 98.6%) and histotype assessment (κ=0.882; SE 0.031; p<0.001; observed agreement 97.6%). Compared with histopathology, EVFCM showed high performance, with an overall diagnostic accuracy of 96.4%. The AUC for the combined assessment was 0.875 (SE 0.074; 95% CI 0.730-1.000). Only two discrepancies were observed between EVFCM and histopathology: one false-negative margin assessment and one discordance attributable to differences in sample processing. These findings support EVFCM as a reliable tool for intraoperative margin assessment in NMSC. Comparable performance between dermatologist and pathologist readers supports its potential integration into Mohs surgery workflows; however, potential workflow advantages of the standardized sample-processing approach require prospective validation using quantitative time metrics.

title: Adaptive local region super-resolution for high-field MRI: A diffusion-based approach with structural and frequency-domain constraints.
abstract: High-field MRI offers superior SNR but is constrained by the trade-off between spatial resolution and acquisition time. Existing global deep learning super-resolution (SR) methods often incur computational overhead by ignoring regional image content. This motivates an adaptive local SR strategy to optimize efficiency and detail preservation. To address this, we developed a local SR method that adaptively allocates computational resources to information-rich regions. The proposed framework regularized an entropy-based local region processing strategy with a diffusion model fortified by frequency-domain and structural constraints. We retrospectively evaluated our method on two diverse datasets: a proprietary 7.0 T dental MRI dataset (25 T2-weighted DESS sequences from 10 beagle dogs) and a public 5.0 T brain MRI dataset (Diff5T, 50 diffusion-weighted sequences). Image quality was quantified using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FID. On the 7.0 T dental test dataset (2 subjects), our method achieved a PSNR of 27.31 [26.83, 27.79] dB and the lowest LPIPS of 0.19 [0.18, 0.20]. On the 5.0 T brain test dataset (10 subjects), the method achieved a PSNR of 27.15 ± 0.10 dB, an LPIPS of 0.14 ± 0.00 and an FID of 54.01, with lower perceptual metrics than the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies indicated that the proposed frequency-domain and structural constraints reduced LPIPS and FID, with trade-offs in PSNR and SSIM. In conclusion, the evaluated framework showed improvements in perceptual metrics by integrating targeted local processing with frequency-domain and structural regularization, accompanied by a trade-off in pixel-wise fidelity metrics, supporting the technical feasibility of addressing the resolution-time trade-off in high-field MRI. Future work will focus on expanding the dataset and evaluating the framework in human dental cohorts to address anatomical differences between the current canine model and human dental anatomy.

title: Multicenter external validation of a multimodal MRI deep-learning model to predict meningioma bone invasion.
abstract: Background Preoperative detection of meningioma bone invasion lacks objective biomarkers and relies on subjective radiological assessment, posing a risk of excessive bone resection or residual tumor. We therefore developed and externally validated a parsimonious six-feature DenseNet121 signature derived from multiparametric MRI across two independent institutions. Methods In this retrospective diagnostic accuracy study, 438 consecutive patients (mean age, 53 ± 11 years; 77% women) with histologically confirmed meningioma were allocated to training (n = 182), internal validation (n = 77), and external test (n = 179) sets. Following N4 bias-field correction and isotropic resampling, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and diffusion-weighted volumes were fed into a DenseNet121 architecture to extract a six-feature signature via nested cross-validation. Discrimination (area under the ROC curve, AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test), and clinical utility (decision-curve analysis) were evaluated. Results In the external cohort (prevalence 11%), the signature achieved an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.73-0.91), sensitivity 75%, specificity 77% and negative predictive value 96%, with an AUC improvement of 0.155 over conventional radiomics (95% CI, 0.01-0.30; p = 0.035). At a 20% risk threshold, decision-curve analysis confirmed a positive net clinical benefit, primarily driven by the high negative predictive value. SHAP analysis demonstrated the dominant and consistent contribution of low-ADC features. Conclusion The DenseNet121-derived six-feature signature serves as a reliable rule-out aid for preoperative meningioma bone invasion, with a high negative predictive value that may safely support decisions to avoid extensive bone resection in predicted-negative cases. Positive predictions require confirmatory CT or intraoperative biopsy to mitigate false positives. This tool could assist nurses and surgeons in preoperative planning, facilitating personalized patient care and potentially reducing operative time and complications.

Background

Preoperative detection of meningioma bone invasion lacks objective biomarkers and relies on subjective radiological assessment, posing a risk of excessive bone resection or residual tumor. We therefore developed and externally validated a parsimonious six-feature DenseNet121 signature derived from multiparametric MRI across two independent institutions.

Methods

In this retrospective diagnostic accuracy study, 438 consecutive patients (mean age, 53 ± 11 years; 77% women) with histologically confirmed meningioma were allocated to training (n = 182), internal validation (n = 77), and external test (n = 179) sets. Following N4 bias-field correction and isotropic resampling, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and diffusion-weighted volumes were fed into a DenseNet121 architecture to extract a six-feature signature via nested cross-validation. Discrimination (area under the ROC curve, AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test), and clinical utility (decision-curve analysis) were evaluated.

Results

In the external cohort (prevalence 11%), the signature achieved an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.73-0.91), sensitivity 75%, specificity 77% and negative predictive value 96%, with an AUC improvement of 0.155 over conventional radiomics (95% CI, 0.01-0.30; p = 0.035). At a 20% risk threshold, decision-curve analysis confirmed a positive net clinical benefit, primarily driven by the high negative predictive value. SHAP analysis demonstrated the dominant and consistent contribution of low-ADC features.

Conclusion

The DenseNet121-derived six-feature signature serves as a reliable rule-out aid for preoperative meningioma bone invasion, with a high negative predictive value that may safely support decisions to avoid extensive bone resection in predicted-negative cases. Positive predictions require confirmatory CT or intraoperative biopsy to mitigate false positives. This tool could assist nurses and surgeons in preoperative planning, facilitating personalized patient care and potentially reducing operative time and complications.

title: A hierarchical residual Swin transformer with dual-level locality compensation for accelerated MRI reconstruction.
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides high spatial resolution, excellent soft-tissue contrast, and reliable anatomical discrimination, and is therefore widely used in clinical diagnosis. However, long acquisition time still limits imaging efficiency and clinical throughput. Although convolutional neural network (CNN)-based deep learning approaches have shown considerable promise for reconstructing images from undersampled k-space data, existing methods frequently fail to preserve fine structural details and texture continuity under aggressive undersampling conditions. In this study, we propose a novel reconstruction network based on the Swin Transformer, which integrates three key components: (i) long residual connections to facilitate the recovery of high-frequency details; (ii) a dual-level locality compensation mechanism to restore local spatial information; and (iii) a channel recalibration module to explicitly capture global dependencies among channels, thereby enhancing global feature extraction. Extensive experiments conducted on the IXI and MICCAI 2013 datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms several compared generative adversarial network (GAN)-based approaches for MRI reconstruction across all undersampling mask types, achieving a PSNR improvement of approximately 0.6-1 dB over the best competing method under various settings. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/cvgjhuor/HR-SwinGAN.

title: A deep learning radiomics model based on multiparametric MRI for predicting the efficacy of neoadjuvant chemotherapy in axillary lymph nodes of breast cancer.
abstract: Objectives In this study, we developed and validated a deep learning radiomics clinical (DLRC) model integrating multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) and clinical data to predict axillary pathological complete response (apCR) in cN+ breast cancer patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). Materials and methods We retrospectively collected data from 221 eligible breast cancer patients. The DLRC model integrated radiomics features and deep learning scores (DL-Scores) derived from mpMRI, together with clinical risk factors, to predict apCR. Seven classifiers were employed for model construction, and the optimal classifier was selected based on classification performance to build the final model. Model performance was evaluated using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, area under the curve (AUC), calibration curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Classification performance was assessed via the confusion matrix. Additionally, SHAP plots were utilized for interpretability analysis of the model. Results Multivariate analysis confirmed that progesterone receptor (PR), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), clinical T stage (OR = 0.258), and time-intensity curve (TIC) were significantly associated with apCR. The mpMRI based DLRC model achieved AUCs of 0.949 (95% CI, 0.912-0.986) and 0.932 (95% CI, 0.867-0.998) in the training and validation sets. SHAP analysis further revealed the interpretability of the model. The confusion matrix visually demonstrated the consistency between the predicted results and the true labels, validating the classification performance of the model. Conclusion The DLRC model effectively predicts apCR in breast cancer patients after NAC. It can serve as an auxiliary tool for clinicians in identifying potential candidates for axillary de-escalation, offering support for personalized precision treatment. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD-AI reporting checklist.

title: Preoperative breast cancer subtyping using multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging and explainable machine learning.
abstract: Breast cancer exhibits substantial molecular heterogeneity with distinct molecular subtypes that differ markedly in prognosis, treatment response, and clinical management. To enable imaging-based subtype differentiation, this study retrospectively analyzed suspected breast cancer patients who underwent breast MRI between September 2020 and September 2024, finally including 292 breast cancer lesion records from 283 patients with postoperative IHC-confirmed subtypes. All patients received SyMRI, DCE-MRI, and DWI. Quantitative metrics were extracted-pre- and post-contrast T1, T2, and PD values, T1-Ratio, and PD-Ratio, ADC, TIC patterns, BI-RADS categories, and morphological features. Elastic-net logistic regression was embedded within the training folds for feature selection, and five machine-learning classifiers-LR, SVM, KNN, RF, and DT-were evaluated using the historical internal test set and repeated patient-grouped nested cross-validation. After false-discovery-rate adjustment, ADC-Tumor, post-contrast T1, post-contrast T2, T1-Ratio, and Burr sign differed significantly across molecular subtypes. Repeated patient-grouped nested validation selected the random-forest model (macro-average one-vs-rest AUC, 0.946 ± 0.035), which achieved a macro-average AUC of 0.862 (95% CI, 0.789-0.927) in the historical internal test set; class-specific results and confusion matrices were reported with uncertainty intervals. TreeSHAP analysis of the selected random-forest model identified post-contrast T1 (overall mean absolute SHAP, 0.053), post-contrast T2 (0.053), and T1-Ratio (0.050) as the leading overall contributors, with distinct subtype-specific patterns. These findings support further investigation of multiparametric breast MRI as a preliminary adjunct for preoperative subtype assessment; the model cannot replace histopathological and IHC confirmation and requires independent external validation.

title: Association of whole-body Dixon MRI-derived abnormal bone marrow volume with prognosis in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate whether imaging parameters derived from whole-body Dixon MRI are associated with prognosis in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (MM). Methods This retrospective study included 123 patients with newly diagnosed MM who underwent whole-body MRI. A deep learning model was used to segment bone marrow in major regions. Abnormal bone marrow was defined using region-, age-, and sex-specific lower fat fraction (FF) thresholds from a community population. Total, axial, and peripheral abnormal bone marrow volumes and FFs were extracted. Associations with clinical parameters and stages were assessed by Spearman's correlation and group comparisons. Prognostic values were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox regression. Results Abnormal bone marrow volumes correlated negatively with hemoglobin and albumin and positively with β2-microglobulin, M protein, and bone marrow plasma cell percentage (|ρ| = 0.19-0.53; p < 0.05). Abnormal volumes differed across stages (p < 0.05), whereas FFs did not. Total abnormal bone marrow volume ≥ 122.4 cm 3 was independently associated with overall survival (OS) (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.71, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.31-5.58, p = 0.007) and progression-free survival (PFS) (HR = 1.88, 95% CI = 1.10-3.24, p = 0.022). Axial abnormal bone marrow volume ≥ 93.0 cm 3 was independently associated with OS (HR = 2.15, 95% CI = 1.07-4.32, p = 0.032) and PFS (HR = 1.85, 95% CI = 1.07-3.21, p = 0.028). Conclusion Whole-body Dixon MRI-derived abnormal marrow volume was independently associated with OS and PFS in MM, suggesting its potential utility in prognostic assessment.

title: Denoising of multi b-value diffusion-weighted MR imaging using an improved non-local means filter.
abstract: Purpose Intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) maps derived from the quantitative analysis of multiple b-value diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DW-MRI) has shown many clinical applications. However, DW-MRI is affected by Rician noise, which compromises the reliability of IVIM maps. Method To address this issue, we propose an improved non-local means (NLM) filtering method that utilizes a prior image to improve the estimation of similarity weights. Moreover, the proposed method is implemented using a fast version of NLM filtering to efficiently perform image denoising. We used both simulated and real DW-MRI data to evaluate the performance of the proposed method and compared the results with those obtained using three image denoising methods: local principal component analysis, Marchenko-Pastur principal component analysis, and pre-filtered rotationally invariant non-local principal component analysis. Results Results from the simulated DW-MRI data showed that the proposed method outperformed the other three methods in terms of root mean-squared error and improved the quality of IVIM maps. Results from the real DW-MRI data showed that the proposed method yielded IVIM parameter values consistent with those reported in the literature and exhibited lower coefficients of variation compared to the other three methods. Conclusion Overall, the proposed NLM filtering method has the potential to be a fast and reliable denoising technique for multiple b-value DW-MRI.

title: GlioVision: A multimodal MRI framework for non-invasive prediction of glioma molecular biomarkers.
abstract: Gliomas are primary brain tumors for which molecular biomarker assessment plays an important role in clinical evaluation and treatment planning. Traditional assessment relies on analysis of surgical tumor specimens, which carries procedural risks and sampling bias due to tumor heterogeneity. Existing deep learning methods can be computationally demanding and are often trained on narrowly represented datasets, which may limit their clinical deployment. In this study, we propose GlioVision, a multi-modal deep learning framework for non-invasive prediction of glioma molecular biomarkers using multi-parametric MRI, including T1, T1-Gd, T2, and FLAIR sequences. The framework employs a 3D DenseNet-based architecture with channel and spatial feature recalibration, combined with an adaptive processing module that handles variability across multi-institutional datasets. In addition, a confidence-based filtering mechanism (CFPM) is introduced to identify low-confidence predictions and quantify prediction uncertainty. The model is trained and evaluated on a multi-cohort dataset compiled from publicly available sources, comprising 2270 subjects with heterogeneous imaging protocols. Subject-level splitting is used to prevent data leakage, and performance is reported using AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity across all biomarkers. Independent public cohorts were used for testing. GlioVision achieves AUC values of 0.94 for IDH, 0.87 for 1p/19q, 0.86 for MGMT, and 0.92 for tumor grade, indicating consistent performance across biomarkers. The effect of confidence-based filtering is also analyzed to examine the trade-off between prediction coverage and accuracy. Finally, we investigate a simple model obfuscation approach based on controlled image perturbations and evaluate its impact on prediction performance. This study presents a multi-institutional evaluation of a deep learning pipeline for predicting glioma biomarkers from MRI. It may support further research in radiogenomic analysis and non-invasive tumor characterization.

title: The utility of magnetic resonance imaging of the spinal cord in paediatric transverse myelitis: A systematic review.
abstract: Background Spinal cord magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is central to the diagnosis of paediatric acute transverse myelitis (ATM), yet its true diagnostic yield, concordance with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflammation, and prognostic value remain unclear. Objective To quantify the diagnostic yield of spinal cord MRI in paediatric ATM, evaluate agreement with CSF inflammatory markers, and explore associations between MRI features and clinical outcomes. Methods A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and prospectively registered (CRD42024504846). MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO and CENTRAL were searched from 2006 to October 2025. Observational studies including ≥5 children (≤18 years) with monophasic ATM who underwent spinal cord MRI were eligible. The primary outcome was the proportion of clinically diagnosed ATM cases demonstrating inflammatory spinal cord lesions on MRI. Secondary outcomes included MRI-CSF concordance and associations between imaging findings and long-term outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Results Twelve studies comprising 330 children were included. The pooled diagnostic yield of spinal cord MRI was 97.6% (95% CI 92.2 to 100.0%), with substantial heterogeneity (I²=71.8%) and a wide 95% prediction interval of 71.2 to 99.6%, indicating that a future paediatric cohort could plausibly report a yield anywhere within that range. Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and gadolinium enhancement were the most frequently reported features. Paired MRI-CSF data were available for 61 patients; discordance was observed in 36%, most commonly MRI-positive with normal CSF. Follow-up data (n = 237) showed 64% achieved good recovery, whereas 30% had severe residual deficits; persistent bladder dysfunction occurred in 31%. Baseline MRI positivity did not reliably predict outcome. Conclusions Spinal cord MRI demonstrates a high diagnostic yield in imaged children with clinically diagnosed ATM, but imaging was a condition of cohort entry in most included studies and the pooled estimate is strongly influenced by study design. MRI should be interpreted alongside CSF findings, and baseline imaging alone does not reliably stratify prognosis. Standardised prospective studies are required to refine the diagnostic and prognostic role of MRI in paediatric inflammatory myelopathies.

Spinal cord MRI demonstrates a high diagnostic yield in imaged children with clinically diagnosed ATM, but imaging was a condition of cohort entry in most included studies and the pooled estimate is strongly influenced by study design. MRI should be interpreted alongside CSF findings, and baseline imaging alone does not reliably stratify prognosis. Standardised prospective studies are required to refine the diagnostic and prognostic role of MRI in paediatric inflammatory myelopathies.

title: Phase-associated differences in perivascular and glymphatic-related MRI markers in AQP4-IgG-seropositive neuromyelitis Optica spectrum disorder: A cross-sectional study.
abstract: Background Perivascular and brain fluid-homeostasis-related MRI measures reflect distinct structural and diffusion-related features, but their phase-associated profiles in aquaporin-4 immunoglobulin G (AQP4-IgG)-seropositive neuromyelitis Optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) remain unclear. Methods In this single-center cross-sectional study, 78 participants were included, comprising 55 patients with AQP4-IgG-seropositive NMOSD (26 in the acute phase and 29 in remission) and 23 healthy controls. Basal ganglia perivascular space (BG-PVS) and white matter perivascular space (WM-PVS) volumes were quantified from T1-weighted images using automated segmentation, the bilateral mean diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index was derived from diffusion MRI, and total choroid plexus (ChP) volume was measured on three-dimensional T1-weighted images. Principal group comparisons were covariate-adjusted, and the four adjusted omnibus group tests were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) procedure. Results BG-PVS volume showed a significant covariate-adjusted group effect after BH-FDR correction (F(2, 72) =7.03; raw P = 0.00163; q = 0.00651). BG-PVS volume was higher in remission-phase AQP4+ NMOSD than in acute-phase AQP4+ NMOSD (geometric-mean ratio=1.389; 95% CI, 1.058-1.824; Tukey-adjusted P = 0.0139) and healthy controls (geometric-mean ratio=1.486; 95% CI, 1.126-1.960; Tukey-adjusted P = 0.0030), whereas no significant difference was observed between acute-phase NMOSD and healthy controls. WM-PVS volume, the bilateral mean DTI-ALPS index, and total ChP volume showed no significant covariate-adjusted group effects after BH-FDR correction. Conclusions Remission-phase AQP4-IgG-seropositive NMOSD was characterized by higher BG-PVS volume and a distinct peripheral immune profile compared with the acute phase. These findings suggest that glymphatic-related changes may emerge over the course of AQP4-IgG-seropositive NMOSD. Further prospective longitudinal studies are needed to validate these findings and clarify their temporal evolution.

title: Latin American consensus recommendations on the role of magnetic resonance imaging in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder in clinical practice.
abstract: Background Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is a severe autoimmune astrocytopathy in which magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays a central role in diagnosis, relapse confirmation, differential diagnosis, and longitudinal monitoring. Despite its clinical relevance, standardized MRI recommendations tailored to regional practice are lacking, particularly in Latin America (LATAM), where access to imaging resources and expertise is heterogeneous. Methods Using a modified RAND/UCLA Delphi methodology, a multidisciplinary panel of LATAM experts in neurology, neuroimmunology, neuroradiology, and methodology developed consensus recommendations on the use of MRI in NMOSD. Statements were informed by a narrative review of the literature and rated using a 9-point Likert scale across iterative rounds. Consensus was predefined as a median score ≥7 with limited dispersion. Recommendations were stratified according to feasibility in real-world LATAM settings. Results Consensus was achieved for use of MRI at disease onset, relapse assessment, routine follow-up, differential diagnosis, evaluation of disease activity and treatment response, and the role of advanced techniques and artificial intelligence (AI). Standardized brain and spinal cord MRI are recommended at diagnosis, complemented by orbital imaging when optic neuritis is suspected. MRI contributes substantially to relapse adjudication, particularly in clinically mild or ambiguous presentations. During follow-up, MRI assists in differential diagnosis, detection of subclinical activity, prognostication, and treatment monitoring, although routine contrast use is not required in stable patients. Advanced MRI and AI-based tools are considered complementary, with current utility focused on research and registry-based applications. Conclusions These LATAM-adapted consensus recommendations provide a practical, evidence-informed framework for MRI use in NMOSD, aiming to improve diagnostic accuracy, harmonize imaging practices, and optimize patient management across diverse healthcare settings.
