title: Racial residential segregation and receipt of breast cancer screening in the United States: a national cross-sectional study, 2020.
abstract: Objectives Breast cancer is the most common cancer among the U.S. women, with a lifetime risk that exceeds 13%. In 2026, it is projected that approximately 321,910 new cases of invasive breast cancer will be diagnosed. While there are many well-known barriers to breast cancer screening, the effect of residential segregation on access to screening services is not fully understood. Design This study utilized data from the 2020 U.S. Health Information National Trends Survey Data Linkage Project (HDLP2020) for 1329 women aged 40-75 years. Fitting generalized linear models with the maximum likelihood estimation, we explored the relationship between residential segregation and mammography screening rates. Secondary analyses examined the role of race (White vs. non-White) and rural-urban status in these associations. Results Women in higher residential segregation were less likely to have undergone mammography in the past year, relative to those in less segregated areas (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 0.40; 95% CI: 0.16-0.97; p -value = 0.04). Non-White women in moderately segregated regions also exhibited lower screening rates than those in low-segregation areas. Additionally, women in highly segregated urban settings were less likely to report mammography screening than their counterparts in less segregated urban areas (adjusted OR = 0.39; 95% CI: 0.16-0.92; p -value = 0.03). Conclusion The findings demonstrate that in more racially segregated communities, women are less likely to receive screening mammograms, particularly those who are non-White and live in urban settings. Efforts to improve breast cancer screening may account for the contextual and community determinants of health and address the specific needs of women in moderately to highly segregated areas to potentially reduce disparities and promote health equity.

title: Late onset retinoblastoma in a child with 13 q deletion syndrome.
abstract: A nine-year-old boy presented with right leukocoria, prompting an ophthalmic evaluation that revealed an exophytic group E retinoblastoma. Initial systemic assessment revealed intellectual disability and dysmorphic facies. Conventional cytogenetic analysis of peripheral blood lymphocytes revealed male karyotype (46, XY). Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using a locus-specific probe targeting the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14 demonstrated a deletion in approximately 90% of interphase nuclei and consequently the diagnosis of 13 q deletion was established. Chromosomal microarray identified a ~ 20-Mb deletion at 13q13.3-q21.1 (×1) and a ~ 20-Mb duplication at 13q21.31-q31.1 (×3). MRI orbit and brain showed no optic nerve or intracranial extension. Metastatic work up including CSF sample and BM aspirates was free. Due to advanced group E retinoblastoma, the decision was to perform enucleation. Subsequent histopathological examination revealed high risk features in the enucleated eye and the child received post enucleation chemotherapy. One year afterward, there are no detectable recurrences. To our knowledge, this represents one of the oldest reported cases of retinoblastoma in association with 13q deletion syndrome.

title: Cost-effectiveness of RIMS1 methylation-guided gastric cancer surveillance after Helicobacter pylori eradication.
abstract: Background The cost-effectiveness of methylation-guided surveillance after Helicobacter pylori eradication remains uncertain. Research design and methods From a healthcare system perspective, a cohort model compared annual, biennial, and RIMS1 methylation-guided surveillance over 30 years in Japanese patients aged 50 years with open-type gastric atrophy. Differences in stage at diagnosis were calibrated from annual-surveillance data. Costs and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) were discounted at 3.0% annually. Sensitivity analyses examined uncertainty; an exploratory analysis used Korean inputs. Results At US$52,037.74/QALY, methylation-guided surveillance had the highest net monetary benefit (NMB). Compared with biennial surveillance, its incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was US$47,021.24/QALY and incremental NMB was US$62.56/person. It reduced routine endoscopies by 40.9% versus annual surveillance. Cost-effectiveness varied with surveillance duration, endoscopy-related utility loss, implementation costs, and risk misclassification. Across 5,000 probabilistic draws, methylation-guided surveillance had the highest mean NMB, but biennial surveillance was more often optimal (51.2% vs 36.0%). The preferred strategy in the Korean analysis varied with endoscopy costs. Conclusions In the base-case analysis, RIMS1-guided surveillance was cost-effective, increasing QALYs compared with biennial surveillance and reducing endoscopy use compared with annual surveillance. Its estimated cost-effectiveness depends on the assumed improvement in stage at diagnosis with more frequent surveillance.

title: Non-invasive neuromodulation after repetitive head impacts: current evidence and a precision framework for circuit-based rehabilitation.
abstract: Repetitive head impacts (RHIs) are associated with heterogeneous cognitive, behavioral, psychiatric, sleep-related, pain, and neurological symptoms. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) remains a postmortem neuropathological diagnosis, whereas traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES) is a clinical research syndrome assessed during life. No intervention has been shown to modify CTE pathology, but neuromodulation may support the surviving neural circuits. PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar were searched from database inception to August 2026 for this narrative review. The author evaluates magnetic and electrical stimulation, low-intensity ultrasound, photobiomodulation and cranial nerve stimulation as adjuncts to rehabilitation after repetitive head impacts. Direct RHI/TES evidence is distinguished from findings in other traumatic brain injury and concussion populations, other clinical populations and experimental models. The author then proposes a phenotype- and circuit-guided framework for treatment development. Neuromodulation should not be considered a disease-modifying treatment for CTE. Its most credible role is as a phenotype-led adjunct to rehabilitation. This approach requires identification of a viable circuit relevant to the dominant impairment, selection of an individualized stimulation dose, measurement of target engagement and pairing with symptom-relevant rehabilitation. Progress requires credible sham-controlled and factorial trials, multimodal biomarkers, clinically meaningful functional outcomes, and long-term follow-up.

title: Clinical features associated with HFUS-defined vascular occlusion after hyaluronic acid facial injections: a retrospective exploratory study.
abstract: Hyaluronic acid (HA) filler injections are widely used in aesthetic treatments but can cause vascular occlusion. Early diagnosis is often delayed due to reliance on clinical experience. High-frequency ultrasound (HFUS) offers a noninvasive diagnostic method. The study aims to explore the association between clinical warning signs and HFUS-defined vascular occlusion after HA filler injections. This retrospective study analyzed 57 patients with suspected vascular occlusion after HA filler injections. HFUS and a clinical scoring system covering seven symptom categories were used for early evaluation. Occlusion and non-occlusion groups were compared using HFUS and clinical scores. Among 57 clinically suspected cases, 42 (73.7%) were classified as HFUS-defined vascular occlusion and 15 (26.3%) were classified as non-occlusion. In multivariable analysis, skin color change (OR 30.390, 95% CI: 2.482-372.039; p = .008) and delayed capillary refill time (OR 185.936, 95% CI: 2.638- 13,095.200; p = .016) were associated factors of vascular occlusion. A two-variable model incorporating there two features yielded an AUC of 0.944 (95% CI: 0.891-0.998). Skin color change and delayed capillary refill time were associated with HFUS-defined vascular occlusion in this exploratory cohort. These findings may help inform clinical assessment but require prospective validation in independent populations.

title: Post-treatment risks of transcatheter aortic valve implantation: should we be increasing preventative measures?
abstract: Introduction Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an established treatment for severe aortic stenosis across an expanding risk spectrum. As indications extend to younger and lower-risk patients, post-treatment complications with implications for survival, quality of life, and valve durability require attention. Areas covered This narrative review discusses major post-TAVI complications with direct implications for procedural planning and lifetime management, including cerebrovascular events, conduction abnormalities, coronary obstruction and aortic root injury, bioprosthetic valve dysfunction, valve thrombosis, residual regurgitation, and TAVI-associated infective endocarditis. Evidence was reviewed from pivotal randomized trials, contemporary registries, consensus documents, systematic reviews, and mechanistic studies addressing incidence, pathophysiology, predictors, prognosis, prevention, diagnosis, and management of these complications. Expert opinion Post-TAVI risk reduction should move beyond reactive complication management toward individualized prevention. Meticulous computed tomography-based planning, optimized valve selection and implantation technique, rational antithrombotic therapy, structured rhythm and valve surveillance, selective use of cerebral embolic protection, timely correction of clinically or hemodynamically significant residual regurgitation, and infection-prevention pathways are central components of contemporary care. Future progress will depend on better risk stratification, longer-term durability data, and targeted preventive strategies adapted to lower-risk patients with longer life expectancy.

title: Falcon - multicancer early detection (MCED) real-world evidence (RWE) registry.
abstract: Falcon is a multi-site prospective registry study of a blood-based multi-biomarker multi-cancer early detection (mb-MCED) test in individuals who seek cancer screening to characterize clinical care and outcomes and assess the psychological impact of MCED testing.Falcon is enrolling ≥ 25,000 U.S. participants who receive the MCED test annually for 3 years (MCED cohort) and a matched comparison cohort of ≥50,000 participants receiving standard-of-care clinical management only (SOC cohort). Cohorts will include individuals 50-80 years of age presenting for primary care services who have no current suspicion or history of cancer within 3 years. SOC cancer screening will continue as recommended.The MCED cohort will include MCED testing and follow-up IV-contrast computed tomography and, if necessary, positron emission tomography-CT imaging following a positive test. Self-reported measures of anxiety, worry, and distress will be collected from MCED cohort participants for ≥5 years and following an index date for the SOC cohort. Time from positive MCED to diagnostic imaging and biopsy to first oncologic appointment will be recorded. Smart phone applications will be used to remotely interact with patients to improve health care coordination. Data will be collected for ≥5 years. Clinical trial registration: www.clinicaltrials.gov identifier: NCT06589310 (V3, 5-2025).

title: Bone microarchitecture, density, and strength assessment in automotive trauma patients using HR-pQCT: a pilot study.
abstract: Objective Automotive trauma patients enrolled in the Crash Injury Research and Engineering Network (CIREN) typically undergo computed tomography (CT) imaging as part of emergency care. HR-pQCT is a noninvasive imaging technique that enables assessment of bone microarchitecture at the peripheral sites. CT and HR-pQCT can be used to estimate volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) and strength via finite element analysis (FEA). However, HR-pQCT's superior resolution (approximately 10 times higher than conventional clinical CT scanners) captures in vivo trabecular and cortical microarchitecture, enabling high fidelity FEA. This study examines HR-pQCT-derived bone microarchitecture and strength measurements in relation to fracture patterns, bone-related comorbidities, and CT-derived vBMD in CIREN trauma patients, while providing foundational evidence to support HR-pQCT use following motor vehicle crashes (MVC) and pedestrian crashes. Methods Nine automotive trauma patients (ages 17-76; 78% female) enrolled at Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center from the National Highway Safety Administration's CIREN study participated in the HR-pQCT pilot study. HR-pQCT scans were acquired within 1-12 months following the patient's MVC ( n = 7) or pedestrian crash ( n = 2). Scans were acquired at four sites: 1) distal tibia, 2) diaphyseal tibia, 3) distal radius, and 4) diaphyseal radius. HR-pQCT normative percentiles were determined using Indiana University's calculator. Descriptive statistics were used to present HR-pQCT musculoskeletal outcomes based on bone-related comorbidities, BMI, and fracture incidence. Pearson correlations were performed between HR-pQCT-derived distal tibia and radius total vBMD and CT-derived total vBMD at the spine and femoral compartments. Results At the distal tibia, participants without tibia and fibula fractures tended to show greater mean cortical thickness (1.63 ± 0.38 versus 1.15 ± 0.05 mm), cortical area (146.24 ± 46.07 versus 103.70 ± 1.70 mm 2 ), cortical vBMD (943.83 ± 79.18 versus 861.05 ± 26.52 mg HA/cm 3 ), and bone strength (10.25 ± 3.72 versus 7.00 ± 0.70 kN). Additionally, HR-pQCT-derived distal tibia total vBMD demonstrated a strong positive correlation with CT-derived femoral head total vBMD ( r = 0.766; p = 0.045). Normative percentiles showed that participants with bone-related comorbidities had lower bone microarchitectural and strength percentiles than the group without comorbidities. Conclusion This study demonstrates the viability of HR-pQCT for characterizing bone microarchitecture, strength, and density in automotive trauma patients and identifying differences that might relate to fracture and bone-related comorbidities. These preliminary findings support incorporating HR-pQCT imaging into automotive crash research due to its ability to provide detailed cortical and trabecular microarchitectural measurements that are not available from clinical CT.

title: SSH1 knockdown increases autophagosome formation through ATG9A recruitment and promotes tau protein degradation.
abstract: Pathological accumulation of MAPT/tau protein is a defining feature of Alzheimer disease (AD) and related tauopathies, highlighting the need to identify druggable regulators of MAPT/tau clearance. Using Drosophila behavioral assays focused on cytoskeletal remodeling pathways dysregulated in AD, we identified genes whose genetic modulation mitigates MAPT/tau-induced behavioral deficits. These modifiers were validated by histopathology and mechanistically examined in human tauopathy cell models to determine their impact on autophagy-dependent MAPT/tau degradation. Autophagic flux, ATG9A trafficking, and autophagosome biogenesis were further analyzed. Across models, reduction of the phosphatase SSH1 consistently lowered steady-state MAPT/tau levels by enhancing autophagic flux through a mechanism distinct from its canonical regulation of CFL1. Mechanistically, SSH1 functions as a negative regulator of early autophagosome formation: SSH1 depletion promotes ATG9A mobilization to the endoplasmic reticulum-phagophore assembly site (ER-PAS), thereby accelerating autophagic vesicle biogenesis. Importantly, the MAPT/tau-lowering effect of Dmssh attenuation was abolished in flies haploinsufficient for DmAtg9, demonstrating that SSH1-mediated MAPT/tau clearance requires ATG9 function. Consistent with a direct regulatory interaction, in vitro phosphatase assays revealed that recombinant SSH1 decreases ATG9A phosphorylation in the presence of actin, identifying an SSH1-ATG9A regulatory axis controlling autophagosome initiation. These findings position SSH1 as a nodal inhibitor of autophagy initiation whose inhibition enhances MAPT/tau proteolysis. Notably, SSH1 haploinsufficiency also reduces SNCA/α-synuclein accumulation in vivo, indicating broader relevance to neurodegenerative proteopathies. By integrating in vivo functional screening with mechanistic studies in human cells, this work identifies SSH1 as a druggable phosphatase that constrains autophagy at the level of ATG9A-dependent vesicle formation.

title: An interpretable skin cancer detection and classification framework using meta-heuristic driven symmetric convolution-based adaptive MobileNet with LSTM layer.
abstract: Skin cancer requires early and accurate detection for effective treatment. Automated image analysis can help identify skin lesions and support clinical diagnosis.This study aims to develop an efficient framework for accurate skin cancer detection using lesion segmentation, deep learning, and optimization.Skin lesion images are first segmented using MobileUNet++ with Spatial Attention (MUNet++-SA) to identify lesion regions accurately. The segmented images are then classified using the proposed SAMNet-LSTM model. The model parameters are optimized using Rationalized Masterpiece Optimization (RMO) to improve classification performance. The proposed method is compared with existing approaches.The proposed MUNet++-SA achieves improved segmentation performance. Its mean IoU is 16.47%, 15.88%, 14.11%, and 8.23% higher than U-Net, U-Net3+, ResUNet, and DenseUNet, respectively. The RMO-optimized SAMNet-LSTM also provides improved and efficient skin cancer classification.The proposed framework combines accurate lesion segmentation with optimized deep learning for reliable skin cancer detection. It can support faster and more effective clinical decision-making.

title: Artificial intelligence in modern medicine: a comprehensive review of technologies, applications, and future directions.
abstract: Objectives We evaluated the transformative impact of AI modalities on clinical practice, distinguishing between retrospective algorithmic performance and prospective clinical effectiveness. Methods Comprehensive searches were executed [databases searched: January 2016 to October 2024] across PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and Web of Science, identifying peer-reviewed original research and clinical trials. Non-peer-reviewed materials and commercial web sources were strictly excluded. Results AI technologies-particularly deep learning (DL), natural language processing (NLP), and foundation models-demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy in retrospective cohorts across radiology, dermatology, and pathology. In precision therapeutics, AI accelerates drug discovery and facilitates multi-omics integration for individualized treatment planning. Furthermore, autonomous AI systems have proven cost-effective in nationwide diabetic retinopathy screening programs. However, significant gaps remain between in-silico success and real-world clinical utility. Primary barriers include the lack of prospective randomized trials, pervasive risks of algorithmic bias threatening health equity, the "black box" nature of deep neural networks, and stringent interoperability challenges. Conclusion AI serves as a potent computational catalyst for advancing personalized medicine. To transition from retrospective experimental success to standard-of-care clinical integration, future research endeavors must prioritize Explainable AI (XAI), federated learning frameworks for privacy preservation, and rigorous prospective clinical validation under standardized regulatory oversight.

title: Blood-based biomarkers in gastric cancer peritoneal metastases: current evidence and potential clinical applications.
abstract: Gastric cancer remains among the most common malignancies. Peritoneal metastases account for a significant share of mortality in gastric cancer; however, early detection is constrained by the limited sensitivity of current diagnostic approaches. Computed tomography represents the primary imaging modality for initial assessment, whereas staging laparoscopy, combined with peritoneal cytology and/or biopsy, plays a crucial role in detecting occult peritoneal metastases and confirming the diagnosis. The extent of peritoneal disease, the feasibility of complete cytoreduction, and the postoperative quality of life remain the primary requirements for deciding surgical intervention. As clinical staging and management remain challenging, non-invasive diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers are needed to improve risk stratification and optimize therapeutic strategies. This review summarizes the blood biomarkers reported during the last 5 years and their potential role in predicting peritoneal metastases. A literature search was conducted in PubMed on 12 March 2026, covering publications from March 2021 to March 2026. Ten eligible original studies were included. Although blood-based biomarkers show promise for improving the detection and management of peritoneal metastases in gastric cancer, the available evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Further prospective, multicenter studies with external validation are required to establish their clinical utility before their integration into routine practice.

title: Spinal neurocysticercosis: synthesizing evidence on clinical presentations, anatomical patterns, diagnostic approaches, and therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Spinal neurocysticercosis (NCC) is an uncommon manifestation of NCC involving the spinal cord, meninges, nerve roots, and subarachnoid spaces. Although less common than intracranial disease, spinal involvement can cause substantial neurological morbidity because even small lesions within the confined spinal canal may produce progressive myelopathy. Disease may result from hematogenous dissemination or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spread of Taenia solium larvae and may present as intramedullary, intradural extramedullary, subarachnoid, or, rarely, extradural lesions. Clinical manifestations are diverse and include paraparesis, quadriparesis, cauda equina syndrome, and chronic meningitis. Magnetic resonance imaging is the diagnostic modality of choice, providing detailed assessment of lesion location, evolutionary stage, inflammatory activity, and associated complications. CSF analysis and immunological or molecular tests provide supportive evidence, while histopathological examination confirms the diagnosis when tissue is available. Treatment is individualized and may include antiparasitic agents, corticosteroids, and surgery when indicated. Although outcomes are generally favorable with early diagnosis and appropriate treatment, delayed treatment, extensive arachnoiditis, diffuse leptomeningeal disease, and established spinal cord damage may result in permanent neurological deficits. Further prospective studies are needed to refine diagnostic strategies and optimize management. PubMed database was searched from inception to 13 July 2026, for spinal neurocysticercosis and spinal cysticercosis.

title: Clinical management and multimodal imaging features of brucellar mastitis mimicking metastatic breast carcinoma: a rare case report and literature review.
abstract: Brucella mastitis represents a rare infectious disease that is frequently misdiagnosed as metastatic breast carcinoma, particularly when older women present with systemic manifestations. Here, we report a 60-year-old woman presenting with a neck pain and left upper extremity numbness. Initial contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CEMR) and 18 F -FDG PET-CT highly suggested breast malignancy with osseous metastasis, while contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) provided critical microvascular perfusion insights favoring an inflammatory process. The diagnosis was ultimately confirmed via blood culture and pathological examination. The patient was successfully treated with targeted antimicrobial treatment. This case offers important insights into the multimodal imaging differentiation of atypical breast lesions and emphasizes the diagnostic challenges of Brucella mastitis accompanied by systemic osteoarticular involvement.

title: Neuroimaging and neurophysiological changes following structured interventions in children with developmental coordination disorder: a scoping review.
abstract: Background Longitudinal neuroimaging and neurophysiological studies can indicate whether structured interventions in developmental coordination disorder (DCD) are accompanied by neurobiological change, but this literature has not been synthesized across modalities, follow-up intervals, and analytic approaches. Objective To map longitudinal neurobiological outcomes after structured interventions in children and adolescents with DCD or probable DCD and the analytic approaches used, including neurobiological-clinical/functional linkage analyses. Methods We conducted a scoping review following JBI methodology, reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S. Eligible sources included participants aged 0-18 years with confirmed or probable DCD, a structured intervention, and neurobiological assessment at baseline and ≥1 post-intervention time point. Two reviewers independently screened records and charted data. We searched six databases, two trial registries, and preprint platforms on January 10, 2026 (updated August 21, 2026), without date or language restrictions. Formal critical appraisal was not undertaken; methodological and reporting features were charted descriptively. Results Of 747 records identified, 13 sources (eight independent cohorts) published between 2012 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. Neurobiological sample sizes ranged from 20 to 88 (median 49). Designs included randomized controlled, non-randomized controlled, and quasi-experimental pre-post studies. Interventions clustered into Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance (CO-OP; 6 sources), exercise/motor-learning programs (4), and neuromuscular/biomechanical approaches (3). Modalities included diffusion tensor imaging, resting-state functional MRI, structural MRI/voxel-based morphometry, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, electroencephalography/event-related potentials, and surface electromyography. MRI-based longitudinal outcomes were reported exclusively in CO-OP cohorts, with several publications arising from shared registered trials and partial cohort overlap. Six sources included neurobiological follow-up beyond the immediate post-intervention assessment. Analytic approaches varied in pre-post versus group-by-time contrasts, region-of-interest versus whole-brain analyses, and correction for multiple comparisons. Seven sources reported neurobiological-clinical/functional linkage analyses; five tested change-based associations, and statistically significant findings were limited to individualized movement-quality outcomes. Conclusions The evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and unevenly distributed across intervention categories and modalities. Priorities include independent replication, longitudinal neuroimaging of non-CO-OP interventions where scientifically justified, more consistent follow-up, and prespecified, adequately powered linkage analyses.

title: Atypical late neurosyphilis presenting as status epilepticus: diagnostic and screening implications.
abstract: Objectives Neurosyphilis is a serious complication of poorly treated syphilis due to Treponema pallidum invasion of the central nervous system. Symptoms vary from silent infection to severe neurological deficits. Despite progress in diagnostics and treatment, the diagnosis is frequently missed because it is not considered, particularly in atypical presentations and in patients with no evident risk factor. . Methods A 45-year-old man presented with confusion, speech difficulties, and left-sided weakness following subtle behavioral changes. In the emergency department, he had a witnessed focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure starting with head deviation to the left and tonic posturing of the left arm. Brain CT was normal, while MRI revealed right thalamic and bilateral temporal FLAIR hyperintensities with diffusion restriction in the thalamus. CSF showed mild pleocytosis (17 WBC/µL) and raised protein (67.6 mg/dL). Serum treponemal screening was positive with an RPR titre > 1:32. Neurosyphilis was confirmed by a reactive CSF non-treponemal test (RPR 1:2) in a patient with compatible clinical and CSF findings; the CSF TPHA titre was >1:10,240, which is supportive but not in itself a diagnostic criterion.Levetiracetam was started on admission and intravenous penicillin G on day 2, after the diagnosis was confirmed. Because EEG and MRI suggested possible focal status epilepticus, valproate and phenytoin were added. The patient developed respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation and deep vein thrombosis. After extended ICU stay and rehabilitation, he recovered with mild residual critical illness myopathy and cognitive deficits. Conclusion Neurosyphilis is not intrinsically difficult to diagnose, provided it is considered, including outside the classically recognised risk groups such as men who have sex with men.

title: Childhood peer abuse moderates associations of inflammation and cortisol with subcortical brain volume.
abstract: Objective: Childhood peer abuse is a developmentally salient form of interpersonal adversity, yet its role in shaping links between peripheral biological stress markers and brain structure remains poorly understood. The present cross-sectional study examined whether retrospectively reported childhood peer verbal and physical abuse moderated associations of systemic inflammatory burden and hair cortisol with subcortical brain volume.Methods: Participants from a community sample completed the Maltreatment and Abuse Chronology of Exposure scale and structural magnetic resonance imaging. Inflammatory burden was indexed by a composite of standardised IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, and C-reactive protein values (n = 292), and hair cortisol was available in a subsample (n = 172). Bilateral amygdala, hippocampus, putamen, and caudate volumes were extracted from FreeSurfer segmentation. Linear regression models adjusted for gender, age, parental education, and estimated total intracranial volume; false discovery rate correction was applied across the four ROI tests within each marker-by-moderator family.Results: Peer verbal abuse moderated associations of inflammatory burden with bilateral amygdala volume (β = -.095, pFDR = .032) and bilateral putamen volume (β = -.115, pFDR = .017). Peer physical abuse moderated the association between hair cortisol and bilateral amygdala volume (β = .227, pFDR = .035). Caudate models did not survive correction. Core findings remained significant after sensitivity adjustment for broader childhood adversity and current depression/anxiety symptoms.Conclusions: Associations differed across brain regions, biological markers, and peer-abuse subtypes. These findings identify peer adversity as an important interpersonal context for understanding stress-related brain differences.

title: Early extracranial dissemination with prolonged survival in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma: case study and comprehensive literature review.
abstract: Background Extracranial metastasis of glioblastoma (GBM) is rare (0.4-2%) and associated with poor prognosis. For this report, "early extracranial dissemination" is defined as radiographically and histologically confirmed metastatic disease identified at or within one month of the index GBM diagnosis, distinguishing it from metastasis arising later in the disease course. Case presentation A 65-year-old woman with IDH-wildtype, MGMT-methylated GBM presented with seizures, right hemiplegia, and expressive aphasia. She underwent near-total resection followed by chemoradiotherapy with temozolomide. A suspicious right lower lobe pulmonary lesion was identified on initial staging, and biopsy-confirmed GBM involving mediastinal lymph nodes was established within one month of diagnosis. Despite pulmonary and mediastinal involvement, intracranial hemorrhage, seizures, and venous thromboembolism, she survived 25 months from diagnosis and 24 months following confirmation of metastatic disease. Discussion This case is notable for exceptionally early extracranial dissemination, pulmonary and mediastinal involvement, and prolonged post-metastatic survival. MGMT methylation and sustained temozolomide therapy may have contributed to disease control, although these observations remain hypothesis-generating. Conclusion Early extracranial dissemination may be underrecognized and warrants further investigation through risk-stratified approaches to extracranial surveillance.

A 65-year-old woman with IDH-wildtype, MGMT-methylated GBM presented with seizures, right hemiplegia, and expressive aphasia. She underwent near-total resection followed by chemoradiotherapy with temozolomide. A suspicious right lower lobe pulmonary lesion was identified on initial staging, and biopsy-confirmed GBM involving mediastinal lymph nodes was established within one month of diagnosis. Despite pulmonary and mediastinal involvement, intracranial hemorrhage, seizures, and venous thromboembolism, she survived 25 months from diagnosis and 24 months following confirmation of metastatic disease.

Discussion

This case is notable for exceptionally early extracranial dissemination, pulmonary and mediastinal involvement, and prolonged post-metastatic survival. MGMT methylation and sustained temozolomide therapy may have contributed to disease control, although these observations remain hypothesis-generating.

Conclusion

Early extracranial dissemination may be underrecognized and warrants further investigation through risk-stratified approaches to extracranial surveillance.

title: From metastatic disease to no evidence of disease after conversion liver surgery in advanced gastric cancer with liver metastases: A case report.
abstract: Stage IV gastric cancer with liver metastases has a poor prognosis. Conversion surgery may enable long-term disease control in selected patients, but pathological complete response is rare and is usually defined only for surgically resected specimens. Here, a 54-year-old female with initially unresectable, HER2-negative, pMMR-by-IHC, EBER-positive gastric cancer and synchronous liver metastases received first-line XELOX plus tislelizumab for 4 cycles. Because of suspected oxaliplatin hypersensitivity, treatment was changed to cisplatin plus capecitabine plus tislelizumab for 3 cycles. After subsequent suspected platinum hypersensitivity, treatment was changed to capecitabine plus tislelizumab for 7 cycles. After 14 cycles, repeat endoscopic biopsy showed no tumor cells. Imaging showed significant regression of liver lesions. After multidisciplinary discussion, the patient underwent conversion liver surgery comprising resection of selected liver lesions and radiofrequency ablation of other liver lesions. R0 status was confirmed only for the resected liver specimens; ablated lesions had no pathological specimen. Histopathological examination of the resected liver specimens showed no residual viable tumor cells, consistent with pathological complete response in the resected liver lesions. The gastric primary was assessed as clinical complete response by endoscopy and biopsy. At last follow-up 1 month after surgery, imaging showed no evidence of disease; long-term outcome remains unknown. This case illustrates that selected patients with advanced gastric cancer and liver metastases may achieve a strong response to tislelizumab-based immunochemotherapy and liver-directed conversion treatment. However, the long-term benefit, the role of omitting gastrectomy, and the significance of FAPI/FDG discordance remain uncertain.

title: Differentiating disseminated cryptococcosis from pulmonary cryptococcosis: Roles of clinical characteristics and cryptococcal antigen.
abstract: Abstract Distinguishing disseminated cryptococcosis (DC) from localized pulmonary cryptococcosis (PC) is crucial due to divergent management and disparate prognoses. This study aimed to recognize associated factors for DC from PC in non-human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) patients. Accordingly, 475 pathologically confirmed cryptococcosis cases (391 PC and 84 DC) were retrospectively reviewed over a 20-year period at a tertiary hospital in China. Clinical, radiographic, dynamic serum cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) titer profiles, treatment and prognosis were analyzed. Patients with DC were significantly associated with a history of glucocorticoid therapy (16.7% vs. 5.6%; P = 0.001) and autoimmune diseases (16.7% vs. 6.1%; P = 0.001) compared with PC, aggressive thoracic computed tomography findings, including patchy exudation ( P = 0.001) and cavitation ( P = 0.009), and markedly higher baseline median serum CrAg titers (1:1280 vs. 1:80, P < 0.001). By multivariable analysis, CNS symptoms (adjusted OR [aOR] 131.12, 95% CI 10.21-1683.9, P = 0.001), chronic liver disease (aOR 15.21, 95% CI 1.06-217.69, P = 0.045), and baseline serum CrAg ≥1:80 (aOR 13.51, 95% CI 1.39-131.07, P = 0.025) remained independently associated with DC. An initial CrAg titer ≥ 1:80 should prompt careful CNS evaluation and consideration of lumbar puncture. Patients with DC had significantly longer median CrAg clearance ( P = 0.001) and antifungal duration (18 vs. 6 months), with higher mortality (9.5% vs. 1.0%; P < 0.001) compared to PC. Early risk-stratification is imperative to optimize interventions and improve survival.

title: Supermicrosurgical perforator-to-perforator flap reconstruction for lower limb defects: a single-center case series.
abstract: Lower limb soft tissue defects remain a major reconstructive challenge due to frequent exposure of critical structures and compromised vascularity. In complex cases where local tissue is insufficient, free tissue transfer is required. Advances in supermicrosurgery have enabled perforator-to-perforator (P-to-P) anastomoses allowing reliable perfusion while preserving major axial vessels and minimizing donor-site morbidity. A retrospective review was conducted of five patients who underwent P-to-P free flap reconstruction for lower limb defects between January 2018 and January 2023. Preoperative CT angiography and intraoperative duplex ultrasound were used for perforator mapping. Two anterolateral thigh, one medial sural artery perforator, and two gracilis muscle flaps were utilized. Anastomoses were hand-sewn using 10-0 to 12-0 nylon under high-magnification microscopy. Flap perfusion was monitored with Vioptix Tissue Oximeter. The mean age was 60.8 years and defect sizes ranged from 5 × 4 cm to 20 × 8 cm. All flaps survived without partial or total loss. One patient developed minor wound dehiscence that healed without intervention. Reconstruction was successful across varied etiologies including infection, chronic wounds, and postoperative defects, with low morbidity and no re-explorations. P-to-P supermicrosurgical reconstruction offers a reliable, vessel-preserving approach for complex lower limb defects. This technique maintains major vascular axes, minimizes donor-site morbidity, and achieves outcomes comparable to conventional microsurgical methods across diverse etiologies such as infection, chronic wounds, and postoperative defects. In our series, flap survival was universal with no re-explorations and minimal morbidity. Wider clinical adoption and continued experience may further define its role in contemporary lower extremity reconstruction.

title: A clinical-radiological model for predicting in-hospital mortality in acute exacerbation of COPD.
abstract: Background Quantitative computed tomography (QCT) has emerged as a promising tool for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) phenotyping. However, its prognostic value in acute exacerbations of COPD (AECOPD) remains insufficiently explored, and existing risk stratification models have limited integration of imaging-derived metrics. This study aimed to develop and validate a prognostic model that integrates multidimensional clinical variables with QCT-derived metrics, and to compare its predictive performance with traditional clinical scores for in-hospital mortality in AECOPD. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, consecutive patients aged ≥40 years hospitalized with severe AECOPD were enrolled from September 2010 to October 2024, with collection of demographic characteristics, clinical features, laboratory indices, and chest CT imaging data. The cohort was randomly split into training and testing sets (7:3). Candidate predictors were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression followed by multivariable logistic regression. Four classification models were developed and evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. Discriminative performance was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and compared with conventional clinical scores. Results A total of 465 patients with AECOPD were included, of whom 47 (10.1%) died during hospitalization. Five independent predictors were identified: confusion, lymphocyte count <0.8 × 10 9 /L, chronic heart failure, white blood cell count ≥10 × 10 9 /L, and reduced pulmonary vascular fractal dimension. The logistic regression model demonstrated the best performance, achieving an AUC of 0.852 (95% CI, 0.738-0.965) in the testing set, significantly outperforming other models and established clinical scores. Conclusions A predictive model integrating QCT-derived metrics with clinical features improved AECOPD in-hospital mortality prediction over traditional scores, supporting its utility for individualized risk stratification and management.

title: CT image-based evaluation of phantom-derived DLP-to-effective dose conversion factors for adult abdomen-pelvis CT.
abstract: Effective dose is used in computed tomography (CT) as a population-level quantity for radiation protection, dose monitoring, and clinical studies. It is commonly estimated by multiplying scanner-reported dose-length product (DLP) by a conversion coefficient, or k -factor, because organ doses are not available from routine examinations. Most CT k -factors were derived from computational human phantoms, but phantom-derived estimates have not been systematically compared with effective doses calculated directly from CT images across adults with diverse body habitus. We calculated k -factors using a set of adult abdominal CT images combined with deep learning-based automatic organ segmentation and Monte Carlo dose calculation methods and compared them with those calculated from two phantom-derived k -factor approaches: the fixed AAPM TG23 coefficient and body size-dependent k -factors calculated using National Cancer Institute dosimetry system for CT (NCICT). Abdomen-pelvis CT images from 38 adults (18 females, 20 males) spanning water-equivalent diameter (WED) values of 21-41 cm were segmented using TotalSegmentator and an in-house gonad model, converted into voxelised anatomical models, and coupled with a validated CT scanner Monte Carlo model. CT image-based k -factors were calculated as effective dose divided by DLP and evaluated as functions of WED and sex. Image-based k -factors decreased with increasing WED for both sexes, and female values were higher than male values at comparable WED. Over the overlapping WED range, NCICT-based k -factors showed good agreement with CT-based values with the same decreasing trend. The fixed TG23 coefficient introduced systematic bias at smaller and larger body sizes. However, the selected NCICT adult phantoms did not cover the lower-WED end of the CT cohort. These findings support the performance of phantom-based effective dose calculations and indicate the need to extend phantom libraries while continuing CT image-based evaluation across pediatric CT and broader imaging protocols.

title: Determination of local diagnostic reference levels for mammography in Fars Province, Iran.
abstract: The most common cancer that strikes women is breast cancer. It is diagnosed using mammography, which is considered a gold standard diagnostic tool in detecting breast cancer. Despite the use of ionizing radiation, mammography should be performed according to the ALARA principle, ensuring that radiation dose is optimized while maintaining adequate image quality for accurate diagnosis. This study sought to determine the LDRL for mammography in Fars Province, Iran, in line with the guidelines provided in ICRP Publication 135. This analytical study involved the extraction of data from the DICOM header of quality-controlled mammography devices in 62 centers in Fars Province. In total, 27,345 mammogram reports ranging from 2004 to 2025 were analyzed. Technical information about mammography was obtained through kVp, mAs, anode filter combination, and patient information, including age and compressed breast thickness. Data from the past five years and projections of CC and MLO were considered in the analysis.The study determined LDRLs for both Entrance Surface Air Kerma (Kae) and organ dose. For Kae, which does not require breast thickness correction, the LDRL was established at 5.94 mGy for the CC view and 9.49 mGy for the MLO view. The LDRLs for organ dose were further stratified by breast thickness. A comparison with national and international standards revealed that while the LDRL for the CC view was lower than the NDRLs of the UK and Ireland, it remained higher than previously reported levels in Iran. Notably, the LDRL for the MLO view was found to be higher than levels reported in other Iranian studies and international benchmarks. These findings highlight the necessity for protocol optimization, particularly for the MLO view, to align local practices with global dose reduction standards.

title: MPISuperRes-PnP: a super-resolution zero-shot plug-and-play reconstruction algorithm for magnetic particle imaging.
abstract: Objective. Magnetic particle imaging (MPI) is a promising, emerging medical imaging modality. MPI is based on the non-linear response of magnetic nanoparticles to an applied magnetic field and does not expose the specimen to ionizing radiation. The measured signal is the voltage induced in receive coils by the particles' response. Reconstructing the particle concentration from the signal constitutes the imaging task. Even using state-of-the-art measurement-based reconstruction, the associated spatial grid is very coarse, hence super-resolution techniques are important. In this work, we propose an approach for super-resolution in MPI inspired by energy minimization. Approach. Different methods have been proposed for super-resolution in MPI, ranging from upscaling of the associated system matrix to interpolation of the reconstruction. Here we incorporate super-resolution into the reconstruction task via an energy minimization formulation. Following the plug-and-play (PnP) approach to energy minimization we derive a splitting scheme where the arising Gaussian denoising task is treated with a pre-trained learned Gaussian denoiser. Main results. We derive a super-resolution method for MPI based on a PnP approach using a pre-trained denoiser in zero-shot fashion. This way, we incorporate benefits of deep learning without training and avoid the need of training data. Further, we provide a quantitative and qualitative evaluation of the proposed method on simulated data with realistic noise. Hyper-parameters are selected via an extended parameter search. The found parameters are applied for reconstruction on real data. We qualitatively show the applicability of our method on real data (MPIData: EquilibriumModelWithAnisotropy and 2D-OpenMPI Data). Significance. The proposed method employs a deep-learning denoiser without training-thus it does not require presently scarcely available MPI training data. The denoiser behaves conservatively, i.e. no hallucination artifacts were observed. The super-resolution approach is generic such that it can be applied in future MPI contexts involving different regularizers or different imaging tasks.

title: GPT-assisted radiomic modeling for predicting pathological complete response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Objective . To evaluate whether GPT can assist in automating radiomics modeling for predicting pathological complete response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Methods. The study included a training cohort (TC; n = 186), a validation cohort (VC; n = 116), and a prospective multicenter validation cohort (PVC; n = 269). Radiomic and supervised deep learning features were extracted from pretreatment T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging. logistic regression (LR) was first evaluated using radiomic, deep learning, and fused features. Support vector machine, naïve Bayes, random forest, and extreme gradient boosting models were subsequently compared using fused features. GPT was not used as the classifier but assisted with preprocessing, feature selection, hyperparameter optimization, code generation and execution, model training, and probability output. Each GPT-assisted workflow was independently repeated five times. Results. Fused features achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for both manually developed and GPT-assisted LR models. Their AUCs were 0.759 versus 0.763 ± 0.003 in the TC, 0.714 versus 0.741 ± 0.008 in the VC, and 0.700 versus 0.706 ± 0.004 in the PVC. Across five classifiers, GPT-assisted workflows achieved performance broadly comparable to manually developed models. Repeated GPT-assisted runs showed limited variability, with AUC standard deviations ranging from 0.001 to 0.019. Conclusion. Under expert supervision, GPT can automate key radiomics modeling procedures while achieving performance comparable to conventional machine learning workflows, potentially reducing technical workload and facilitating integrated model development.

title: NHPVS: a nodule-aware deep learning method for high-abundance pulmonary vessel segmentation on chest CT.
abstract: Objective. Deep learning-based segmentation of pulmonary vessels is challenged by vessel-nodule confusion and insufficient detection of small vessels. To address these issues, we propose a Nodule-aware High-abundance Pulmonary Vessel Segmentation (NHPVS) framework that enhances nodule differentiation and improves small vessel segmentation. Approach. This multi-center study retrospectively collected 477 chest CT scans comprising non-contrast and contrast scans. A 3D U-Net-based model was trained on 370 scans for pulmonary vessel segmentation. Performance metrics included Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), sensitivity, centerline DSC (cl DSC), 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95), and nodule misclassification rate (NMR). Visual and quantitative assessments were conducted on the external test set. Main Results. NHPVS outperformed existing methods, achieving a DSC of 89.2%, a sensitivity of 89.2%, a cl DSC of 93.2%, an HD95 of 1.4 mm, and an NMR of 1.8%. Compared with the state-of-the-art method (nnUNet-v2), NHPVS showed superior segmentation accuracy, vascular continuity, and branch abundance, with improvements of 31.1% in vessel length and 60.5% in branch counts. The volume of small pulmonary vessels (diameter <3 mm) segmented by NHPVS was significantly greater than that segmented by nnUNet-v2 ( p < 0.001). Significance. By enabling the precise visualization of pulmonary arteries and veins on chest CT, NHPVS has the potential to assist radiologists in disease diagnosis and surgical planning.

title: Pulse width-dependent Monte Carlo source modeling for ultra-high dose rate electron beams.
abstract: Objective. The emergence of ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) electron beams has highlighted the need for accurate Monte Carlo (MC) source models after recent measurements revealed pulse width (PW)-dependent discrepancies in dose profiles. This work aims to develop and validate a MC source model for conventional and FLASH modes using GATE 10, including PW dependence. Approach. Percentage depth dose (PDD) curves and lateral dose profiles were measured in water using a flashDiamond detector for PWs of 0.5-5s. These data were used to optimize the parametric source model throughminimization and gamma analysis. Validation was performed using a mouse collimator and PMMA slabs. Relative dose distributions and cumulative dose-volume histograms were computed in a CT-based voxelised mouse, with and without bolus. Main results. The optimized FLASH source model features a dual-peak energy spectrum with a PW-dependent energy component (7.0-7.8 MeV for 0.5-5s) and low-energy component probability. In conventional mode, a two-component spectrum (1.51.0 and 6.81.5 MeV) was used. Simulations showed good agreement with measurements (gamma-index 2 mm/2% anddifferences for,and). Differences in the mouse lung volume receiving at least 95% of the maximum dose (V95) were 1% across FLASH PWs, increasing to 5% and 12% in CONV without and with bolus, respectively. Bolus increased V95in FLASH by 17%, indicating improved target coverage. Significance. A GATE 10 MC-based source model of the ElectronFLASH LINAC was developed for both UHDR (PW-dependent) and conventional modes. Despite PW-dependent energy variations, no significant dosimetric differences were observed between PWs in FLASH in the preclinical mouse model. The model provides a reliable tool for optimization of preclinical irradiation setups for FLASH biological studies in the absence of a treatment planning system.

title: Anatomy-prior-guided and scan-aware 3D segmentation of the pediatric pancreas in CT images.
abstract: Objective. Pediatric pancreas CT segmentation is challenging because developmental anatomy and scan-protocol variability jointly affect organ size, image appearance, and boundary visibility. This study evaluated whether explicitly incorporating anatomy-related and scan-related case-level descriptors could improve pediatric pancreas segmentation relative to an image-only baseline. Approach. We developed APSC-Net, an anatomy-prior-guided and scan-aware 3D segmentation framework based on SegResNet. Structured anatomy-related and scan-related descriptors were encoded as separate context vectors and injected through bottleneck anatomy-prior guidance and decoder-stage low-rank FiLM modulation. The model was trained and internally tested on GE pediatric CT cases, then evaluated without retraining on a held-out Siemens subset in a cross-vendor evaluation within the same cohort and institution. Main results. On the full held-out GE test set, APSC-Net improved the mean dice similarity coefficient (DSC) from 0.665 to 0.770 and reduced the 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95) from 22.2 to 11.6 mm compared with an image-only SegResNet baseline. Stratified analysis showed DSC gains across pediatric age groups, including the youngest subgroup (0.718-0.751 for 0-5 years), and across exposure-stage strata. In the GE stream ablation, the full and scan-only configurations performed similarly. In secondary testing on held-out Siemens cases, the full model achieved lower average symmetric surface distance (ASSD) than either single-stream variant and achieved the lowest HD95 and ASSD among the compared methods, while age-group domain-regularized baselines remained competitive in DSC. Significance. On the evaluated cohorts, APSC-Net achieved lower boundary-distance errors than the image-only SegResNet baseline. The findings support further evaluation of case-level metadata conditioning for pediatric imaging tasks affected by developmental and acquisition-related variability.

title: Deep learning-based prediction of diffusion MRI responses from microvascular OCT angiograms.
abstract: Objective. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) signals are sensitive to microvascular geometry and hemodynamics, but current approaches rely on computationally intensive simulations on optical coherence tomography (OCT)-derived vascular graphs. We investigated whether three-dimensional deep learning models can serve as fast surrogates that predict diffusion MRI responses directly from microvascular OCT angiograms. Approach. Five mouse cortical OCT angiograms were segmented into 4792 vascular subgraphs and converted into nine-channel image volumes encoding vascular geometry, magnetic field gradient, hematocrit, oxygen saturation, partial oxygen pressure, blood velocity magnitude, and three velocity components. For each sample, a physics-based framework generated spin echo (SE) and diffusion-weighted signals for three-values (50, 100, 500 s mm), three gradient timing pairs, and ten gradient directions. We trained five 3D architectures (AutoEncoder, BasicUNet, DenseNet169, EfficientNetB4 and ResNet) with late fusion of acquisition parameters and evaluated performance using MSE, MAE and. Main results. Under within-distribution (random-split) evaluation, testvalues were at least 0.87. DenseNet169 achieved the best overall accuracy (MSE, MAE,) and maintainedacross all diffusion settings, while ResNet provided near-perfect reconstruction of the SE sequence alone (). Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation gave MSE, MAE, and, with 34.4% of held-out samples reaching. Channel ablation revealed velocity magnitude and velocity components as dominant predictors. Once trained, the models predicted full diffusion responses in milliseconds, providing speedups of four to six orders of magnitude compared with simulations. Significance. These results demonstrate that deep learning surrogates can accurately and efficiently approximate diffusion MRI responses from microvascular OCT angiograms, enabling rapid exploration of microvascular configurations and acquisition protocols.

title: DiffINR: conditional neural field diffusion for deformation-driven volumetric image estimation from limited measurements.
abstract: Objective. We propose DiffINR for rapid deformation-driven estimation of patient-specific target volumes from limited measurements. DiffINR uses a coordinate-based implicit neural representation (INR) to estimate a dense deformation vector field (DVF) that warps a high-quality prior volume (source) to the target anatomy, with patient-specific INR initialization provided by a population-based conditional hyperdiffusion model. Approach. During offline training, INRs were optimized on fully sampled source-target image volume pairs to represent DVFs. A Transformer diffusion model, hyperdiffusion, learned the distribution of the resulting INR weights. The model was jointly conditioned on anatomical features extracted from the training source and target volumes by a foundation model and on features encoded directly from limited measurements. At inference, hyperdiffusion generated INR initial weights, which were further fine-tuned by patient-specific optimization using measurement-domain fidelity and DVF-smoothness losses. We evaluated DiffINR on two tasks: cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) estimation from limited-angle x-ray projections and real-time volumetric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) estimation from ultra-sparse k-space data. Main Results. For orthogonal-view 90° CBCT estimation, DiffINR achieved a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.962 ± 0.021, relative error of 6.84% ± 1.70%, and target registration error of 3.61 ± 1.27 mm, outperforming the iterative methods, population-based models, and randomly initialized INR baselines. For volumetric MRI estimation with 13 radial spokes per slice, DiffINR achieved an SSIM of 0.985 ± 0.007, Dice coefficient of 0.89 ± 0.04, and center-of-mass error of 1.30 ± 1.09 mm. DiffINR showed high robustness to data distribution shifts at test time, including dataset changes, limited-angle setting variations, and different MRI sampling sparsity levels. Test-time runtime was 23 s for CBCT estimation and 27 s for MRI estimation, compared with 795 s and 928 s, respectively, for INR optimization from scratch. Significance. By combining hyperdiffusion-based INR initialization with patient-specific data consistency, DiffINR achieves fast and accurate deformation-driven volumetric image estimation.

title: Characterizing magnetic field coupling in MRI-guided radiotherapy by solving a dirichlet problem with sparsely sampled boundary conditions.
abstract: Objective. Integrating medical linear accelerators and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners for MRI-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) is complicated by mutual magnetic field coupling, making efficient field mapping crucial. This study proposes a computationally efficient methodology to characterize an MR scanner's magnetic fringe field by solving a boundary value problem (BVP) from sparsely sampled data. This approach accurately maps fields in free space and near ferromagnetic materials without requiring proprietary internal MR coil models or full-scale room simulations. Approach. A full-scale finite element method (FEM) model of a proximity-type MRgRT system, validated against experimental measurements, was used as the reference. A hybrid BVP methodology was developed where Laplace's equation was first solved using sparsely sampled magnetic field boundary conditions. To account for the linac, this free-space solution was subsequently used as an initial condition for a refined model that incorporated the ferromagnetic properties of the linac head and was solved using Maxwell's equations. Accuracy was assessed by comparing the BVP solutions to the full-scale FEM reference across various sampling resolutions. Main results. The BVP approach reconstructed the magnetic field to within 1 G of the reference using a coarse 40 cm boundary sampling. The hybrid method successfully characterized field distortions from the linac; ignoring the ferromagnetic structure led to errors of -7 G to 2 G near the component, whereas including it reduced the discrepancy to within 1 G. The methodology was efficient, reducing computation time from 2 h for the full-scale model to under 10 min, while using a fraction of the memory. Significance. This study presents a validated, efficient, and accessible BVP-based methodology for magnetic field characterization in MRgRT systems. By enabling accurate field mapping from sparse data, accounting for ferromagnetic components, and drastically reducing computational demands, this approach offers a robust tool for rapid engineering assessments and serves as a practical alternative to complex full-scale simulations.

title: Multi-GPU parallel framework for DOI-enabled long axial field-of-view PET image reconstruction.
abstract: Objective. Depth-of-interaction (DOI)-enabled long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) positron emission tomography (PET) can mitigate parallax-induced resolution degradation, but DOI modeling substantially expands the lines-of-response space and increases computational cost. This study aimed to develop a scalable reconstruction framework for DOI-enabled LAFOV-PET. Approach. We present an optimized multi-GPU reconstruction framework based on list-mode ordered-subsets expectation maximization. The framework targets the major computational bottlenecks of DOI-enabled LAFOV-PET reconstruction, including sensitivity image calculation and Monte Carlo-based scatter estimation. Main results. The extended IQ phantom demonstrated near-linear scalability across multiple GPUs for sensitivity image calculation and Monte Carlo-based scatter estimation. Additional Derenzo and hybrid anthropomorphic phantom studies validated the imaging benefits of DOI modeling, including improved spatial resolution and performance under realistic imaging conditions. Significance. The proposed framework improves the scalability of DOI-enabled LAFOV-PET reconstruction by enabling its dominant computational components to efficiently utilize available GPU resources, establishing a foundation for high-performance reconstruction in next-generation PET systems.

title: Applying exponential data consistency conditions to non-homogeneous attenuation.
abstract: Objective. Exponential data consistency conditions (eDCCs) have shown feasibility for motion correction and attenuation map alignment in single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). The eDCCs require all the activity to be contained within a convex region of homogeneous attenuation. In a non-homogeneous attenuation, activity outside the convex region can violate this assumption, introducing an additional source of inconsistency and inhibiting eDCC-based methods. We present the mathematical foundations of the sine-amplitude approach for coping with activity outside the region of constant attenuation and validate it using SPECT computer simulations. Approach . The sine-amplitude method uses the time-varying aspect of the cardiac signal in ECG-gated SPECT studies to extract a component of the measured data that satisfies the eDCCs, even if the overall activity does not. Four noise-free activity distributions were simulated: a time-varying point source inside the heart, the point source with static liver activity, time-varying left-ventricle (LV) activity, and the LV with static liver activity. The liver activity violated the eDCC constraints. The method was evaluated with different levels of Poisson noise and liver activity. Consistency between exponential projections was assessed using the mean normalised difference (MND) over single- and multi-slice axial ranges. Main Results . In noise-free simulations, the liver activity outside the region of constant attenuation increased the LV activity single-slice MND fromto. For the eleven-slice range, the presence of liver increased the LV activity MND fromto. The sine-amplitude method reduced the LV single-slice MND toand the eleven-slice MND to. With noisy data, the sine-amplitude method improved the average MND values for all tested liver levels when the total heart counts were 2.1-53 times a typical clinical acquisition, depending on the axial range. Significance. For time-varying SPECT data, the sine-amplitude approach can broaden the applicability of exponential data consistency conditions in non-homogeneous attenuation.

title: Towards artificial intelligence based preoperative dosimetry for liver 90 Y selective internal radiation therapy.
abstract: Objective. Selective internal radiation therapy delivers Y-90 microspheres through the hepatic arterial system to achieve tumoricidal absorbed dose while limiting normal-tissue irradiation. Current pre-treatment dosimetry requires angiography and 99 mTc-MAA imaging, resulting in an invasive and resource-intensive workflow. This study evaluates the feasibility of estimating post-therapy Y-90 dose distribution directly from diagnostic multiphasic CT using an automated deep-learning pipeline, without requiring angiography or surrogate-particle imaging. Approach. In 152 treatments from the multicenter PROACTIF registry, arterial- and portal-phase CT, together with clinically documented perfusion territories and injected activities, were processed through automated segmentation, rigid registration, differential CT generation, and a generative model synthesizing a PET-like Y-90 activity map. Absorbed-dose maps were computed using the Local Dose Deposition method, and predictive accuracy was assessed using tumor dose-volume metrics and voxelwise spatial agreement. Main results. For the best-performing configuration, the median tumor D70 error was 23 Gy, with substantial inter-patient variability reflecting the challenges of CT-only dose prediction. High-dose coverage (V200) showed a similar pattern. In contrast, spatial agreement was consistently strong, with perfused-volume gamma passing rates around 93% and tumor-level rates around 85%, indicating that the macro-scale distribution of microspheres can be approximated from diagnostic CT. The full pipeline was fully automated and produced predictive dosimetry in under 30 S. Significance. Pre-angiography CT contains exploitable information about arterial enhancement and perfusion patterns that enables feasible CT-only prediction of Y-90 spatial distribution. While tumor-level absorbed-dose metrics remain variable, the strong spatial agreement suggests potential utility as an early planning tool to support patient selection or guide catheterization strategy prior to angiography.

title: An imaging framework for nuclei-based three-dimensional cell quantification in intact tissue using phase-contrast x-ray CT.
abstract: Objective. Quantitative analysis of cellular morphology and spatial organisation within intact tissue remains challenging, particularly when three-dimensional information must be preserved. This study investigates whether laboratory propagation-based phase-contrast x-ray computed tomography (CT) can support nuclei-based quantitative analysis in unstained tissue while retaining the surrounding tissue architecture. Approach. We propose a nuclei-based quantitative imaging workflow that combines laboratory propagation-based phase-contrast x-ray CT with volumetric segmentation. Intact unstained liver tissue was imaged at cellular resolution, then nuclei were segmented throughout the reconstructed volume and quantitative metrics describing the nuclear morphology and spatial organisation were extracted. The resulting measurements were evaluated in two non-overlapping volumes of interest and compared with histological reference data using thickness-matched virtual CT slices. Main results. The proposed workflow enabled visualisation and segmentation of individual nuclei throughout intact unstained liver tissue. Comparable nuclear morphology and spatial organisation metrics were obtained from two non-overlapping volumes of interest, indicating stable segmentation performance within the analysed specimen. Comparison with H&E histology demonstrated broad agreement in nuclear morphology. Significance. This work demonstrates the feasibility of nuclei-based quantitative analysis using laboratory phase-contrast x-ray CT in intact unstained tissue. The approach provides volumetric cellular information while preserving tissue architecture and may complement conventional histological assessment in applications requiring three-dimensional analysis. These findings highlight the potential of laboratory phase-contrast CT for quantitative tissue characterisation and spatial cellular analysis.

title: Decay-time correction for dual-panel in-beam PET monitoring of carbon-ion SOBP irradiation.
abstract: Objective. In-beam positron emission tomography (PET) is a promising technique for monitoring beam range and activity distribution in carbon-ion radiotherapy. However, spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) delivery introduces a challenge because sequentially delivered energy layers experience different decay times in-beam and off-beam PET acquisitions. This study developed a decay-time correction method to reduce temporal bias in measured PET activity distributions under SOBP irradiation. Approach. A dual-panel LYSO-SiPM PET system in a 4 × 1 module arrangement, with an effective detection area of 21.28 × 5.32 cm 2 , was used to acquire in-beam and off-beam PET images during homogeneous solid-water phantom irradiation. The beam was delivered in scanning mode using sequential high-to-low energy layers, with up to 11 layers ranging from 216.50-263.23 MeV u -1 . Four irradiation schemes were evaluated: physical-dose, relative biological effectiveness-weighted dose (RWD), full-opposing-field RWD, and half-opposing-field RWD SOBP. A Monte Carlo-based decay-time correction framework was established by incorporating beam delivery timing, radionuclide decay characteristics, and activity accumulation. Corrected PET images were compared with Monte Carlo-simulated activity distributions generated using a platform consistent with the experimental setup. Main Results. Sequential energy-layer delivery and radionuclide decay affected measured PET activity distributions under SOBP irradiation. After correction, experimental PET profiles showed improved agreement with corresponding Monte Carlo profiles across all four SOBP schemes. Depending on the irradiation scheme and acquisition mode, the correction reduced root-mean-square error by approximately 7.1%-73.1%, reduced SOBP-region mean absolute deviation by approximately 7.0%-72.2%, and increased the Pearson correlation coefficient from 0.861-0.973 before correction to 0.947-0.980 after correction. Significance. This study addressed temporal bias in PET activity distributions caused by decay-time differences among sequentially delivered energy layers during carbon-ion SOBP irradiation. The proposed correction improved the reliability and interpretability of dual-panel in-beam PET under sequential multi-energy carbon-ion irradiation, extending planar PET monitoring toward more treatment-relevant verification scenarios.

title: Comparison of proton, helium-ion, and carbon-ion CT imaging for hadron radiotherapy using Monte Carlo simulations.
abstract: Objective . To perform a comprehensive comparative analysis of proton, helium-ion, and carbon-ion computed tomography (CT) as direct imaging modalities for hadron therapy treatment planning, focusing on relative stopping power (RSP) reconstruction accuracy and patient radiation dose. Approach . High-fidelity Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using the GATE/Geant4 platform to model a standard CTP404 phantom. RSP maps were reconstructed using two iterative algorithms: the simultaneous algebraic reconstruction technique and the Richardson-Lucy deconvolution. Imaging performance was evaluated by comparing reconstructed RSP values against ground truth data for various tissue-equivalent inserts, while integral doses were estimated for a human head geometry using a Shepp-Logan-like phantom. Main results . All investigated particle modalities demonstrated a significant dose reduction compared to conventional x-ray CT protocols (which are approximately 40 mGy). The estimated imaging doses weremGy for protons,mGy for helium ions, andmGy for carbon ions. In terms of accuracy, carbon-ion imaging achieved promising accuracy for soft-tissue materials (mean absolute error). Helium ions offered a balanced performance with sub-errors for most materials and a dose burden significantly lower than carbon ions. Protons exhibited the widest range of RSP deviations. Significance . Direct particle imaging eliminates the systematic uncertainties inherent in photon-to-hadron conversion, which typically introduce RSP deviations of 1.6%-3.5% in standard single-energy x-ray CT. While carbon ions provide better RSP reconstruction precision essential for complex treatment plans in heterogeneous anatomy, helium and proton imaging offer exceptional dose sparing, making them particularly advantageous for pediatric patients and frequent adaptive replanning scenarios.

title: Impact of depth-of-interaction and spatially-variant point-spread-function model on the performance of ultra-high resolution brain PET.
abstract: Objective. To implement a spatially-variant point spread function (VarPSF) model for the NeuroEXPLORER (NX) brain positron emission tomography (PET) scanner in the open-source Yale Reconstruction Toolkit for PET, and investigate the interplay between depth-of-interaction (DOI) resolution and resolution modeling. Approach. PSF parameters were estimated from simulated and physically measured point sources. Three primary DOI configurations were evaluated: eight-layer DOI (8DOI), two-layer DOI (2DOI), and no DOI (noDOI), with an additional 4DOI comparison in the off-center simulated Derenzo study. Reconstructions using VarPSF, a spatially-invariant PSF measured at the field-of-view center (SinglePSF), and no PSF modeling (noPSF) were assessed using simulated Derenzo and brain phantoms, a physical Derenzo phantom, and one non-human primate (NHP) scan. Main results. In simulated and physical Derenzo studies, VarPSF yielded higher peak-to-valley ratios than SinglePSF and noPSF at the final evaluated iterations, with pronounced gains at large radial offsets. In the simulated brain phantom, VarPSF reduced the estimated transverse blur by 0.3 mm relative to SinglePSF and 0.5 mm relative to noPSF in 2DOI, and by 0.6 mm and 0.8 mm, respectively, in noDOI. In the NHP study, VarPSF improved contrast and structural delineation with reduced DOI encoding at approximately matched white-matter coefficient of variation, while its incremental benefit over SinglePSF was small with 8DOI at clinically relevant iteration settings. Significance. Spatially-variant PSF modeling can partially compensate for limited DOI information. The findings motivate combining modest DOI capability with accurate resolution modeling, while further validation is required for redesigned detectors and fully corrected acquisitions. The open-source implementation enables controlled investigation of the complementary roles of DOI encoding and resolution modeling.

title: AnF-DiffPET: anatomy- and frequency-guided diffusion for simulated low-dose PET/CT denoising.
abstract: Objective. Positron emission tomography (PET) provides essential functional information for disease assessment. However, reducing injected activity or acquisition time produces low-dose (LD) PET with stronger count-dependent noise and less reliable uptake quantification. Diffusion models offer a promising solution for PET denoising by progressively recovering high-dose (HD) PET images from LD inputs. However, LD-to-HD PET denoising remains challenging because of limited anatomical guidance, unstable multi-scale feature propagation, and inaccurate recovery of uptake patterns in the frequency domain. Approach. We propose AnF-DiffPET, an anatomy- and frequency-guided diffusion framework for computed tomography (CT)-conditioned LD PET denoising. The framework integrates anatomical-frequency guidance, Multi-Scale Cross-Transformer Reconstruction, and Frequency-Contrastive Hard Mining to enhance anatomy-aware feature modulation and frequency-domain consistency during denoising. Main results. Experimental results across four simulated LD PET/CT datasets show that the proposed method improves image fidelity, anatomical consistency, and quantitative fidelity over representative CNN-based, GAN-based, Transformer-based, Mamba-based, and diffusion-based methods. Significance. AnF-DiffPET provides a PET/CT-specific diffusion restoration framework that combines anatomical guidance, multi-scale feature reconstruction, and frequency-domain regularization for LD PET denoising. The code and trained models will be publicly released upon acceptance.
