title: X-ray projection-guided deformation vector field estimation and dynamic CBCT imaging using patient-specific vector-quantized diffusion.
abstract: Objective. To develop a conditional vector-quantized (VQ) diffusion-based dynamic cone beam computed tomography imaging framework using dual-view x-ray projections for accurate reconstruction of respiratory-induced lung tumor motion, with the potential to enable four-dimensional (4D) target verification during lung radiotherapy. Methods. Patient-specific respiratory motion models were constructed from planning 4D- computed tomography(CT) images using deformable image registration and principal component analysis (PCA). Synthetic DVFs were generated by sampling PCA coefficients and applied to the reference-phase CT images to produce dynamic three-dimensional (3D) volumes, from which paired dual-view DRRs were generated. A conditional VQ diffusion framework was developed, consisting of separate two-dimensional and 3D vector quantized variational autoencoder s for encoding DRRs and DVFs into discrete latent representations, followed by a conditional diffusion model to learn the mapping from x-ray projection features to deformation vector field (DVF) latent representations. During inference, dual-view x-ray projections were encoded and processed by the conditional diffusion model to estimate DVFs, which were then used to deform the reference CT image and reconstruct temporally resolved 3D volumes. Results. The simulation study demonstrates that the estimated DVFs effectively captured the respiratory-induced deformation of lung tumors, and the reconstructed dynamic volume CT images demonstrated accurate anatomical motion characteristics across respiratory phases. Conclusion. The proposed patient-specific VQ diffusion framework enables accurate estimation of respiratory-induced lung tumor motion from dual-view x-ray projections and facilitates the high-temporal-resolution dynamic volume CT reconstruction. The results demonstrate its potential as an image-guided solution for tumor motion tracking in lung tumor radiotherapy.

title: Generative modeling of complex-valued brain MRI data.
abstract: Objective. Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction pipelines discard phase information captured during acquisition, despite its sensitivity to tissue properties that are not represented by magnitude alone. The aim of this study is to develop a generative framework that jointly models magnitude and phase information in complex-valued brain MRI data and enables the conditional generation of MRI samples representing normal and abnormal brain tissue. Approach. The proposed generative framework combines a conditional variational autoencoder, which compresses complex-valued MRI scans into latent representations while preserving phase coherence, with a flow-matching-based generative model. Synthetic sample quality is assessed using a real-versus-synthetic classifier, image-space coverage tests, and downstream classifiers trained on synthetic data for abnormal tissue detection. Main results. The autoencoder preserves phase coherence above 0.997. Real-vs-synthetic classifiers yielded low AUROCs between 0.53 and 0.64 for generated phase images supporting realistic phase modeling. Magnitude was moderately distinguishable, with AUROCs between 0.53 and 0.82, suggesting appreciable overlap between real and synthetic sample distributions while also indicating a distribution shift for several sequences. Image-space coverage was broad. On the held-out test split, no consistent directional difference from the matched real-to-real references was detected in any evaluated setting, while the training split showed slight to moderate undercoverage depending on acquisition sequence and tissue condition. In downstream normal-versus-abnormal classification, classifiers trained entirely on synthetic data achieve an AUROC of 0.880, surpassing the real-data baseline of 0.842 on the fastMRI dataset. This advantage persists on an independent external test set with biopsy-confirmed labels. Significance. The proposed framework demonstrates the feasibility of jointly modeling magnitude and phase information for normal and abnormal complex-valued brain MRI data. Beyond synthetic data generation, the framework enables future investigation of how magnitude and phase jointly encode pathology-specific features once sufficiently large raw MRI datasets with fine-grained, pathology-confirmed labels become available.

title: A wavelet-guided diffusion method for brain magnetic resonance parameter mapping using MOLED-based datasets: proof-of-principle.
abstract: Objective. Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (qMRI) can noninvasively acquire parametric maps, providing quantitative biomarkers for clinical assessment. Parametric maps, such as T 2 , T 2 * , and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), characterize distinct biophysical processes in tissue in an interpretable, numerical manner. Owing to their distinct physical origins, various parametric maps differ in physical units, numerical magnitudes, and dynamic ranges. Even for the same type of parametric map, inter-subject differences may still exist in anatomical morphology, tissue characteristics, and the local distributions of parameter values. However, deep learning methods trained in image-domain directly learn pixel-level parameter values, and variations in numerical scales and subject-specific parameter distributions may result in anatomical detail loss and localized artifacts in certain tasks. To address this challenge and to deliver dependable quantitative references for clinical assessment, we propose a wavelet-guided diffusion method. Approach. We extend the discrete convolution wavelet transform (DCWT) to two dimensions and combine it with a conditional denoising diffusion method to develop a diffusion-based DCWT (Diff-DCWT) for parameter mapping. Diff-DCWT achieves accurate parameter mapping under the guidance of wavelet coefficient maps, thereby reducing reliance on image domain learning. The performance of Diff-DCWT is evaluated through simulation and in vivo experiments across T 2 , T 2 * , and ADC mapping tasks. Main Results. Both simulation and healthy volunteer experiments demonstrate that T 2 , T 2 * , and ADC maps obtained from Diff-DCWT maintain excellent visual quality and quantitative accuracy. Clinical case studies suggest the potential utility of Diff-DCWT-derived T 2 and ADC maps for stroke staging and help distinguish lesional from normal brain regions in glioma. Significance. Diff-DCWT establishes a high-fidelity framework for parameter mapping and exhibits preliminary clinical value in stroke staging and glioma characterization. Moreover, this work demonstrates the potential of wavelet-domain prior guidance for deep learning-based qMRI applications.

title: Learned proximal gradient flow matching for limited-angle CT reconstruction.
abstract: Objective. The primary objective of this research is to address the challenges of limited-angle computed tomography (CT) reconstruction, which arises when projection data is acquired over an angular range smaller than required for theoretically exact reconstruction. This ill-posed problem leads to serious artifacts that compromise diagnostic quality. The study aims to develop a robust and efficient framework to achieve high-fidelity image reconstruction. Approach. The proposed method, termed learned proximal gradient flow matching (LPGFM), introduces a novel framework that synergistically combines explicit optimization principles with deep generative models. First, a pre-trained flow matching network is applied to transform the initialized solution along a learned gradient field, effectively removing artifacts while preserving anatomical details. Secondly, a proximal correction step enforces strict data consistency, enhancing robustness against deviations. This approach decouples data fidelity from prior application, preventing error propagation and ensuring stability, particularly under out-of-distribution conditions. Main results. The proposed LPGFM method demonstrates significant advantages in limited-angle CT (LACT) reconstruction. Experiments on the medical and head datasets show that LPGFM outperforms comparative methods. Quantitative evaluations reveal that LPGFM achieves the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index scores with the lowest RMSE. For instance, in the 150medical data, LPGFM attains a PSNR of 30.14 dB, indicating superior artifact suppression and detail preservation. Under the more challenging 120condition, LPGFM maintains robustness with minimal quality degradation, highlighting its generalization capability. Significance. This work signifies a paradigm shift in LACT reconstruction by bridging the gap between model-based optimization and data-driven generative models. The LPGFM framework offers theoretical advantages, such as interpretability and robustness, while practical benefits include reduced reliance on large training datasets and adaptability to diverse scanning geometries. Its ability to deliver high-quality reconstructions under extreme limited-angle conditions has implications for clinical applications.

title: Smooth total variation regularization for interference detection and elimination (STRIDE) for MRI.
abstract: Objective. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is increasingly required to operate near electronic devices that emit dynamic electromagnetic interference (EMI). Existing reference-channel EMI removal methods estimate a transfer function between EMI sensors and imaging coils from the measured data alone, and do not use prior knowledge about the structure of MR images. We develop and validate an EMI removal method that uses the inherent spatial smoothness of MR images as an additional prior, demonstrated on a head-only 0.5 T scanner. Approach. Smooth total variation regularization for interference detection and elimination (STRIDE) operates in the image domain. For each image column, EMI sensor data are combined and subtracted from the imaging coil data such that the2 norm of the total variation (TV) along the readout direction is minimized. This exploits the smoothness of MR images, a property well-known in compressed sensing but not previously used in EMI removal. STRIDE was evaluated on phantom and in-vivo brain datasets under EMI scenarios replicating sources encountered at our affiliated hospitals, and compared against two implementations of External Dynamic Interference Estimation and Removal (EDITER). Main results. STRIDE produced visually better EMI removal and generally higher temporal signal-to-noise ratio than both EDITER implementations, with comparable EMI removal percentage. STRIDE also resulted in lower or equal root-mean-square error than both EDITER implementations in all 8 phantom EMI conditions tested. These results held across both phantom and in-vivo datasets. Significance. STRIDE shows that incorporating known properties of MR images into the EMI removal problem provides meaningful improvements over methods that rely on measured data alone. The approach is deterministic, training-free, sequence-independent, and compatible with existing EMI sensor hardware. STRIDE therefore extends reference-channel EMI removal to scenarios where existing methods fail, particularly point-of-care and interventional MRI outside fully shielded environments, providing a deterministic, training-free alternative to machine-learning approaches.

title: Domain-aligned self-supervision: CT-specialized DINOv3 enhances PET/CT tumor segmentation.
abstract: Objective. This study investigates how domain-aligned self-supervised pretraining influences downstream PET/CT tumor segmentation, with a focus on disentangling the roles of domain proximity and pretraining dataset scale. Approach. We compared nnU-Net segmentation models initialized from random weights or from DINOv3 encoders pretrained on natural images, x-ray mammography, CT, or PET, using datasets of different sizes. To disentangle the effects of pretraining domain and dataset size, CT-DINOv3 encoders were pretrained using different numbers of 2D CT slices, including subsets matched in size to the pretraining datasets from other domains. Models were evaluated on two PET/CT benchmarks, autoPET (whole-body, FDG/prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)) and HECKTOR (head-and-neck primary tumors and metastatic lymph nodes), using five-fold cross-validation with frozen encoders. Main results. CT-pretrained models achieved the highest Dice scores for lymph nodes, FDG lesions, and PSMA lesions. For primary tumors, PET pretraining produced the highest observed Dice score, followed by CT pretraining, suggesting the potential benefit of in-domain representations when PET data are sufficient. Notably, PET pretraining exceeded size-matched CT pretraining for PSMA but remained below models pretrained on larger CT datasets for both PSMA and FDG targets. In contrast, natural-image pretraining did not outperform from-scratch training despite its much larger pretraining scale, indicating that scale alone is insufficient when domain proximity is low. Across comparisons, strong transfer reflected the combination of domain proximity and sufficient pretraining scale, especially for CT-based models with broad data availability. Significance. These results demonstrate that both domain proximity and dataset scale jointly determine the effectiveness of self-supervised pretraining. While higher domain alignment improves performance at comparable scale, sufficient data is required to realize this benefit. CT-based pretraining provides a favorable balance between domain relevance and data availability, leading to robust performance across tasks. This study provides practical guidance for selecting pretraining strategies in PET/CT segmentation.

title: ReCo-Diff: residual-conditioned deterministic sampling for cold diffusion in sparse-view CT.
abstract: Objective. Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation dose and acquisition time but introduces structured streak artifacts that make reconstruction severely ill-posed. Cold-diffusion approaches can model such deterministic degradation processes, but existing sampling strategies may rely on scalar similarity criteria and predefined thresholds to trigger sample-adaptive resets of the degradation-level trajectory. We aim to replace this threshold-based sampling control with spatially resolved residual conditioning. Approach. We propose ReCo-Diff, a residual-conditioned cold-diffusion framework for sparse-view CT reconstruction. At each reverse step, a zero-residual baseline prediction is re-degraded using the CT degradation operator, and the resulting signed image-domain re-degradation discrepancy is used as a spatial conditioning map for a second restoration pass. ReCo-Diff does not require an adaptive reset during residual-conditioned sampling and instead follows a predetermined degradation schedule. A one-time level transition is additionally used for highly sparse inputs. The method was evaluated on the AAPM Low-Dose CT dataset under 18-, 36-, and 72-view settings using a patient-wise split with one held-out test volume. Main results. ReCo-Diff achieved PSNR values of 38.54, 42.57, and 46.98 dB at 18, 36, and 72 views, respectively. At 18 views, matched-computation analysis showed that ReCo-Diff achieved 38.54 dB compared with 38.25 dB for a two-pass zero-residual control under the same 18-NFE budget. A spatially shifted-residual control achieved 37.65 dB, indicating that effective residual conditioning benefits from spatial correspondence with the current degraded state. Significance. ReCo-Diff replaces adaptive trajectory control with step-wise spatial residual conditioning in deterministic cold diffusion. Matched-computation analysis shows that the reconstruction benefit depends on spatially aligned residual information rather than on the additional network evaluation alone. The proposed strategy provides an alternative approach to controlling error propagation under a predetermined degradation schedule without relying on sample-adaptive reset decisions.

The method was evaluated on the AAPM Low-Dose CT dataset under 18-, 36-, and 72-view settings using a patient-wise split with one held-out test volume.Main results.ReCo-Diff achieved PSNR values of 38.54, 42.57, and 46.98 dB at 18, 36, and 72 views, respectively. At 18 views, matched-computation analysis showed that ReCo-Diff achieved 38.54 dB compared with 38.25 dB for a two-pass zero-residual control under the same 18-NFE budget. A spatially shifted-residual control achieved 37.65 dB, indicating that effective residual conditioning benefits from spatial correspondence with the current degraded state.Significance.ReCo-Diff replaces adaptive trajectory control with step-wise spatial residual conditioning in deterministic cold diffusion. Matched-computation analysis shows that the reconstruction benefit depends on spatially aligned residual information rather than on the additional network evaluation alone. The proposed strategy provides an alternative approach to controlling error propagation under a predetermined degradation schedule without relying on sample-adaptive reset decisions.

title: A harmonisation framework for multi-centre preclinical PET imaging across a national research infrastructure.
abstract: Objective. Quantitative preclinical positron emission tomography (PET) imaging plays an important role in translational research, yet variability across scanners, sites, and analysis workflows remains a major barrier to robust multi-centre studies. In this work, we developed and evaluated a harmonisation framework across a national network of preclinical PET facilities. Approach. Six identical National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) NU 4-2008 image quality phantoms were manufactured and distributed to six sites, where they were imaged using local acquisition and reconstruction protocols across multiple scanner platforms. Main Results. Substantial variability in contrast recovery, uniformity, and spill-over ratios was observed under site-specific conditions. Centralised automated re-analysis produced only minor reductions in variability, indicating that inter-user effects were relatively small, compared to site-specific protocol variations. In contrast, optimisation of reconstruction parameters led to a marked reduction in inter-scanner variability (an average of 60% reduction across larger rods), particularly for voxel-wise maximum contrast recovery coefficients (CRC), which are more sensitive to noise and reconstruction settings than the standard axial averaging NEMA CRC metric. Following harmonisation, the variability of CRCapproached and was lower that of conventional axial-averaged NEMA analysis (CRC), with reductions ranging 7%-33% across the 1-5 mm rods, demonstrating improved quantitative consistency even at the voxel level. Significance. These findings show that scanner and site-specific protocol variations are the dominant factors for harmonisation in preclinical PET. By systematically evaluating acquisition, image reconstruction and analysis related sources of variability across a national network of heterogeneous preclinical PET systems, this work provides a practical framework for harmonisation. The proposed framework is conceptually aligned with clinical harmonisation initiatives such as EARL and provides a practical basis for the future development of harmonised performance ranges across preclinical scanners. This enables more reliable multi-centre studies and supports the use of quantitative, voxel-wise imaging biomarkers in translational research.

title: High-fidelity 3D geometric reconstruction of pelvic organs from MRI: a hybrid deep learning and iterative optimization approach.
abstract: Objective The generation of high-fidelity, high-quality three-dimensional (3D) pelvic organ geometries from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived segmentation masks remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a hybrid framework for reconstructing the bladder, uterus, and rectum, and to assess its geometric fidelity, mesh-quality proxy performance, and reconstruction efficiency. Approach. We developed a hybrid deformable shape modeling framework that integrates deep learning prediction with iterative optimization for the reconstruction of the bladder, uterus, and rectum. The framework consists of three core components: (1) a geometry-aware multi-level deep learning architecture that preserves topological consistency of pelvic organs; (2) a two-stage amortized optimization training strategy that balances global shape capture and local surface refinement; and (3) a holistic synergy mechanism-where iterative optimization provides supervision for deep learning during the training phase, and during inference, deep learning rapidly predicts the global organ morphology, followed by iterative optimization to refine local surfaces and mesh quality. Main results. Before iterative refinement, the proposed model outperformed representative deep learning-based reconstruction methods in geometric fidelity, achieving CD/DSC values of 5.5 × 10⁻³/0.788 for the bladder, 3.7 × 10⁻³/0.839 for the rectum, and 4.2 × 10⁻³/0.900 for the uterus. Deep learning-based initialization enabled the complete hybrid framework to converge within approximately 100 iterations, with a reconstruction time of approximately 35 s per organ on a CPU and 1.5 s on a GPU. At the patient level, the mean minSICN and minSIGE values of the 10 worst volumetric elements were 0.0807 and 0.0844, respectively, exceeding those achieved by traditional geometric post-processing methods. Significance. The proposed framework connects image-domain segmentation with structural-domain applications by efficiently generating high-fidelity, high-quality pelvic organ geometries with improved mesh-quality proxy performance. These geometries may support statistical shape assessment and may provide candidate surface representations for subsequent volumetric meshing and solver-specific biomechanical validation.

title: Adaptive physics-inspired angular-spatial modeling for multi-shell diffusion MRI denoising.
abstract: Objective . Multi-shell diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) provides rich q-space information but is susceptible to noise, which can disrupt spatial anatomy, intra-shell directional relationships, inter-shell signal attenuation, and downstream diffusion parameter estimation. We aim to develop a denoising method that jointly preserves spatial structure, directional information, and shell-specific signal characteristics. Approach . We propose ASD-NCSM, an adaptive physics-inspired angular-spatial framework with a fixed three-stage alternating architecture. It combines intra-shell differential angular graph message passing with 2.5D spatial residual refinement. Noise-Conditioned Shell Modulation (NCSM) adaptively regulates angular updates according to b -value, spatial residual and angular dispersion proxies, and local gating. A Shell-wise Physical Attenuation and Angular Relation Consistency objective further constrains shell-wise signal fidelity, logarithmic attenuation, and local angular structure. The model was evaluated on Human Connectome Project multi-shell dMRI with simulated noise and independently acquired real in vivo brain dMRI data. Main results . Across five simulated noise levels from 2% to 10%, ASD-NCSM achieved the best overall DWI restoration among MPPCA, 1D-CNN, ECDM, SAN2N, and dMRI-Swin, with consistent subject-level advantages in PSNR, SSIM, and NRMSE. At 6% noise, principal-direction angular nRMSE was 32.68 ± 2.76%, with significant differences from all five baselines after Holm correction. ASD-NCSM also achieved the lowest mean MAE for FA, MD, AD, and RD, and the lowest relative MAE for ODI and FISO, while NDI was comparable to 1D-CNN and dMRI-Swin. For real data without noise-free references, Q-PEFT yielded the lowest angular cross-fit inconsistency (2.29 ± 0.10%) across three test subjects while maintaining limited signal and downstream-parameter changes. Significance. ASD-NCSM jointly preserves spatial continuity, directional geometry, and shell-level attenuation, providing balanced signal recovery, directional preservation, and downstream parameter stability for multi-shell dMRI denoising.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
abstract: Objective. Limited-angle cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is attractive for image-guided radiotherapy and imaging-guided procedures when full-arc acquisition is impractical, but the incomplete angular sampling leads to severe streaking, shading, and structural distortion. This study aimed to develop a physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction framework for recovering anatomically faithful volumetric CBCT from short-arc limited-angle projections. Approach. We propose a physics-constrained and geometry-aware network (PCGA-Net), a dual-domain reconstruction framework that combines projection completion, analytic geometric reconstruction, and image-domain refinement within a unified cross-domain design. Specifically, a projection completion module first estimates missing-angle information from the measured limited-angle projections. A geometry-aware reconstruction module then maps the completed projections into image space using differentiable cone-beam forward and backward-projection operators. Finally, a volumetric refinement module suppresses residual artifacts and restores anatomical detail under geometry-guided cross-domain consistency supervision. The framework was evaluated on three clinically distinct cohorts: gynecologic (GYN) high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy, abdominal liver four-dimensional computed tomography (4DCT), and head-and-neck (H&N) CBCT. Main results. Across all three cohorts, fully adapted PCGA-Net consistently outperformed conventional limited-angle Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstruction and the compared learning-based baselines, a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) and PatRecon-Net, in both qualitative and quantitative evaluation under matched patient-specific adaptation conditions. On the GYN HDR brachytherapy cohort, PCGA-Net achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 34.47 ± 6.28 Hounsfield units (HU), a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.87 ± 0.04, and a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 35.79 ± 0.95 dB, compared with 178.63 ± 31.58 HU, 0.51 ± 0.03, and 18.97 ± 1.31 dB for FDK. On the abdominal liver 4DCT cohort, PCGA-Net achieved 39.27 ± 6.10 HU MAE, 0.82 ± 0.03 SSIM, and 36.85 ± 1.16 dB PSNR, versus 195.21 ± 40.08 HU, 0.50 ± 0.06, and 18.50 ± 1.50 dB for FDK. On the H&N CBCT cohort, PCGA-Net achieved 28.42 ± 4.88 HU MAE, 0.91 ± 0.05 SSIM, and 38.52 ± 0.95 dB PSNR, compared with 165.30 ± 25.40 HU, 0.61 ± 0.05, and 21.13 ± 1.14 dB for FDK. In all three cohorts, PCGA-Net also exceeded cGAN and PatRecon-Net across all evaluated metrics. Significance. These results indicate that jointly enforcing projection-domain completion, analytic imaging geometry, and image-domain refinement is an effective strategy for limited-angle CBCT reconstruction. PCGA-Net provides a robust short-arc reconstruction framework across multiple anatomical sites and clinical workflows, supporting its potential utility in constrained image-guided therapeutic and procedural settings.

title: Dimensionality reduction for partial-volume correction in quantitative SPECT.
abstract: Objective . The aim of this paper is to develop a method for region-based post-reconstruction partial-volume correction (PVC) of single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) images, which explicitly estimates the mean activity concentration in regions without assuming strict intra-regional uniformity. Approach . PVC was applied to 177 Lu-SPECT images obtained from the simulation of eight anthropomorphic phantoms as well as two example patients. Both sets of data were reconstructed using OS-EM with ten subsets and up to 40 iterations, including compensation for attenuation, scatter, and spatial resolution. Reconstructed images were deconvolved using the van Cittert algorithm and Lucy-Richardson algorithm, both implemented on images represented as standard cuboid voxels or as regional voxels, consisting of regions defined from whole-image segmentation. Methods embedding regional voxels were applied both assuming region-wise uniform activity concentration and incorporating perturbations in the form of cosine series to relax the uniformity assumption. For comparison, images were also processed with the iterative Yang method and MIRD recovery coefficients. Evaluation was performed with respect to the estimated activity concentration for kidneys, spleen, and tumours, as well as the total activity in the images. Main results . Mean activity-concentration errors prior to PVC were (-22.6 ± 11.5) %, (-13.8 ± 2.1) %, and (-7.4 ± 2.8) % for tumours, kidneys, and spleen, respectively. Region-perturbed van Cittert deconvolution with order 4 reduced these errors to (2.3 ± 7.7) %, (0.3 ± 2.2) %, and (4.0 ± 1.6) % while the errors for region-perturbed Lucy-Richardson deconvolution of order 4 were (0.3 ± 8.0) %, (0.0 ± 1.6) %, (2.6 ± 0.5) %. Corresponding results for the iterative Yang method were (2.8 ± 21) %, (-0.3 ± 2.1) %, and (3.8 ± 2.4) % and using MIRD recovery coefficients (-5.0 ± 14.2) %, (-7.1 ± 1.9) %, and (-0.6 ± 3.1) %. Significance . Region-based PVC improves the accuracy of quantitative SPECT, and the inclusion of cosine perturbations allows for a gradual relaxation of the uniformity assumption.

title: Nonlinear stability phenotypes and collapse dynamics of multi-organ radiomics in total-body PET imaging: toward digital twin-oriented robustness assessment.
abstract: Objective. Radiomics analysis in positron emission tomography (PET) offers a high-dimensional representation of tissue characteristics, yet its reliability is limited by sensitivity to acquisition perturbations, particularly dose reduction. This study aims to introduce a nonlinear stability phenotyping framework to characterize dose-response behavior of multi-organ radiomics and evaluate their potential relevance for future digital twin-oriented applications. Approach. A multi-center dataset of 550 total-body PET scans was analyzed. Dose reduction was simulated using list-mode subsampling (dose reduction factor - DRF = 2-100). A total of 107 radiomics features were extracted per organ. Stability was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficient and summarized as stability fractions. Nonlinear models were fitted to organ- and feature-level trajectories. Stability phenotypes and critical thresholds were derived, along with organ-level instability metrics. Main results. Radiomics stability exhibited strongly nonlinear, organ-dependent behavior. Feature-level analysis identified frequent sigmoid-associated collapse patterns with high descriptive model fits ( R 2 > 0.90). The liver showed the highest instability burden (30.8% unstable features), followed by esophagus and kidneys (18%-20%). Texture features were the primary source of instability, whereas shape features remained robust. Organ-level trajectories demonstrated heterogeneous responses, with some organs maintaining high stability (0.80-0.95) across DRFs, while others showed sharp declines (down to 0.64). Linear (stable) behavior dominated at the organ level, though masking underlying nonlinear feature dynamics. Significance. Radiomics stability in total-body PET follows nonlinear, phenotype-driven dynamics with identifiable tipping points and organ-specific sensitivity. The proposed framework provides a behavior-based approach for evaluating radiomics robustness and supports the selection of reliable features and organs for robust quantitative imaging and may inform future digital twin-oriented applications.

title: Spot-wise compensation of proton beam deflection and radiation field deformation in the transverse magnetic field of an in-beam MR scanner using a research version of a commercial treatment planning system.
abstract: Objective Magnetic resonance-integrated proton therapy (MRiPT) offers the potential for high-precision, image-guided particle therapy but is challenged by magnetic field (MF)-induced proton beam deflection and radiation field deformation. Unless compensated for, these effects compromise dose conformity and prohibit clinical implementation. This work aims to develop and experimentally validate a spot-wise compensation method capable of restoring proton dose distributions in the presence of a measured 3D magnetic vector field map within a clinical treatment planning system (TPS). Approach A spot-wise compensation framework was implemented in a research version of RayStation, a TPS commercially available for clinical use. The method compensates both lateral beam deflection and MF-induced radiation field deformation by shifting individual pencil-beam spots based on displacement vectors derived from dose calculations in water phantoms using the measured MF of an in-beam MR scanner integrated with a horizontal proton beamline. Two complementary strategies were implemented: a patient-specific approach based on plan-specific displacement calculations, and a generic approach using precomputed displacement maps derived from a reference phantom. Compensation performance was evaluated in representative clinical cases. Dose distributions were experimentally validated using 2D ionisation chamber array measurements. Main Results Both compensation methods effectively restored target coverage, dose homogeneity, and organ-at-risk sparing to the level of no-MF reference plans. The patient-specific method generally achieved a higher performance, whereas the generic compensation method enabled rapid automated correction with sufficient accuracy for clinical workflows involving deep-seated tumours. Local γ-analysis demonstrated excellent agreement between measured and calculated doses, with pass rates exceeding 98.5% for 3%/3 mm criteria. Significance This work demonstrates that compensation of MF-induced proton beam deflection and field deformation can be achieved entirely within a research version of the RayStation TPS using measured, MR scanner-specific MF data. The proposed method provides a scalable, robust framework for future MRiPT clinical applications.&#xD.

title: Scatter correction for multi-source linear static CT via a geometry-aware parameter regression network with differentiable forward modeling.
abstract: Objective. Multi-source linear static CT (SLCT) offers high temporal resolution and a compact form factor by eliminating mechanical rotation. However, lateral offsets of peripheral x-ray beams break the rotational symmetry assumed by conventional scatter correction methods, resulting in location-dependent and asymmetric scatter point spread functions (PSFs). Approach. To address this challenge, we propose a scatter correction framework that integrates a geometry-aware analytical kernel with a parameter regression network (GAPR-Net). An explicit correction term is incorporated into the conventional cone-beam scatter kernel to model asymmetric PSF distortion induced by lateral source offsets. GAPR-Net learns scatter kernel hyperparameters associated with source geometry and object thickness from Monte Carlo pencil-beam data, while a differentiable forward model analytically estimates scatter and enables stable optimization under a geometric consistency loss. Main results. Extensive simulation experiments were performed using water, electron-density, and ICRP phantoms, together with a DICOM-derived head phantom reconstructed using the derived three-dimensional SLCT reconstruction algorithm. Compared with scatter kernel superposition, DSE, ResNet, and a static-computed tomography-specific 1D U-Net, GAPR-Net achieved consistent improvements. For the electron-density and ICRP phantoms, GAPR-Net achieved scatter-estimation mean absolute percentage errors (MAPEs) of 4.43% and 5.31%, respectively. In the reconstructed images, it achieved a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 29.51 dB for the electron-density phantom and reduced the MAPE of the ICRP thorax phantom from 14.69% to 6.07%. Head-phantom experiments at 80 kVp, 100 kVp, and 120 kVp further demonstrated stable performance across different x-ray spectra. A physical testbed experiment was conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed GAPR-Net under real conditions. Significance. GAPR-Net provides a physically interpretable and computationally efficient approach for correcting non-stationary asymmetric scatter artifacts in SLCT.

title: A cascade deep learning network for simultaneous prediction of dose and linear energy transfer in proton therapy of prostate cancer.
abstract: Objective Prediction of dose-averaged linear energy transfer (LETd) may facilitate LET-aware evaluation of proton therapy plans. This study developed a cascade deep learning framework for simultaneous three-dimensional prediction of dose and LETd distributions for conventional dose-based optimization (DoseOpt) and LETd-incorporated optimization (LETOpt) in prostate intensity-modulated proton therapy. Approach A total of 150 patients with prostate cancer were included, each with DoseOpt and LETOpt plans. Planning CT images and anatomical structure masks were used as inputs. The cascade network transferred an intermediate latent representation from the dose prediction pathway to the LETd prediction pathway. Stepwise, multitask, and anatomy-only LETd (only-LET) networks served as comparators. Model performance was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation. Main results All dose-predicting models showed high spatial agreement, with cascade Dice similarity coefficients of approximately 0.93, 0.96, and 0.95 for the 50%, 75%, and 95% prescription isodose volumes. No significant differences in structure-specific dose errors remained after false discovery rate correction. The cascade model achieved the lowest global LETd MAE for DoseOpt and LETOpt, 0.108 ± 0.025 and 0.111 ± 0.025 keV/μm, respectively, significantly lower than those of the multitask, stepwise, and only-LET models. Structure-specific LETd performance was endpoint dependent, with favorable cascade performance for several CTV and organ-at-risk endpoints. LETOpt primarily redistributed LETd while largely preserving dose, and the cascade model reproduced the principal plan-specific changes, including reductions in rectal and rectal-wall LETd. Mean inference time was 0.505 ± 0.020 s per patient. Significance The proposed framework enables rapid simultaneous prediction of dose and LETd for predefined planning strategies from patient anatomy without requiring a precomputed dose distribution, supporting LET-aware plan comparison and providing a basis for future LETd-guided biological optimization.

title: An uncertainty-aware deep learning-based registration model for adaptive lung cancer radiotherapy.
abstract: Objective To develop a deep learning (DL) based probabilistic 3D deformable image registration framework for uncertainty-aware dose accumulation in magnetic resonance imaging-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) of lung cancer. Approach: We propose TransMorph-prob (TM-prob), a variational Bayesian model that predicts the voxel-wise mean and variance of dense displacement fields (DDFs). Two TM-prob models were trained on an internal CT dataset (725 patients) and a low-field MR-linac dataset (102 patients), and benchmarked against Monte Carlo dropout TransMorph (TM-MCD) and DIRUncertainty with B-spline initialization (ASDIR) on the DIRLAB 4DCT dataset (10 patients, 3000 landmarks), and an annotated MR-linac dataset (16 patients, 107 image pairs, 227 landmarks) with target and seven organ-at-risk (OAR) contours. Both datasets contained an additional 1239/13,289 algorithm-generated landmarks. Performance was evaluated using target registration error (TRE), Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), landmark- and voxel-wise expected calibration errors (LECE/ECE), and dose distributions derived from 2000 DDF samples per patient. Main results: On the DIRLAB dataset, TM-prob achieved a median TRE of \qty{1.8}{\mm}/\qty{2.8}{\mm} on manual/algorithm-generated landmarks, versus \qty{1.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.4}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{2.1}{\mm}/\qty{3.0}{\mm} for TM-MCD. On the MRI dataset, TM-prob achieved the median TRE of \qty{3.9}{\mm}/\qty{2.6}{\mm} and a mean DSC of 0.87, matching ASDIR (\qty{3.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.7}{\mm}, and DSC of 0.87) while outperforming TM-MCD (\qty{4.4}{\mm}/\qty{2.9}{\mm}, and 0.84). In uncertainty calibration, TM-prob achieved a LECE of \qty{1.74}{\mm}/\qty{0.30}{\mm} on MRI manual/algorithm-generated landmarks versus \qty{2.41}{\mm}/\qty{0.56}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{6.65}{\mm}/\qty{3.92}{\mm} for TM-MCD, and an average contour ECE of 5.8% versus 7.0% and 21.2%. Two patients with indistinct GTV boundaries exhibited substantially wider target D95 distributions, demonstrating that calibrated DDF uncertainty translates into clinically relevant dose-coverage uncertainty. Significance: TM-prob is an end-to-end DL model, achieving fast, well-calibrated, uncertainty-aware registration for lung cancer patients, enabling reliable DDF uncertainty propagation into dose accumulation for clinical decision-making in online adaptive radiotherapy.

title: Generative structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model for MR to CT image synthesis in radiotherapy planning.
abstract: Objective Radiotherapy (RT) planning uses magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for soft tissue information, while computerized tomography (CT) imaging is necessary for dose calculation. Synthetic CTs generated from MR images streamline the clinical workflow by reducing the need for an actual CT acquisition while minimizing radiation exposure, enabling adaptive RT workflows. Appraoch: We propose a radiotherapy planning model combining stable structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) with MRI conditioning, for generating synthetic CT (sCT). The model combines a hybrid network with a dynamic guidance mechanism, conditioned on MR, to direct the reverse diffusion process and preserve structural details. The model integrates both a denoising and a refinement network, while the guidance strength adapts at each timestep based on the noise level. The training process includes a weighted structure-guided loss function that combines the DDPM noise loss with a dynamic guidance regularizer term for sCT image generation, with a refinement network. Main results: Evaluated on three paired MR/CT datasets (head and neck, brain), our model outperforms recent MR to CT synthesis models, showing the best performance in image quality based on the Mean Absoluate Error (MAE) in Hounsfield units, as well as improved Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) and Gradient Magnitude Similarity Deviation (GMSD) compared to other DDPM and GAN approaches. When comparing tumor segmentation quality, it achieves the best results in Dice score (0.76 ± 0.04) for segmented tumor regions in the generated sCT images. Finally, it achieves the best Mean Square Error (MSE) of 10.1 ± 2.6 Gray in the head and neck cohort, when evaluating dose planning on sCT, with a Conformity Index (CI) of 0.61 ± 0.02 and a Homogeneity Index (HI) of 0.10 ± 0.02. Significance: Performance shows promise in integration for radiotherapy in head and neck, as well as in brain cancers.

title: golgi: an open-source graphical platform for image-to-recruitment modeling of peripheral nerve stimulation.
abstract: Objective Computational models of peripheral nerve stimulation-coupling finite-element bioelectric fields to biophysical axon models-are essential for designing electrodes and waveforms for neuromodulation, but established open tools are code-first, assume substantial modeling expertise, and often depend on commercial finite-element solvers. We present golgi, an open-source platform that takes a peripheral nerve from image to stimulated fiber population. Approach golgi integrates the full pipeline through a single graphical interface, with an equivalent scriptable Python API and command-line interface: image segmentation (or import of surfaces or masks), automated multi-region tetrahedral meshing, anisotropic finite-element solution of the extracellular field with explicit perineurium contact impedance, generation of realistic fiber populations and their three-dimensional trajectories (straight, or curved via a quasi-static streamline solver), and biophysical activation thresholds through interchangeable NEURON and a GPU-accelerated surrogate backend. Main results We demonstrate golgi on extruded multifascicular swine and human cervical vagus nerves and on real three-dimensional, branching human and rabbit vagus nerves reconstructed from micro-computed tomography. It reproduces the physiological fiber-diameter recruitment order, quantifies fascicular selectivity and current steering with a multi-contact cuff, and resolves anatomically defined branches. Selectively engaging a vagal cardiac branch from a proximal cuff depends on anatomy: in the rabbit, whose cardiac fibers are predominantly small and whose superior cardiac branch forms a discrete tract, current steering isolates even its small cardiac (B-type) fibers; in the human only large myelinated fibers are separable, because the high thresholds of small cardiac fibers force currents that also recruit off-target fibers. Significance Every study exports as an integrity-hashed, self-contained bundle whose finite-element-to-recruitment provenance is verifiable byte-for-byte-a reproducibility guarantee absent from existing tools. By combining non-specialist usability, anatomical realism, and verifiable reproducibility, golgi lowers the barrier to in-silico peripheral nerve stimulation modeling. golgi is freely available as open-source software.

Computational models of peripheral nerve stimulation-coupling finite-element bioelectric fields to biophysical axon models-are essential for designing electrodes and waveforms for neuromodulation, but established open tools are code-first, assume substantial modeling expertise, and often depend on commercial finite-element solvers. We present golgi, an open-source platform that takes a peripheral nerve from image to stimulated fiber population.

Approach

golgi integrates the full pipeline through a single graphical interface, with an equivalent scriptable Python API and command-line interface: image segmentation (or import of surfaces or masks), automated multi-region tetrahedral meshing, anisotropic finite-element solution of the extracellular field with explicit perineurium contact impedance, generation of realistic fiber populations and their three-dimensional trajectories (straight, or curved via a quasi-static streamline solver), and biophysical activation thresholds through interchangeable NEURON and a GPU-accelerated surrogate backend.

Main results

We demonstrate golgi on extruded multifascicular swine and human cervical vagus nerves and on real three-dimensional, branching human and rabbit vagus nerves reconstructed from micro-computed tomography. It reproduces the physiological fiber-diameter recruitment order, quantifies fascicular selectivity and current steering with a multi-contact cuff, and resolves anatomically defined branches. Selectively engaging a vagal cardiac branch from a proximal cuff depends on anatomy: in the rabbit, whose cardiac fibers are predominantly small and whose superior cardiac branch forms a discrete tract, current steering isolates even its small cardiac (B-type) fibers; in the human only large myelinated fibers are separable, because the high thresholds of small cardiac fibers force currents that also recruit off-target fibers.

Significance

Every study exports as an integrity-hashed, self-contained bundle whose finite-element-to-recruitment provenance is verifiable byte-for-byte-a reproducibility guarantee absent from existing tools. By combining non-specialist usability, anatomical realism, and verifiable reproducibility, golgi lowers the barrier to in-silico peripheral nerve stimulation modeling. golgi is freely available as open-source software.

title: Towards improving Alzheimer's intervention: a machine learning approach for biomarker detection through combining MEG and MRI pipelines.
abstract: Objective To identify robust biomarkers for early cognitive decline, classification performance was evaluated for healthy controls (HC) versus mild cognitive impairment (MCI) using MEG-derived spectral features at the sensor and source levels, and by testing whether adding MRI anatomical features improves discrimination in the BioFIND cohort. Approach Data from 324 participants (166 HC and 158 MCI) were analyzed using automated artifact rejection and source reconstruction. Spectral biomarkers, including sensor-space and sourcespace representations, were extracted from the magnetometer and gradiometer signals. Five inverse-solution methods were assessed (including linearly constrained minimum variance [LCMV] and exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography analysis [eLORETA]) to increase the robustness of source-based biomarker selection. Multiple classifiers, including a support vector machine (SVM) and L1-regularized logistic regression (GLMNET), were compared using nested K-fold cross-validation embedded in Monte Carlo replications to limit overfitting. Main results The best performance was obtained by combining MRI features with source-based MEG features using GLMNET, achieving 76.31 ± 1.47% accuracy and 82.44 ± 1.44% AUC. MEG-only models showed strong discrimination and outperformed MRI-only analyses, particularly those based on the LCMV and eLORETA features. Across settings, the SVM and GLMNET were the most consistently effective classifiers. Significance These findings support MEG/EEG spectral biomarkers, particularly source-based representations, as sensitive markers of early AD-related functional changes. Integrating MEG with MRI can further improve HC-versus-MCI classification. The study also demonstrated that rigorous validation (nested cross-validation with Monte Carlo replication) is essential for reliable biomarker assessment and for comparing preprocessing, inverse-solution, and classifier choices in translational neuroimaging pipelines.

title: Silver sodium nitroprusside nano-aggregates for ultrasound-activated immunomodulatory therapy of MRSA pneumonia.
abstract: The clinical management of methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) pneumonia is hindered by biofilm infections and cytokine storms. A key challenge is the lack of real-time monitoring tools for the inflammatory microenvironment during treatment. In this study, we developed a theranostic platform (CS@EAgNP) using TPP-modified chitosan to load silver sodium nitroprusside nano-aggregates (AgNP) and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG). This system combines ultrasound (US) imaging with US-activated therapy. The CS@EAgNP nano-aggregates can act as an excellent US contrast enhancer. In vivo US imaging indicated that AgNP generated significantly enhanced echo signals at the infection site, providing real-time and high-contrast visualization of the inflammatory foci that was unattainable with normal lung tissue. Moreover, these nano-aggregates release NO, silver and EGCG under US. The NO and silver penetrate biofilms to kill MRSA, while EGCG scavenges reactive oxygen species and modulates inflammation. This reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and TNF- α , mitigating the cytokine storm. In vivo results further confirm that this image-guided strategy achieves significant bacterial clearance and promotes lung tissue regeneration without detectable toxicity to major organs. This integrated approach bridges diagnosis and treatment, offering a promising solution for managing MRSA pneumonia.

title: Pre-clinical evaluation of a smartphone-assisted navigation system for surgical pin positioning in total knee arthroplasty.
abstract: Total knee arthroplasty success is highly dependent on accurate implant alignment, however, 80% of procedures globally are performed manually. Manual procedures have higher alignment errors compared to robotic platforms and patient-specific instrumentation, yet these have limitations of high cost and intraoperative inflexibility, respectively. This study aimed to evaluate the intraoperative pin positioning accuracy and flexibility of a smartphone-assisted navigation system using computerised-tomography (CT)-derived surgical plans. Three participants used the navigation system to perform 108 guide pin insertions (54 femoral, 54 tibial) on surrogate bone models based on CT-derived surgical plans. Testing included both default mechanical axis targets (0°) and user-selected navigated targets ranging from -3° to 3°. Accuracy was assessed by comparing achieved pin trajectories with the preoperative surgical plan. Median absolute angular deviations achieved ranged from 0.9° to 1.6° across all component-plane combinations, with an overall median deviation of 1.3° (IQR 0.6-2.1°). The proportion of insertions within a predefined ±3° clinical accuracy threshold ranged from 83.3% to 100%, and all component-plane combinations demonstrated deviations significantly within this threshold ( p < 0.00001). These findings support the technical feasibility of the smartphone-assisted navigation system for surgical pin positioning under controlled pre-clinical conditions. Further studies will evaluate the navigation system in cadaveric models with experienced orthopaedic surgeon participants.

title: A practical pipeline for patient-specific musculoskeletal modeling: a comprehensive MRI-based framework.
abstract: Patient-specific musculoskeletal (MS) modeling can provide estimates of internal joint loading that canot be measured directly. However, limitations in automated segmentation due to data-scarce environments, morphing difficulty caused by anatomical variability, and functional nonalignment are major bottlenecks that hinder the practical application of modeling and reduce productivity in MS research. To comprehensively address these practical issues, this study proposes and validates an integrated, automated modeling framework. First, we automatically segmented the lower extremity bones of the 4 knee osteoarthritis patients using a multi-atlas-based segmentation algorithm. By integrating the segmented bone with motion capture and force plate data, a modeling pipeline including multi-stage morphing and functional alignment processes was implemented. Using the constructed customized model, the medial and lateral knee contact forces ( F MC and F LC ) were estimated during a single-leg step-up exercise, and these were compared and evaluated against the results based on manual segmentation. The contact forces estimated through the automated segmentation framework demonstrated high consistency with the manual results. The mean absolute error ranged from 0.04 ± 0.03-0.06 ± 0.03 BW for F MC , and from 0.06 ± 0.04-0.09 ± 0.07 BW for F LC , and the intraclass correlation coefficient demonstrated a high correlation of over 0.99 across all patients. This study demonstrated that the proposed automated pipeline provides a practical approach to address misalignment caused by anatomical variability, while generating joint load estimates equivalent to the manual approach. By addressing key methodological challenges, this study will bring patient-specific models closer to future clinical application, where they could help assess individual loading across different activities and inform treatment and rehabilitation strategies.

title: A compact teacher-student knowledge-distillation framework for lumbar MRI segmentation.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of lumbar magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is important for quantitative assessment of degenerative spine disease, but it remains challenging because spinal structures show low contrast, variable morphology, and severe pixel-class imbalance. This study evaluates a compact teacher-student knowledge-distillation framework for multi-class lumbar MRI segmentation. The student network integrates a Res2Net encoder-decoder, a lightweight transformer bottleneck, and deep supervision; a manifold-constrained hyper-skip (MHC) module is evaluated as an optional constrained skip-fusion variant rather than assumed to be the sole source of improvement. A UNet++ teacher transfers soft probability, class-focused, and boundary-weighted information to guide boundary-sensitive anatomical regions. Under five-fold case-level GroupKFold validation on the primary public axial lumbar MRI dataset, the MHC full-KD variant achieved Dice 0.9141 ± 0.0021, foreground Dice 0.8934 ± 0.0026, IoU 0.8519 ± 0.0033, and HD95 3.1451 ± 0.2101. A no-MHC student trained with the same full distillation objective achieved essentially the same Dice (0.9141 ± 0.0021) with lower HD95 and lower measured latency, indicating that the full distillation objective, rather than the MHC block alone, explained most of the performance recovery toward the teacher. Replication on the 2026 Medical Lumbar Spine 3D Axial MRI Dataset achieved Dice 0.8960 ± 0.0032 and IoU 0.8224 ± 0.0047. A fixed label-harmonized train-on-primary/test-on-2026 transfer stress test achieved macro Dice 0.7002 ± 0.0181 and foreground Dice 0.6280 ± 0.0225. The results suggest that compact class-aware distillation can support reproducible lumbar MRI segmentation for future computer-aided measurement pipelines, while prospective and strict cross-institutional validation remain necessary.

title: 3D ViT network with selective feature enhancement and cross-dimensional interaction for colorectal T-stage classification in CT images.
abstract: Background. Obstructive colorectal cancer (OCC) often manifests on computed tomography (CT) as highly variable in morphology and location, with indistinct margins, atypical infiltration signs, and frequent adherence to surrounding structures. In addition, motion artifacts caused by intestinal peristalsis further degrade image quality and interfere with the identification of subtle structures. These factors readily lead to misassessment in T-stage evaluation, and accurately distinguishing between T4 and non-T4 stages is critical as it directly influences surgical planning and clinical decision-making. Purpose. To address challenges of imaging heterogeneity and motion artifacts in T-stage evaluation, we proposed a 3D vision transformer (ViT) based model with feature enhancement and cross-dimensional interaction for T4/non-T4 classification of OCC. Methods. First, we extended ViT into 3D and incorporate a selective feature enhancement module. This module computes attention weights based on feature means, adaptively enhancing discriminative information while suppressing redundant responses. It effectively mitigates difficulties in identifying subtle structures like serosal invasion caused by motion artifacts and low contrast in CT images, enabling the model to focus on diagnostically critical regions. Second, we introduced a cross-dimensional adaptive feature aggregation mechanism that established multi-scale 3D spatial dependencies, integrating global context with fine-grained local details. This significantly improves the model's ability to characterize tumors with complex and variable morphological features, thereby reducing staging inaccuracies due to underutilized spatial information. Furthermore, cross-domain knowledge transfer was employed to enrich the model's representational capacity and alleviate the inherent data scarcity in 3D medical image analysis. Results. Evaluated on a private dataset of 127 CT scans, the proposed model achieved an AUC of 0.8917 and an accuracy of 0.7917 in T4/non-T4 classification, significantly outperforming mainstream 3D medical image classification networks. Conclusions. Our approach offers clinicians a reliable decision support tool for accurate OCC staging, allowing surgeons to tailor operative strategies based on quantitatively reliable imaging assessments.

title: 3D SE-ResUNet for accurate dose prediction in head and neck IMRT: a structure-specific ensemble approach.
abstract: Accurate three-dimensional dose prediction is important for automated treatment planning and radiotherapy in head and neck cancer. This study investigates an ensemble-based deep learning framework for dose prediction from computed tomography images and anatomical structures, with particular emphasis on structure-specific model weighting. A dataset of 340 head and neck cancer patients from the Open Knowledge-Based Planning dataset was used for model development and evaluation. Three three-dimensional convolutional neural network architectures, including U-Net, SE-UNet, and SE-ResUNet, were trained for dose prediction. Their predictions were first combined using a global weighted ensemble. To account for differences in prediction performance across anatomical structures, a structure-specific ensemble was subsequently developed. For each structure, the relative contribution of the three models was optimized independently on the validation set using an exhaustive grid search with weight increments of 0.1. Performance was evaluated using the Dose Score and dose-volume histograms (DVHs) Score. Among the individual models, SE-ResUNet achieved the lowest DVH Score (2.067 Gy), while the global weighted ensemble achieved a Dose Score of 2.77 Gy and a DVH Score of 2.068 Gy. The proposed structure-specific ensemble substantially reduced the DVH Score to 1.75 Gy, although its overall Dose Score increased slightly to 2.81 Gy. The proposed structure-specific ensemble provides an anatomy-aware strategy for combining complementary dose predictions from heterogeneous deep learning models. While it does not improve the overall Dose Score relative to the global weighted ensemble, it substantially improves the DVH Score and provides a more structure-aware characterization of dose prediction performance. The approach may therefore be useful for deep learning-based dose prediction in head and neck intensity-modulated radiation therapy.

title: Integrating radiomic features and spatial semantic features from multiparametric MRI for IDH genotyping in glioma.
abstract: Gliomas, one of the most prevalent primary tumors of the central nervous system, have IDH molecular subtypes that are strongly linked to patient survival, prognosis, and treatment plans. However, there are currently few noninvasive preoperative prediction techniques, and postoperative pathology and genetic testing are the main approaches used to assess IDH status. Radiomics features can quantitatively characterize intratumoral heterogeneity, whereas spatial semantic features may provide additional information related to tumor location and macroscopic growth patterns. When it comes to characteristics like glioma invasiveness, growth patterns, and angiogenesis, spatial semantic features can enhance radiomics features. In order to predict IDH molecular subtypes in gliomas, this study suggests a combined analytical approach that incorporates clinical data, spatial semantic features, and multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomic features. This technique uses the IBSI standard to extract radiomic data from raw multiparametric MRI images and combines morphological analysis, gradient statistics, and 3D geometric modeling to create spatial semantic information. To eliminate redundant features and account for multicollinearity, Pearson correlation analysis and the variance inflation factor were utilized. The best feature subset was then obtained through a multi-stage feature selection procedure that combined random forests (RFs), LASSO regression, and recursive feature elimination. Lastly, imaging characteristics and clinical data were combined using a RF model to identify IDH molecular subtypes in gliomas. According to experimental findings, the suggested model's area under the ROC curve (AUC) in a five-fold cross-validation was 96.08%. The model had the AUC of 95.62%, ACC of 91.67%, sensitivity of 88.89%, and specificity of 93.94% in the final test set. The limitations of radiomics in conveying tumor macroscopic development patterns and spatial invasion relationships can be somewhat compensated for by spatial semantic aspects, according to additional investigation. title: External evaluation of a deep learning-based algorithm for automated lung tumor and esophagus segmentation on CBCT.
abstract: Online adaptive radiotherapy requires fast and accurate delineation of targets and organs at risk on cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). Although deep learning (DL)-based CBCT auto-segmentation methods have been proposed, their clinical generalizability remains insufficiently validated. This study aimed to externally evaluate a pretrained DL model for lung tumor and esophagus segmentation on CBCT. Originally trained using C-arm linac CBCT images, the model was directly applied to an independent cohort of 12 lung cancer patients, each with 5 CBCT images acquired at a separate institution on an O-ring linac. Rigid propagation of planning CT contours served as a minimal baseline to determine whether the model matched or outperformed conventional rigid registration for gross tumor volume (GTV) and esophagus segmentation using geometric and dosimetric measures. Compared with rigid contour propagation, the model significantly improved GTV segmentation accuracy, with mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) increasing from 0.66 to 0.76. Significant differences in GTV D98% were observed between the model-generated contours and the reference contours (50.69 vs 53.58 Gy). The model showed a statistically non-significant decrease in performance compared with previously reported results on its original testing dataset (mean DSC = 0.84), which shared the same distribution as the training dataset. For esophagus segmentation, evaluation of 26 scans from 6 patients showed that the model achieved geometric accuracy within peri-target contour rings comparable to rigid propagation, with mean DSC of 0.72 and 0.70, respectively. Similar esophagus V32Gy values were observed between the model-generated and reference contours (0.06 vs 0.06 cc). Significantly reduced accuracy was observed compared with previously reported results, with mean DSC decreasing from 0.79 to 0.72. These findings highlight that DL-based CBCT auto-segmentation may suffer performance degradation under domain shifts across patient populations, clinical workflows, and imaging systems, emphasizing the necessity of external evaluation beyond the original development environment.

title: Patient-specific dosimetric impact of online adaptive radiotherapy for locally advanced cervical cancer.
abstract: Background: When cervical cancer patients are treated with external beam radiation therapy, patient-specific anatomical changes, particularly bladder filling, alter the position and shape of the target volume throughout treatment. Online adaptive radiotherapy (oART) accounts for these interfractional changes by generating a treatment plan based on the patient's daily anatomy. Purpose: This study evaluated the dosimetric impact of oART and investigated the relationship between patient-specific anatomical changes and the dosimetric of benefit of adaptation using standard cone-beam CT (CBCT) images for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC). Methods: Ten patients previously treated for LACC at our institution were identified. A reference treatment plan incorporating a 5 mm clinical target volume (CTV)-to-planning target volume (PTV) margin was generated within the planning system simulator. Three CBCT images (Fractions 1, 13, and 25) were used to retrospectively simulate an adaptive treatment session. For each CBCT, the reference plan was recalculated on the daily anatomy to generate a scheduled plan, and an adapted plan was generated for comparison based on target coverage and organ at risk (OAR) dose metrics. The relationship between interfraction anatomical variation and the dosimetric benefit of adaptation was evaluated. Results: Adapted plans improved target coverage while generally maintaining or reducing OAR dose relative to the scheduled plans. However, the magnitude of benefit from adaptation varied between patients. Moderate associations were observed between interfraction anatomical variation of the bladder volume change and improvements in target coverage. Conclusion: The dosimetric benefit of oART was patient-specific and was partially associated with interfraction anatomical variation. These findings support an individualized approach to identify patient-specific characteristics that may help determine what patients would benefit the most from adaptive radiotherapy.

title: Dosimetric comparison of the anisotropic analytical algorithm and Acuros XB for single-fraction cranial stereotactic radiosurgery with a 6 MV flattening filter-free beam.
abstract: Stereotactic radiosurgery delivers an ablative single-fraction dose to small intracranial targets, and the reported dose depends on the calculation algorithm. This exploratory case series quantified the change in reported dosimetry when plans clinically finalised with the anisotropic analytical algorithm (AAA) were recalculated with Acuros XB (AXB) in dose-to-medium mode. Seven consecutive brain metastases in six patients, treated with 6 MV flattening filter-free volumetric modulated arc therapy, were recalculated on the same CT dataset using identical arc geometry, control points, multileaf collimator sequences and monitor units, without re-optimisation or renormalisation. Dose-volume histogram parameters were compared for the planning target volume (PTV), normal brain and organs at risk, and plan quality with the RTOG prescription-isodose-to-target-volume (PITV) ratio, the Paddick conformity index (PCI) and the gradient index (GI). Paired comparisons used exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and are interpreted as exploratory. AXB reported lower PTV dose metrics than AAA for the same deliverable plans, with mean D95% falling from 21.66 to 21.10 Gy, D98% from 21.19 to 20.58 Gy and Dmean from 24.58 to 24.13 Gy (all p = 0.016). The mean paired D98% difference was 3.00 ± 0.80% of the prescription dose. The PITV ratio fell from 1.19 to 1.10 and GI rose from 3.23 to 3.43 (both p = 0.016), whereas PCI did not differ (0.79 versus 0.82, p = 0.188). Normal-brain V12Gy and V10Gy were unchanged. Routine electronic portal imaging device dosimetry of the delivered plans gave a mean 2%/2 mm gamma passing rate of 98.5 ± 1.7%, documenting deliverability rather than validating either algorithm. These findings support careful review of target-dose metrics when an established AAA workflow is transitioned to AXB. The cohort is small and no independent reference dosimetry was available, so the study establishes neither clinical superiority nor an effect on tumour control or toxicity.

title: A multi-atlas ensemble learning framework for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis.
abstract: Objective. Clinical autism spectrum disorder (ASD) relies on subjective scales and neuroimaging, with traditional approaches suffering from high subjectivity and insufficient feature extraction, increasing misdiagnoses risk. Approach. To improve the diagnostic accuracy, we propose a multimodal ASD prediction network (APN) that integrates resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging with non-imaging data. Algorithmically, we first introduce a novel cumulative distribution divergence score (CDDS) feature selection method based on the multi-atlas functional connectivity (FC), which quantifies statistical distributional differences between positive and negative samples, effectively addressing the limitations of the traditional F -score in overlapping or weakly discriminative features. Building upon this, we adapt existing deep learning (DL) paradigms to construct a deep neural architecture (variational autoencoder-denoising autoencoder (VAEA)), combining a variational autoencoder (VAE), a denoising autoencoder, and a multilayer perceptron. The combination of these modules is non-trivial: the novel CDDS first purifies the high-dimensional feature space, enabling the VAEA to learn robust latent probabilistic representations via unsupervised pre-training without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. This is followed by the supervised fine-tuning to optimize parameters. We further incorporate demographic factors including age, full-scale intelligence quotient, and gender via a late-fusion strategy to prevent them from being overshadowed by imaging features, thereby enhancing the discriminability. FC features from three atlases including AAL, CC400, and Dosenbach160 are weighted and integrated to achieve the effective multi-source fusion. Main results. We conduct 10-fold cross-validations on the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) dataset, and the proposed APN achieves 81.63% accuracy, 81.89% sensitivity and 81.46% specificity, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Interpretability analysis identifies hippocampus, amygdala, and cingulate gyrus as strongly ASD-associated regions, offering neural mechanistic insights. Significance. This study provides an efficient, objective, and interpretable multimodal DL framework for ASD assisted diagnosis, with substantial clinical application and neuroscience value.

title: CT protocol optimization for oncologic surveillance imaging: phantom-based comparison of multi-scan and single-scan acquisition strategies.
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) plays an important role in oncologic surveillance after treatment of gynecological malignancies, including patients treated with vaginal electronic brachytherapy. This phantom study evaluated CT acquisition strategies for oncologic surveillance, focusing on radiation dose reduction and objective image quality in the cranial, thoracic, and upper abdominal regions assessed quantitatively. CT acquisition protocols were investigated using an anthropomorphic Kyoto Kagaku phantom. Two acquisition strategies were analyzed: a multi-scan approach with separate acquisitions for the head, neck, thorax, and abdomen-pelvis, and a single-scan head-torso acquisition with region-specific reconstructions. Different exposure parameter settings and reconstruction kernels were evaluated. Objective image quality was assessed using semi-automated region-of-interest measurements with a custom FIJI/ImageJ macro. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and Artifact Index (AI) were calculated for cranial, thoracic, and abdominal regions. For the single-scan protocols, CTDIvol decreased from 4.21 mGy in the standard protocol to 2.97-3.99 mGy in the optimized protocols, while DLP decreased from 410 mGy.cm to 287-388 mGy.cm. Across all anatomical regions, SNR and CNR remained comparable with the standard protocol. Thoracic CNR ranged from 2.68 to 3.01, abdominal CNR remained stable in both liver and aortic regions, and AI demonstrated only moderate variability across the optimized protocols. Optimized CT acquisition protocols reduced radiation dose while preserving the evaluated objective image quality metrics in the cranial, thoracic, and upper abdominal regions. Among the evaluated configurations, a reduced dose single scan head-torso acquisition using reduced tube voltage and tube current modulation showed a favorable balance between radiation dose reduction and objective image quality under the investigated phantom conditions and was identified as a candidate protocol for subsequent clinical and reader performance validation.

title: Wavelet-based adaptive image fusion of CT and MRI with local neighborhood variance for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
abstract: Multimodal imaging of nasopharyngeal carcinoma requires complementary representation of CT-derived bony anatomy and MRI-derived soft-tissue contrast. Existing fusion methods may fail to preserve both structural detail and soft-tissue information in a transparent and reproducible manner. We present a wavelet-based fusion framework that employs local neighborhood variance for adaptive weighting. This interpretable variance-driven strategy selectively integrates CT bony structures and MRI soft-tissue textures according to regional information content. The neighborhood configuration was selected through an ablation analysis of 232 clinical cases. Quantitative evaluation showed improved image-quality performance over the selected comparison methods across entropy, spatial frequency, average gradient, standard deviation, and edge information preservation factor, with respective gains of approximately 5.5%, 2.4%, 6.7%, 5.1%, and 3.2% relative to the best-performing baseline for each metric. These findings support the proposed method as an image fusion methodology for preserving complementary multimodal information; direct effects on target delineation, workflow efficiency, or dosimetric outcomes require future clinical validation.

title: Self-Supervised, Physics-Driven Sparse-Array XACT Reconstruction Using Sinusoidal Implicit Neural Representation.
abstract: X-ray induced acoustic computed tomography (XACT) enables high-contrast bone imaging but typically relies on dense and expensive transducer arrays. Sparse array sampling introduces severe streak artifacts and loss of fine structural details in conventional reconstruction. This work aims to establish a robust reconstruction framework that achieves high-fidelity structural imaging under sparse sampling, thereby overcoming hardware density limitations and facilitating low-cost, high-resolution skeletal health assessment. We propose a self-supervised, physics-driven framework based on sinusoidal implicit neural representation. The unknown initial pressure distribution is parameterized as a continuous coordinate-to-pressure function via a sinusoidal representation network, and is coupled end-to-end with a differentiable acoustic forward simulator implemented in j‑Wave. Network optimization is performed by minimizing waveform residuals between measured and predicted signals, eliminating the need for paired ground-truth data. To improve training stability and accelerate convergence, an adjoint-based warm start and total variation regularization are employed. In experiments on simulated hand and femoral bone sparse array datasets, the proposed method consistently outperforms conventional approaches under various sparse sampling conditions. Notably, for an osteoporotic femur imaged with only 64 transducer elements, the method effectively suppresses artifacts and faithfully preserves fine trabecular structures, achieving a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 32.43 dB and a root mean square error of 0.0239, surpassing the structural and quantitative accuracy of traditional reconstruction using a full 256‑element array. These results demonstrate that the framework supports stable XACT reconstruction under sparse array conditions and, with its favorable artifact suppression and microstructural preservation capabilities, offers a practical computational pathway toward low-cost, high-quality XACT imaging.
